Algorithmic Guarantees, `RMM1`/`RMM2` Memory, and the 5 Golden Rules of `template`\n\n- **Algorithmic & Safety Guarantee**: Default XSS prevention in `tmpl render html` (escaping `&`, `<`, `>`, `\"`, `'`), while triple-stache `{{{var}}}` explicitly opts into raw trusted markup.\n- **$O(1)$ Stack Complexity via TCO**: Every recursive loop in `src/main/ridgun/lib/template.ridgun` is in tail position, so `ridgunc` compiles them into native jumps with zero stack growth.\n- **Deterministic Memory (`RMM1`/`RMM2`)**: Zero garbage-collector pauses; all intermediate allocations are reclaimed deterministically on scope exit.\n- **Continuous Verification**: Statically checked via `stable check` and tested by the automated suite in `src/test/ridgun/test template.ridgun`.\n\n### The 5 Golden Rules When Programming with `template`\n\n1. **Declare `import template` at the top of your file** and call its functions with spaces, exactly as they are declared, so your code reads like natural prose.\n2. **Align your data pipelines with `=`**: chain `template` calls into named intermediate steps and let `stable format` align the columns.\n3. **Leverage `template`'s total functions inside `|` guards**: inspect return values or unwrap ADTs via pattern matching rather than assuming external input is valid.\n4. **Avoid cloning large structures when only reading**: remember that under `RMM2`, function input arguments incur zero reference-count overhead (`+0` / `-0`).\n5. **Pair `template` with `test` (`import test`)**: always lock in your domain invariants with `assert equals` or `assert true`.\n\n---\n\nIn **Chapter 15**, we will explore the **`fmt`** lib in full depth (The `fmt` Lib — Canonical 2D Tabular Formatter and 9-Target Syntax Highlighter).\n"}, {"num": "14", "slug": "15-lib-fmt-tabular-formatter-and-highlighter", "file": "15-lib-fmt-tabular-formatter-and-highlighter.md", "title": "Chapter 15: The `fmt` Lib — Canonical 2D Tabular Formatter and 9-Target Syntax Highlighter", "short_title": "The `fmt` Lib — Canonical 2D Tabular Formatter and 9-Target Syntax Highlighter", "markdown": "# Chapter 15: The `fmt` Lib — Canonical 2D Tabular Formatter and 9-Target Syntax Highlighter\n\n## 15.1. Why Does the `fmt` Lib Exist? (The Real-World Problem & Ridgun Philosophy)\n\n> *\"Why do I need a `fmt` lib written from scratch in pure Ridgun instead of just linking a legacy C library?\"*\n\nThat is the first question every systems engineer asks when meeting `fmt`. And the answer captures the entire philosophy of `ridgun-libs`:\n\nLet's be honest: the beauty of Ridgun lies in its crisp tabular columns (`::`, `=`, `|`, `->`, `--`), but aligning spaces by hand or exporting syntax-highlighted code to ANSI terminals, HTML, and LaTeX without a dedicated engine is tedious.\n\nThe **`fmt`** lib is Ridgun's official 2D tabular formatter and lexical syntax highlighter: it aligns `fn ::` headers, equations, `|` guards, and `--` comments, and renders into **9 output targets** (`FmtPlain`, `FmtTty`, `FmtTrueColor`, `FmtHtmlInline`, `FmtHtmlCss`, `FmtMarkdown`, `FmtPango`, `FmtLatex`, `FmtRtf`).\n\nIn a traditional ecosystem, solving **`FMT`** tasks means pulling in external C dependencies, wrestling with raw pointers, opaque type conversions, unchecked exceptions, or unpredictable garbage-collector pauses. In Ridgun, the **`fmt`** lib (`src/main/ridgun/lib/fmt.ridgun`) tackles the problem with four non-negotiable principles:\n\n1. **Declare `import fmt` (or `import fmt as alias`) at the top of your file**: every lib defines its `module :: fmt` namespace, and under `--strict` multi-word functions are always called with natural spaces.\n2. **Chain your data pipelines left-to-right with `->`**: write `input step one -> step two -> result`, use `(+ _ _ +)` sequence masks to destructure tuples/lists, and omit `_ =` on sequential statements (or discard with `-> ()`).\n3. **Tail-Call Optimization (TCO)**: all internal loops in `fmt` are tail-recursive and compile into native hardware loops using $O(1)$ stack space.\n4. **Deterministic Memory (`RMM1` / `RMM2`)**: every intermediate allocation is reclaimed at the exact instruction where its last read finishes, with no Garbage Collector.\n\n---\n\n## 15.2. Native Artifacts, Imports, and Complete `fmt` API Catalog\n\nIn `ridgun-libs`, **`fmt`** is a first-class **lib** located at `src/main/ridgun/lib/fmt.ridgun` (domain `FMT`). When built with `stable bundle`, it compiles into one native artifact:\n\n| Artifact | Path | Purpose |\n|---|---|---|\n| **Ridgun Bundle** | `target/bundles/fmt.ridgunlib` | Portable distribution and direct `import fmt` resolution |\n\n> Every lib declares its own namespace via `module :: fmt`: simply write `import fmt` (or `import fmt as alias`) at the top and call its functions with natural spaces (`my fn x`) and left-to-right `->` pipelines (`x my fn -> result`).\n\n### 15.2.1. Summary of `fmt` Functional Families\n\n| Signature / Function / Type | Purpose & Usage |\n|---|---|\n| `format ridgun source / fmt source with config` | Format Ridgun source with the canonical tabular column alignment, with the default configuration or a given `FmtConfig` |\n| `default fmt config / fmt config` | Build a `FmtConfig`: indent width, alignment limits, line width, target and theme |\n| `fmt to tty / fmt to truecolor / fmt to html / fmt to html css / fmt to markdown / fmt to pango / fmt to latex / fmt to rtf` | Format and highlight source for a terminal, HTML, Markdown, Pango, LaTeX or RTF |\n| `fmt highlight line / fmt highlight lines` | Highlight one line or a list of lines for a `FmtTarget` and a `FmtTheme` |\n\n### 15.2.2. Deep Dive into `fmt`: Step-by-Step Examples for Every Feature\n\nA signature table alone is never enough: let's explore **every capability** of the `fmt` lib through progressive, runnable Ridgun examples. We will start with two everyday tabular recipes and then walk through every functional scenario, transformation, and boundary condition verified in `src/test/ridgun/test fmt.ridgun`.\n\n### 15.3.1. Example 1: Core Tabular Workflow with `fmt`\n\nNotice how in Ridgun the `=` signs and transformation steps using `fmt` align into a clean, scannable table without unnecessary mutable variables or hidden side effects:\n\n```ridgun\nimport fmt\n\nfn :: formatear y verificar String => String Bool\n formatear y verificar codigo =\n format ridgun source codigo -> limpio\n (limpio, (format ridgun source limpio) == limpio)\n```\n\n### 15.3.2. Example 2: Safe Composition and Boundary Handling\n\nEvery function in the `fmt` lib is designed to compose cleanly with boolean guards `|` and with the rest of the 38 libs in `ridgun-libs`:\n\n```ridgun\nimport fmt\n\nfn :: exportar bloque html String => String\n exportar bloque html codigo =\n fmt to html css codigo\n```\n\n### 15.3.3. Example 3: Canonical Tabular Alignment (`format ridgun source`, `fmt source with config`) of `=>` Signatures, `=` Clauses, `->` Bindings, and `--` Comments\n\nIn this hands-on walkthrough we thoroughly exercise how `fmt` behaves across this functional area, covering standard inputs, parameter combinations, and corner cases:\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: test fmt canonical alignment and config => ()\n test fmt canonical alignment and config =\n nl = char from code 10\n raw_src = \"fn :: add Int Int => Int\" + nl + \"add x y = x + y\" + nl + \"add 0 y_long = y_long\" + nl\n expected_2d = \"fn :: add Int Int => Int\" + nl + \" add x y = x + y\" + nl + \" add 0 y_long = y_long\" + nl\n out_2d = format ridgun source raw_src\n out_2d -> assert str eq expected_2d \"AC1: canonical 2D tabular alignment\"\n\n -- Unaligned config (`is_aligned = False`) uses single-space separation\n cfg_unaligned = fmt config 2 4 80 False FmtPlain FmtThemeNone\n out_unaligned = fmt source with config raw_src cfg_unaligned\n expected_unaligned = \"fn :: add Int Int => Int\" + nl + \" add x y = x + y\" + nl + \" add 0 y_long = y_long\" + nl\n out_unaligned -> assert str eq expected_unaligned \"AC1: unaligned FmtConfig\"\n\n -- Guard and `where` alignment with custom indent_width = 4\n guard_src = \"fn :: clamp Int => Int\" + nl + \"clamp x\" + nl + \"| x < 0 = 0\" + nl + \"| otherwise = x\" + nl + \"where\" + nl + \"lo -> 0\" + nl\n cfg_ind4 = fmt config 4 4 80 True FmtPlain FmtThemeNone\n out_ind4 = fmt source with config guard_src cfg_ind4\n str contains out_ind4 \" | x < 0 = 0\" -> assert true \"AC1: custom indent_width = 4 guard indentation\"\n str contains out_ind4 \" lo -> 0\" -> assert true \"AC1: custom indent_width = 4 where binding alignment\"\n ()\n```\n\n### 15.3.4. Example 4: ANSI 16-Color and 24-Bit TrueColor Lexical Highlighting with Automatic TTY and `NO_COLOR` Detection\n\nIn this hands-on walkthrough we thoroughly exercise how `fmt` behaves across this functional area, covering standard inputs, parameter combinations, and corner cases:\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: test fmt terminal highlighting tty and truecolor => ()\n test fmt terminal highlighting tty and truecolor =\n nl = char from code 10\n esc = char from code 27\n interp_tok = (char from code 123) + \"name\" + (char from code 125)\n sample = \"-- @implements FR-FMT-001\" + nl + \"-- comment line\" + nl + \"fn :: greet String => String\" + nl + \"greet name = \\\"Hello \" + interp_tok + \"\\\" + (int to str 0x2A)\" + nl\n\n tty_dark = fmt to tty sample\n str contains tty_dark (esc + \"[1;32m-- @implements FR-FMT-001\" + esc + \"[0m\") -> assert true \"AC2: TTY pragma highlight\"\n str contains tty_dark (esc + \"[90m-- comment line\" + esc + \"[0m\") -> assert true \"AC2: TTY comment highlight\"\n str contains tty_dark (esc + \"[1;35mfn\" + esc + \"[0m\") -> assert true \"AC2: TTY keyword highlight\"\n str contains tty_dark (esc + \"[1;34mgreet\" + esc + \"[0m\") -> assert true \"AC2: TTY function name highlight\"\n str contains tty_dark (esc + \"[33mString\" + esc + \"[0m\") -> assert true \"AC2: TTY type highlight\"\n str contains tty_dark (esc + \"[36m\" + interp_tok + esc + \"[0m\") -> assert true \"AC2: TTY string interpolation highlight\"\n str contains tty_dark (esc + \"[36m0x2A\" + esc + \"[0m\") -> assert true \"AC2: TTY hex number highlight\"\n\n tty_none = fmt to tty with theme sample FmtThemeNone\n str contains tty_none esc -> assert false \"AC2: FmtThemeNone emits no ANSI escape codes\"\n\n tc_dark = fmt to truecolor sample\n str contains tc_dark (esc + \"[1;38;2;198;120;221mfn\" + esc + \"[0m\") -> assert true \"AC2: TrueColor dark keyword RGB\"\n str contains tc_dark (esc + \"[1;38;2;97;175;239mgreet\" + esc + \"[0m\") -> assert true \"AC2: TrueColor dark function RGB\"\n\n tc_light = fmt to truecolor with theme sample FmtThemeLight\n str contains tc_light (esc + \"[1;38;2;166;38;164mfn\" + esc + \"[0m\") -> assert true \"AC2: TrueColor light keyword RGB\"\n ()\n```\n\n### 15.3.5. Example 5: Exporting Highlighted Documents to HTML5 (`
    `), Pango Markup, LaTeX, RTF, and Vector SVG\n\nIn this hands-on walkthrough we thoroughly exercise how `fmt` behaves across this functional area, covering standard inputs, parameter combinations, and corner cases:\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: test fmt enriched document targets => ()\n      test fmt enriched document targets =\n        nl = char from code 10\n        src = \"fn :: cmp Int Int => Bool\" + nl + \"cmp a b = a < b AND b > 0\" + nl\n\n        -- 1. Inline HTML\n        html_out = fmt to html src\n        str starts with html_out \"
     assert true \"AC3: HTML inline wrapper\"\n        str contains html_out \"fn\" -> assert true \"AC3: HTML inline keyword span\"\n        str contains html_out \"<\" -> assert true \"AC3: HTML escapes < operator\"\n        str contains html_out \">\" -> assert true \"AC3: HTML escapes > operator\"\n\n        -- 2. CSS-class HTML + Stylesheet\n        css_html = fmt to html css src\n        str contains css_html \"fn\" -> assert true \"AC3: HTML CSS keyword class\"\n        str contains css_html \"cmp\" -> assert true \"AC3: HTML CSS function class\"\n        str contains css_html \"Int\" -> assert true \"AC3: HTML CSS type class\"\n        str contains css_html \"AND\" -> assert true \"AC3: HTML CSS logic operator class\"\n        sheet_dark = fmt html stylesheet FmtThemeDark\n        sheet_light = fmt html stylesheet FmtThemeLight\n        str contains sheet_dark \".ridgun-kw\" -> assert true \"AC3: Dark CSS stylesheet\"\n        str contains sheet_light \"#fafafa\" -> assert true \"AC3: Light CSS stylesheet\"\n\n        -- 3. Markdown\n        md_out = fmt to markdown src\n        str starts with md_out (\"```ridgun\" + nl) -> assert true \"AC3: Markdown fenced code block\"\n\n        -- 4. Pango Markup\n        pango_out = fmt to pango src\n        str starts with pango_out (\"\" + nl) -> assert true \"AC3: Pango  wrapper\"\n        str contains pango_out \"fn\" -> assert true \"AC3: Pango span markup\"\n\n        -- 5. LaTeX Verbatim\n        latex_out = fmt to latex src\n        str contains latex_out \"Verbatim\" -> assert true \"AC3: LaTeX Verbatim environment\"\n        str contains latex_out \"textcolor[HTML]\" -> assert true \"AC3: LaTeX textcolor macro\"\n\n        -- 6. RTF\n        rtf_out = fmt to rtf src\n        str contains rtf_out \"rtf1\" -> assert true \"AC3: RTF header\"\n        str contains rtf_out \"colortbl\" -> assert true \"AC3: RTF color table\"\n        str contains rtf_out \"\\\\cf1\\\\b fn\" -> assert true \"AC3: RTF bold color span\"\n        ()\n```\n\n        -- 4. Pango Markup\n        pango_out = fmt to pango src\n        _ = assert true (str starts with pango_out (\"\" + nl)) \"AC3: Pango  wrapper\"\n        _ = assert true (str contains pango_out \"fn\") \"AC3: Pango span markup\"\n\n        -- 5. LaTeX Verbatim\n        latex_out = fmt to latex src\n        _ = assert true (str contains latex_out \"Verbatim\") \"AC3: LaTeX Verbatim environment\"\n        _ = assert true (str contains latex_out \"textcolor[HTML]\") \"AC3: LaTeX textcolor macro\"\n\n        -- 6. RTF\n        rtf_out = fmt to rtf src\n        _ = assert true (str contains rtf_out \"rtf1\") \"AC3: RTF header\"\n        _ = assert true (str contains rtf_out \"colortbl\") \"AC3: RTF color table\"\n        _ = assert true (str contains rtf_out \"\\\\cf1\\\\b fn\") \"AC3: RTF bold color span\"\n        ()\n```\n\n### 15.3.6. Example 6: Signature-Aware Highlighting of `fn ::` and `op ::` Declarations and Contextual Keywords\n\nIn this hands-on walkthrough we thoroughly exercise how `fmt` behaves across this functional area, covering standard inputs, parameter combinations, and corner cases:\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: test fmt signature aware fn and op highlighting => ()\n      test fmt signature aware fn and op highlighting =\n        nl = char from code 10\n        fn_src = \"fn :: copy to with otherwise String Int => String\" + nl + \"copy to with otherwise src opt = copy src\" + nl\n        fn_css = fmt to html css fn_src\n        str contains fn_css \"copy to with otherwise String Int\" -> assert true \"AC2/AC3: fn :: highlights keyword-named fn words as rg-fn and types as rg-type\"\n        str contains fn_css \"      copy to with otherwise src    opt =  copy src\" -> assert true \"AC2/AC3: fn = clause highlights fn words as rg-fn, parameters as plain, and RHS invocation as non-rg-fn\"\n        str contains fn_css \"src\" -> assert false \"AC2/AC3: fn = clause parameter src is not highlighted as rg-fn\"\n        str contains fn_css \"otherwise\" -> assert false \"AC2/AC3: otherwise inside fn declaration/definition is not highlighted as rg-kw\"\n        str contains fn_css \"with\" -> assert false \"AC2/AC3: with inside fn declaration/definition is not highlighted as rg-kw\"\n        str contains fn_css \"to\" -> assert false \"AC2/AC3: to inside fn declaration/definition is not highlighted as rg-kw\"\n\n        op_src = \"op :: Int unwrap or Int with to Int => Int\" + nl + \"a unwrap or b with to c = a + b + c\" + nl\n        op_css = fmt to html css op_src\n        str contains op_css \"Int unwrap or Int with to Int\" -> assert true \"AC2/AC3: op :: highlights mixfix op words (or, with, to) as rg-fn and parameter types as rg-type\"\n        str contains op_css \"      a   unwrap or b   with to c   =\" -> assert true \"AC2/AC3: op = clause highlights mixfix op words as rg-fn and interleaved parameter slots (a, b, c) as plain\"\n        str contains op_css \"or\" -> assert false \"AC2/AC3: or inside op declaration/definition is not highlighted as rg-logic\"\n\n Algorithmic Guarantees, `RMM1`/`RMM2` Memory, and the 5 Golden Rules of `fmt`\n\n- **Algorithmic & Safety Guarantee**: Strict idempotence (`fmt source (fmt source s) == fmt source s`) and 100% preservation of semantic tokens.\n- **$O(1)$ Stack Complexity via TCO**: Every recursive loop in `src/main/ridgun/lib/fmt.ridgun` is in tail position, so `ridgunc` compiles them into native jumps with zero stack growth.\n- **Deterministic Memory (`RMM1`/`RMM2`)**: Zero garbage-collector pauses; all intermediate allocations are reclaimed deterministically on scope exit.\n- **Continuous Verification**: Statically checked via `stable check` and tested by the automated suite in `src/test/ridgun/test fmt.ridgun`.\n\n### The 5 Golden Rules When Programming with `fmt`\n\n1. **Declare `import fmt` at the top of your file** and call its functions with spaces, exactly as they are declared, so your code reads like natural prose.\n2. **Align your data pipelines with `=`**: chain `fmt` calls into named intermediate steps and let `stable format` align the columns.\n3. **Leverage `fmt`'s total functions inside `|` guards**: inspect return values or unwrap ADTs via pattern matching rather than assuming external input is valid.\n4. **Avoid cloning large structures when only reading**: remember that under `RMM2`, function input arguments incur zero reference-count overhead (`+0` / `-0`).\n5. **Pair `fmt` with `test` (`import test`)**: always lock in your domain invariants with `assert equals` or `assert true`.\n\n---\n\nIn **Chapter 16**, we will explore the **`cli`** lib in full depth (The `cli` Lib — Flags, Options, `--` Barrier, Subcommands, and Typed Env Readers).\n"}, {"num": "15", "slug": "16-lib-cli-flags-options-and-env", "file": "16-lib-cli-flags-options-and-env.md", "title": "Chapter 16: The `cli` Lib — Flags, Options, `--` Barrier, Subcommands, and Typed Env Readers", "short_title": "The `cli` Lib — Flags, Options, `--` Barrier, Subcommands, and Typed Env Readers", "markdown": "# Chapter 16: The `cli` Lib — Flags, Options, `--` Barrier, Subcommands, and Typed Env Readers\n\n## 16.1. Why Does the `cli` Lib Exist? (The Real-World Problem & Ridgun Philosophy)\n\n> *\"Why do I need a `cli` lib written from scratch in pure Ridgun instead of just linking a legacy C library?\"*\n\nThat is the first question every systems engineer asks when meeting `cli`. And the answer captures the entire philosophy of `ridgun-libs`:\n\nLet's be honest: hand-rolling `argv` parsing always starts as an innocent loop and breaks the moment a user passes bundled `-la` flags, `--port=9090`, or `--` followed by a filename starting with a dash.\n\nThe **`cli`** lib handles long flags (`--verbose`), short flags (`-v`), bundled short flags (`-la`), valued options (`--port=8080`, `--port 8080`, `-p 8080`), the POSIX `--` end-of-options barrier, positional arguments, subcommands, and typed environment variable readers.\n\nIn a traditional ecosystem, solving **`CLI`** tasks means pulling in external C dependencies, wrestling with raw pointers, opaque type conversions, unchecked exceptions, or unpredictable garbage-collector pauses. In Ridgun, the **`cli`** lib (`src/main/ridgun/lib/cli.ridgun`) tackles the problem with four non-negotiable principles:\n\n1. **Declare `import cli` (or `import cli as alias`) at the top of your file**: every lib defines its `module :: cli` namespace, and under `--strict` multi-word functions are always called with natural spaces.\n2. **Chain your data pipelines left-to-right with `->`**: write `input step one -> step two -> result`, use `(+ _ _ +)` sequence masks to destructure tuples/lists, and omit `_ =` on sequential statements (or discard with `-> ()`).\n3. **Tail-Call Optimization (TCO)**: all internal loops in `cli` are tail-recursive and compile into native hardware loops using $O(1)$ stack space.\n4. **Deterministic Memory (`RMM1` / `RMM2`)**: every intermediate allocation is reclaimed at the exact instruction where its last read finishes, with no Garbage Collector.\n\n---\n\n## 16.2. Native Artifacts, Imports, and Complete `cli` API Catalog\n\nIn `ridgun-libs`, **`cli`** is a first-class **lib** located at `src/main/ridgun/lib/cli.ridgun` (domain `CLI`). When built with `stable bundle`, it compiles into one native artifact:\n\n| Artifact | Path | Purpose |\n|---|---|---|\n| **Ridgun Bundle** | `target/bundles/cli.ridgunlib` | Portable distribution and direct `import cli` resolution |\n\n> Every lib declares its own namespace via `module :: cli`: simply write `import cli` (or `import cli as alias`) at the top and call its functions with natural spaces (`my fn x`) and left-to-right `->` pipelines (`x my fn -> result`).\n\n### 16.2.1. Summary of `cli` Functional Families\n\n| Signature / Function / Type | Purpose & Usage |\n|---|---|\n| `cli has flag : [String] -> String -> String -> Bool` | Detect `--long`, `-s`, or bundled `-xyz` before `--` |\n| `cli get opt / cli get int opt` | Extract string or integer option (`--k=v`, `--k v`, `-k v`) with default |\n| `cli positionals / cli subcommand` | Collect non-flag positional arguments (including everything after `--`) |\n| `env get or / env get int or / env get bool or` | Read environment variables with typed fallback defaults |\n\n### 16.2.2. 4) \"AC2: cli_get_int_opt negative int\"\n        cli get int opt args \"--host\" \"-h\" 8080 -> assert int equals 8080 \"AC2: non-numeric option falls back to default int\"\n\n        short_eq_args = [\"-p=3000\", \"--empty=\"]\n        cli get int opt short_eq_args \"--port\" \"-p\" 80 -> assert int equals 3000 \"AC2: short option -p=3000\"\n        cli get opt short_eq_args \"--empty\" \"-e\" \"def\" -> assert str eq \"\" \"AC2: explicit empty --empty= returns empty string\"\n        ()\n```\n\n### 16.3.4. Under the Hood: How `cli` Is Built in Pure Ridgun (`src/main/ridgun/lib/cli.ridgun`)\n\nOne of the biggest advantages of `ridgun-libs` is that **there are no C black boxes**. Internal Implementation: Internal String & List Helpers\n\nObserve how `cli.ridgun` declares explicit `fn :: ... => ...` contracts first and resolves each case through aligned equations and tail calls:\n\n```ridgun\nmodule :: cli\n\nfn :: cl str contains char String Int Int Int => Bool\n      cl str contains char s ch idx len =\n        | idx >= len                = False\n        | (str char at s idx) == ch = True\n        | otherwise                 = cl str contains char s ch (idx + 1) len\n\nfn :: cl is bundled short String String => Bool\n      cl is bundled short arg short_flag =\n        | (str len short_flag) != 2        = False\n        | (str char at short_flag 0) != 45 = False\n        | (str len arg) < 2                = False\n        | (str char at arg 0) != 45        = False\n        | (str char at arg 1) == 45        = False\n        | otherwise                        = cl str contains char arg (str char at short_flag 1) 1 (str len arg)\n\nfn :: cl list contains str [String] String => Bool\n      cl list contains str [] _ = False\n      cl list contains str (x:rest) tgt =\n        | x == tgt  = True\n        | otherwise = cl list contains str rest tgt\n\nfn :: cl is digits loop String Int Int => Bool\n      cl is digits loop s idx len =\n        | idx >= len                                           = True\n        | (str char at s idx) < 48 or (str char at s idx) > 57 = False\n        | otherwise                                            = cl is digits loop s (idx + 1) len\n\nfn :: cl is signed int len String Int => Bool\n      cl is signed int len s n =\n        | n == 0                  = False\n        | (str char at s 0) == 45 =\n          | n <= 1    = False\n          | otherwise = cl is digits loop s 1 n |.\n        | otherwise               = cl is digits loop s 0 n\n\nfn :: cl is signed int String => Bool\n      cl is signed int s      =  cl is signed int len s (str len s)\n\nfn :: cl is ws Int => Bool\n      cl is ws c   =  c == 32 or c == 9 or c == 10 or c == 13\n\nfn :: cl lower char String Int Int => String\n      cl lower char s idx c =\n        | c >= 65 and c <= 90 = char from code (c + 32)\n        | otherwise           = str slice s idx (idx + 1)\n\nfn :: cl trim lower loop String Int Int => String\n      cl trim lower loop s idx len =\n        | idx >= len                   = \"\"\n        | cl is ws (str char at s idx) = cl trim lower loop s (idx + 1) len\n        | otherwise                    = (cl lower char s idx (str char at s idx)) + (cl trim lower loop s (idx + 1) len)\n```\n\n### 16.4.2. Internal Implementation: Positional Arguments & Subcommand Extraction\n\nObserve how `cli.ridgun` declares explicit `fn :: ... => ...` contracts first and resolves each case through aligned equations and tail calls:\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: cl is flag tok String => Bool\n      cl is flag tok a      =\n        | (str len a) <= 1        = False\n        | (str char at a 0) == 45 = True\n        | otherwise               = False\n\nfn :: cli positionals with opts [String] [String] => [String]\n      cli positionals with opts [] _ = []\n      cli positionals with opts (a:[]) _ =\n        | a == \"--\"        = []\n        | cl is flag tok a = []\n        | otherwise        = [a]\n      cli positionals with opts (a:b:rst) val_opts =\n        | a == \"--\"                       = [b] :: rst\n        | cl list contains str val_opts a = cli positionals with opts rst val_opts\n        | cl is flag tok a                = cli positionals with opts ([b] :: rst) val_opts\n        | otherwise                       = [a] :: (cli positionals with opts ([b] :: rst) val_opts)\n\nfn :: cli positionals [String] => [String]\n      cli positionals args     =  cli positionals with opts args []\n\nfn :: cl first str [String] => String\n      cl first str []       =  \"\"\n      cl first str (x:_)    =  x\n\nfn :: cli subcommand [String] => String\n      cli subcommand args     =  args cli positionals -> cl first str\n```\n\n### 16.4.3. Internal Implementation: Typed Environment Variable Readers\n\nObserve how `cli.ridgun` declares explicit `fn :: ... => ...` contracts first and resolves each case through aligned equations and tail calls:\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: cl env val or String String => String\n      cl env val or val fallback =\n        | (str len val) == 0 = fallback\n        | otherwise          = val\n\nfn :: env get or String String   => String\n      env get or key    fallback =  cl env val or (sys getenv key) fallback\n\nfn :: env get int or String Int => Int\n      env get int or key fallback = cl parse int opt (sys getenv key) fallback\n\nfn :: cl parse bool val String Bool => Bool\n      cl parse bool val val fallback =\n        | val == \"1\" or val == \"true\" or val == \"yes\" or val == \"on\"  = True\n        | val == \"0\" or val == \"false\" or val == \"no\" or val == \"off\" = False\n        | otherwise                                                   = fallback\n\nfn :: env get bool or String Bool => Bool\n      env get bool or key fallback =\n        key sys getenv -> raw\n        cl trim lower loop raw 0 (str len raw) -> norm\n        cl parse bool val norm fallback\n```\n\n---\n\n## 16.5. Algorithmic Guarantees, `RMM1`/`RMM2` Memory, and the 5 Golden Rules of `cli`\n\n- **Algorithmic & Safety Guarantee**: Strict adherence to the POSIX `--` barrier: no token after `--` is ever misinterpreted as a flag or option.\n- **$O(1)$ Stack Complexity via TCO**: Every recursive loop in `src/main/ridgun/lib/cli.ridgun` is in tail position, so `ridgunc` compiles them into native jumps with zero stack growth.\n- **Deterministic Memory (`RMM1`/`RMM2`)**: Zero garbage-collector pauses; all intermediate allocations are reclaimed deterministically on scope exit.\n- **Continuous Verification**: Statically checked via `stable check` and tested by the automated suite in `src/test/ridgun/test cli.ridgun`.\n\n### The 5 Golden Rules When Programming with `cli`\n\n1. **Declare `import cli` at the top of your file** and call its functions with spaces, exactly as they are declared, so your code reads like natural prose.\n2. **Align your data pipelines with `=`**: chain `cli` calls into named intermediate steps and let `stable format` align the columns.\n3. **Leverage `cli`'s total functions inside `|` guards**: inspect return values or unwrap ADTs via pattern matching rather than assuming external input is valid.\n4. **Avoid cloning large structures when only reading**: remember that under `RMM2`, function input arguments incur zero reference-count overhead (`+0` / `-0`).\n5. **Pair `cli` with `test` (`import test`)**: always lock in your domain invariants with `assert equals` or `assert true`.\n\n---\n\nIn **Chapter 17**, we will explore the **`path`** lib in full depth (The `path` Lib — POSIX Normalization (`path clean`) and Path-Traversal Confinement).\n"}, {"num": "16", "slug": "17-lib-path-posix-paths-and-confinement", "file": "17-lib-path-posix-paths-and-confinement.md", "title": "Chapter 17: The `path` Lib — POSIX Normalization (`path clean`) and Path-Traversal Confinement", "short_title": "The `path` Lib — POSIX Normalization (`path clean`) and Path-Traversal Confinement", "markdown": "# Chapter 17: The `path` Lib — POSIX Normalization (`path clean`) and Path-Traversal Confinement\n\n## 17.1. Why Does the `path` Lib Exist? (The Real-World Problem & Ridgun Philosophy)\n\n> *\"Why do I need a `path` lib written from scratch in pure Ridgun instead of just linking a legacy C library?\"*\n\nThat is the first question every systems engineer asks when meeting `path`. And the answer captures the entire philosophy of `ridgun-libs`:\n\nLet's be honest: joining file paths with `base + \"/\" + user_path` without lexical `..` resolution and boundary confinement is an open invitation for a `../../etc/passwd` path-traversal exploit.\n\nThe **`path`** lib implements POSIX lexical normalization (`path clean`), safe joining (`path join`), component extraction (`dirname`, `basename`, `stem`, `ext`, `path replace ext`), and the **`path is safe subpath`** (`VUL-INJ-001`) directory-confinement guard.\n\nIn a traditional ecosystem, solving **`PATH`** tasks means pulling in external C dependencies, wrestling with raw pointers, opaque type conversions, unchecked exceptions, or unpredictable garbage-collector pauses. In Ridgun, the **`path`** lib (`src/main/ridgun/lib/path.ridgun`) tackles the problem with four non-negotiable principles:\n\n1. **Declare `import path` (or `import path as alias`) at the top of your file**: every lib defines its `module :: path` namespace, and under `--strict` multi-word functions are always called with natural spaces.\n2. **Chain your data pipelines left-to-right with `->`**: write `input step one -> step two -> result`, use `(+ _ _ +)` sequence masks to destructure tuples/lists, and omit `_ =` on sequential statements (or discard with `-> ()`).\n3. **Tail-Call Optimization (TCO)**: all internal loops in `path` are tail-recursive and compile into native hardware loops using $O(1)$ stack space.\n4. **Deterministic Memory (`RMM1` / `RMM2`)**: every intermediate allocation is reclaimed at the exact instruction where its last read finishes, with no Garbage Collector.\n\n---\n\n## 17.2. (The Real-World Problem & Ridgun Philosophy)\n\n> *\"Why do I need a `time` lib written from scratch in pure Ridgun instead of just linking a legacy C library?\"*\n\nThat is the first question every systems engineer asks when meeting `time`. And the answer captures the entire philosophy of `ridgun-libs`:\n\nLet's be honest: `libc` date functions (`localtime`, `gmtime`, `mktime`) rely on hidden mutable global state (`TZ`), aren't thread-safe, and trip developers up on century leap-year rules.\n\nThe **`time`** lib implements **Howard Hinnant's $O(1)$** proleptic Gregorian UTC civil calendar algorithm, strict **ISO-8601 / RFC 3339** formatting and parsing (`YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ`), human-readable durations (`1h 1m 1s 5ms`), and bounded exponential backoff.\n\nIn a traditional ecosystem, solving **`TIME`** tasks means pulling in external C dependencies, wrestling with raw pointers, opaque type conversions, unchecked exceptions, or unpredictable garbage-collector pauses. In Ridgun, the **`time`** lib (`src/main/ridgun/lib/time.ridgun`) tackles the problem with four non-negotiable principles:\n\n1. **Declare `import time` (or `import time as alias`) at the top of your file**: every lib defines its `module :: time` namespace, and under `--strict` multi-word functions are always called with natural spaces.\n2. **Chain your data pipelines left-to-right with `->`**: write `input step one -> step two -> result`, use `(+ _ _ +)` sequence masks to destructure tuples/lists, and omit `_ =` on sequential statements (or discard with `-> ()`).\n3. **Tail-Call Optimization (TCO)**: all internal loops in `time` are tail-recursive and compile into native hardware loops using $O(1)$ stack space.\n4. **Deterministic Memory (`RMM1` / `RMM2`)**: every intermediate allocation is reclaimed at the exact instruction where its last read finishes, with no Garbage Collector.\n\n---\n\n## 18.2. Internal Implementation: Leap Year, Month Length & Day of Week\n\nObserve how `time.ridgun` declares explicit `fn :: ... => ...` contracts first and resolves each case through aligned equations and tail calls:\n\n```ridgun\nmodule :: time\n\nfn :: time is leap year Int  => Bool\n      time is leap year year =\n        | (year % 400) == 0 = True\n        | (year % 100) == 0 = False\n        | (year % 4) == 0   = True\n        | otherwise         = False\n\nfn :: tm feb days Int  => Int\n      tm feb days year =\n        | time is leap year year = 29\n        | otherwise              = 28\n\nfn :: time days in month Int Int => Int\n      time days in month year month =\n        | month < 1 or month > 12                                      = 0\n        | month == 2                                                   = tm feb days year\n        | month == 4 or month == 6 or month == 9 or month == 11        = 30\n        | otherwise                                                    = 31\n```\n\n### 18.4.2. Internal Implementation: Howard Hinnant Civil Calendar <-> Epoch Days\n\nObserve how `time.ridgun` declares explicit `fn :: ... => ...` contracts first and resolves each case through aligned equations and tail calls:\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: tm adj year Int Int => Int\n      tm adj year y   m   =\n        | m <= 2    = y - 1\n        | otherwise = y\n\nfn :: tm calc era Int   => Int\n      tm calc era y_adj =\n        | y_adj >= 0 = y_adj / 400\n        | otherwise  = (y_adj - 399) / 400\n\nfn :: tm calc mp Int => Int\n      tm calc mp m   =\n        | m > 2     = m - 3\n        | otherwise = m + 9\n\nfn :: tm days from civil Int Int Int => Int\n      tm days from civil y m d =\n        tm adj year y m -> y_adj\n        y_adj tm calc era -> era\n        y_adj - (era * 400) -> yoe\n        m tm calc mp -> mp\n        (((153 * mp) + 2) / 5) + d - 1 -> doy\n        (yoe * 365) + (yoe / 4) - (yoe / 100) + doy -> doe\n        (era * 146097) + doe - 719468\n\nfn :: time day of week Int Int Int => Int\n      time day of week year month day =\n        tm days from civil year month day -> z\n        (((z + 4) % 7) + 7) % 7\n\nfn :: time utc to epoch Int Int Int Int Int Int => Int\n      time utc to epoch y m d hh mm ss =\n        | m < 1 or m > 12                          = 0 - 1\n        | d < 1 or d > (time days in month y m)    = 0 - 1\n        | hh < 0 or hh > 23                        = 0 - 1\n        | mm < 0 or mm > 59                        = 0 - 1\n        | ss < 0 or ss > 59                        = 0 - 1\n        | otherwise =\n          days = tm days from civil y m d\n          (days * 86400) + (hh * 3600) + (mm * 60) + ss\n\nfn :: tm z era Int     => Int\n      tm z era z_shift =\n        | z_shift >= 0 = z_shift / 146097\n        | otherwise    = (z_shift - 146096) / 146097\n\nfn :: tm mp to month Int => Int\n      tm mp to month mp  =\n        | mp < 10   = mp + 3\n        | otherwise = mp - 9\n\nfn :: tm finish year Int Int => Int\n      tm finish year y0  m   =\n        | m <= 2    = y0 + 1\n        | otherwise = y0\n\nfn :: tm civil from days Int Int Int Int => Int Int Int Int Int Int\n      tm civil from days z hh mm ss =\n        z_shift = z + 719468\n        era     = tm z era z_shift\n        doe     = z_shift - (era * 146097)\n        yoe     = (doe - (doe / 1460) + (doe / 36524) - (doe / 146096)) / 365\n        y0      = yoe + (era * 400)\n        doy     = doe - ((365 * yoe) + (yoe / 4) - (yoe / 100))\n        mp      = ((5 * doy) + 2) / 153\n        d       = doy - (((153 * mp) + 2) / 5) + 1\n        m       = tm mp to month mp\n        y       = tm finish year y0 m\n        (y, m, d, hh, mm, ss)\n\nfn :: time epoch to utc Int       => Int Int Int Int Int Int\n      time epoch to utc epoch_sec =\n        rem_raw = ((epoch_sec % 86400) + 86400) % 86400\n        days    = (epoch_sec - rem_raw) / 86400\n        hh      = rem_raw / 3600\n        mm      = (rem_raw % 3600) / 60\n        ss      = rem_raw % 60\n        tm civil from days days hh mm ss\n```\n\n### 18.4.3. Internal Implementation: ISO-8601 / RFC 3339 Formatting & Parsing\n\nObserve how `time.ridgun` declares explicit `fn :: ... => ...` contracts first and resolves each case through aligned equations and tail calls:\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: tm pad2 Int => String\n      tm pad2 n   =\n        | n < 10    = \"0\" + (int to str n)\n        | otherwise = int to str n\n\nfn :: tm pad4 Int => String\n      tm pad4 n   =\n        | n < 10   = \"000\" + (int to str n)\n        | n < 100  = \"00\" + (int to str n)\n        | n < 1000 = \"0\" + (int to str n)\n        | otherwise = int to str n\n\nfn :: tm fmt utc tuple (Int Int Int Int Int Int) => String\n      tm fmt utc tuple (y, m, d, hh, mm, ss)     =\n        (tm pad4 y) + \"-\" + (tm pad2 m) + \"-\" + (tm pad2 d) + \"T\" + (tm pad2 hh) + \":\" + (tm pad2 mm) + \":\" + (tm pad2 ss) + \"Z\"\n\nfn :: time format iso8601 Int       => String\n      time format iso8601 epoch_sec =  epoch_sec time epoch to utc -> tm fmt utc tuple\n\nfn :: tm all digits String Int Int => Bool\n      tm all digits s idx end_idx =\n        | idx >= end_idx                                       = True\n        | (str char at s idx) < 48 or (str char at s idx) > 57 = False\n        | otherwise                                            = tm all digits s (idx + 1) end_idx\n\nfn :: tm is sep at String Int Int Int => Bool\n      tm is sep at s idx c1 c2 =\n        ch = str char at s idx\n        (ch == c1) or (ch == c2)\n\nfn :: tm parse iso8601 len String Int => Int\n      tm parse iso8601 len s n =\n        | n < 19 or n > 20                         = 0 - 1\n        | not (tm all digits s 0 4)                = 0 - 1\n        | (str char at s 4) != 45                  = 0 - 1\n        | not (tm all digits s 5 7)                = 0 - 1\n        | (str char at s 7) != 45                  = 0 - 1\n        | not (tm all digits s 8 10)               = 0 - 1\n        | not (tm is sep at s 10 84 32)            = 0 - 1\n        | not (tm all digits s 11 13)              = 0 - 1\n        | (str char at s 13) != 58                 = 0 - 1\n        | not (tm all digits s 14 16)              = 0 - 1\n        | (str char at s 16) != 58                 = 0 - 1\n        | not (tm all digits s 17 19)              = 0 - 1\n        | n == 20 and (str char at s 19) != 90     = 0 - 1\n        | otherwise =\n          y  = str to int (str slice s 0 4)\n          m  = str to int (str slice s 5 7)\n          d  = str to int (str slice s 8 10)\n          hh = str to int (str slice s 11 13)\n          mm = str to int (str slice s 14 16)\n          ss = str to int (str slice s 17 19)\n          time utc to epoch y m d hh mm ss\n\nfn :: time parse iso8601 String => Int\n      time parse iso8601 s      =  tm parse iso8601 len s (str len s)\n```\n\n### 18.4.4. Internal Implementation: Human-Readable Duration & Exponential Backoff\n\nObserve how `time.ridgun` declares explicit `fn :: ... => ...` contracts first and resolves each case through aligned equations and tail calls:\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: tm join part String Int String => String\n      tm join part acc val unit =\n        | val <= 0           = acc\n        | (str len acc) == 0 = (int to str val) + unit\n        | otherwise          = acc + \" \" + (int to str val) + unit\n\nfn :: time format duration ms Int => String\n      time format duration ms ms  =\n        | ms <= 0 = \"0ms\"\n        | otherwise =\n          h  = ms / 3600000\n          m  = (ms % 3600000) / 60000\n          s  = (ms % 60000) / 1000\n          rm = ms % 1000\n          p1 = tm join part \"\" h \"h\"\n          p2 = tm join part p1 m \"m\"\n          p3 = tm join part p2 s \"s\"\n          tm join part p3 rm \"ms\"\n\nfn :: tm pow2 loop Int Int Int => Int\n      tm pow2 loop rem cur max_ms =\n        | rem <= 0 or cur >= max_ms =\n          | cur > max_ms = max_ms\n          | otherwise    = cur |.\n        | otherwise = tm pow2 loop (rem - 1) (cur * 2) max_ms\n\nfn :: time backoff ms Int Int Int => Int\n      time backoff ms attempt base_ms max_ms =\n        | base_ms <= 0              = 0\n        | max_ms <= base_ms         = base_ms\n        | attempt <= 0              = base_ms\n        | otherwise                 = tm pow2 loop attempt base_ms max_ms\n```\n\n---\n\n## 18.5. Algorithmic Guarantees, `RMM1`/`RMM2` Memory, and the 5 Golden Rules of `time`\n\n- **Algorithmic & Safety Guarantee**: $O(1)$ calendar conversion with zero year-by-year loops and strict per-month day validation (rejecting Feb 29 on non-leap years).\n- **$O(1)$ Stack Complexity via TCO**: Every recursive loop in `src/main/ridgun/lib/time.ridgun` is in tail position, so `ridgunc` compiles them into native jumps with zero stack growth.\n- **Deterministic Memory (`RMM1`/`RMM2`)**: Zero garbage-collector pauses; all intermediate allocations are reclaimed deterministically on scope exit.\n- **Continuous Verification**: Statically checked via `stable check` and tested by the automated suite in `src/test/ridgun/test time.ridgun`.\n\n### The 5 Golden Rules When Programming with `time`\n\n1. **Declare `import time` at the top of your file** and call its functions with spaces, exactly as they are declared, so your code reads like natural prose.\n2. **Align your data pipelines with `=`**: chain `time` calls into named intermediate steps and let `stable format` align the columns.\n3. **Leverage `time`'s total functions inside `|` guards**: inspect return values or unwrap ADTs via pattern matching rather than assuming external input is valid.\n4. **Avoid cloning large structures when only reading**: remember that under `RMM2`, function input arguments incur zero reference-count overhead (`+0` / `-0`).\n5. **Pair `time` with `test` (`import test`)**: always lock in your domain invariants with `assert equals` or `assert true`.\n\n---\n\nIn **Chapter 19**, we will explore the **`uuid`** lib in full depth (The `uuid` Lib — RFC 9562 `UUIDv4`/`UUIDv7`, Checksums (`CRC-32`), and PRNG).\n"}, {"num": "18", "slug": "19-lib-uuid-identifiers-checksums-and-prng", "file": "19-lib-uuid-identifiers-checksums-and-prng.md", "title": "Chapter 19: The `uuid` Lib — RFC 9562 `UUIDv4`/`UUIDv7`, Checksums (`CRC-32`), and PRNG", "short_title": "The `uuid` Lib — RFC 9562 `UUIDv4`/`UUIDv7`, Checksums (`CRC-32`), and PRNG", "markdown": "# Chapter 19: The `uuid` Lib — RFC 9562 `UUIDv4`/`UUIDv7`, Checksums (`CRC-32`), and PRNG\n\n## 19.1. Why Does the `uuid` Lib Exist? (The Real-World Problem & Ridgun Philosophy)\n\n> *\"Why do I need a `uuid` lib written from scratch in pure Ridgun instead of just linking a legacy C library?\"*\n\nThat is the first question every systems engineer asks when meeting `uuid`. And the answer captures the entire philosophy of `ridgun-libs`:\n\nLet's be honest: using random `UUIDv4` values as database primary keys fragments B-Tree indexes, while rolling ad-hoc IDs without kernel CSPRNG entropy leads to collisions.\n\nThe **`uuid`** lib implements **RFC 9562 `UUIDv4`** (kernel CSPRNG) and time-ordered **`UUIDv7`** (48-bit millisecond prefix for B-Tree locality), fast checksums (**FNV-1a**, **Adler-32**, **IEEE 802.3 CRC-32**), and a deterministic seeded PRNG.\n\nIn a traditional ecosystem, solving **`UUID`** tasks means pulling in external C dependencies, wrestling with raw pointers, opaque type conversions, unchecked exceptions, or unpredictable garbage-collector pauses. In Ridgun, the **`uuid`** lib (`src/main/ridgun/lib/uuid.ridgun`) tackles the problem with four non-negotiable principles:\n\n1. **Declare `import uuid` (or `import uuid as alias`) at the top of your file**: every lib defines its `module :: uuid` namespace, and under `--strict` multi-word functions are always called with natural spaces.\n2. **Chain your data pipelines left-to-right with `->`**: write `input step one -> step two -> result`, use `(+ _ _ +)` sequence masks to destructure tuples/lists, and omit `_ =` on sequential statements (or discard with `-> ()`).\n3. **Tail-Call Optimization (TCO)**: all internal loops in `uuid` are tail-recursive and compile into native hardware loops using $O(1)$ stack space.\n4. **Deterministic Memory (`RMM1` / `RMM2`)**: every intermediate allocation is reclaimed at the exact instruction where its last read finishes, with no Garbage Collector.\n\n---\n\n## 19.2. Native Artifacts, Imports, and Complete `uuid` API Catalog\n\nIn `ridgun-libs`, **`uuid`** is a first-class **lib** located at `src/main/ridgun/lib/uuid.ridgun` (domain `UUID`). Under the Hood: How `uuid` Is Built in Pure Ridgun (`src/main/ridgun/lib/uuid.ridgun`)\n\nOne of the biggest advantages of `ridgun-libs` is that **there are no C black boxes**. You can open `src/main/ridgun/lib/uuid.ridgun` and read exactly how every operation is implemented using pattern matching, `|` / `|.` guard trees, and tail-call optimization (TCO). Let's inspect the key building blocks of its real implementation:\n\n### 19.4.1. Internal Implementation: RFC 9562 UUIDv4 & UUIDv7 Generation & Validation (CSPRNG + wall clock)\n\nObserve how `uuid.ridgun` declares explicit `fn :: ... => ...` contracts first and resolves each case through aligned equations and tail calls:\n\n```ridgun\nmodule :: uuid\n\n-- Random bytes go through `getrandom` into a `Tensor[U8]`; the clock is the built-in `sys wall time ms` (ADR-0010).\n\nfn :: uu bytes to hex loop Tensor[U8] Int Int => String\n      uu bytes to hex loop t          idx len =\n        | idx >= len = \"\"\n        | otherwise =\n          b   = t_(idx)\n          hi  = b / 16\n          lo  = b % 16\n          tbl = uu hex lut 0\n          (str slice tbl hi (hi + 1)) + (str slice tbl lo (lo + 1)) + (uu bytes to hex loop t (idx + 1) len)\n\nfn :: uu random hex16 => String\n      uu random hex16 =\n        raw = Tensor[U8 * 16]\n        sys call (nr getrandom) raw 16 0 0 0 0\n        uu bytes to hex loop raw 0 16\n\nfn :: uu hex val Int => Int\n      uu hex val c   =\n        | c >= 48 and c <= 57  = c - 48\n        | c >= 65 and c <= 70  = (c - 65) + 10\n        | c >= 97 and c <= 102 = (c - 97) + 10\n        | otherwise            = 0 - 1\n\nfn :: uu variant char String => String\n      uu variant char hex1   =\n        v   = uu hex val (str char at hex1 0)\n        idx = 8 + (v % 4)\n        tbl = uu hex lut 0\n        str slice tbl idx (idx + 1)\n\nfn :: uuid v4 => String\n      uuid v4 =\n        h  = uu random hex16\n        p1 = str slice h 0 8\n        p2 = str slice h 8 12\n        p3 = \"4\" + (str slice h 13 16)\n        p4 = (uu variant char (str slice h 16 17)) + (str slice h 17 20)\n        p5 = str slice h 20 32\n        \"{p1}-{p2}-{p3}-{p4}-{p5}\"\n\nfn :: uu hex48 loop Int Int => String\n      uu hex48 loop val rem =\n        | rem <= 0 = \"\"\n        | otherwise =\n          nib = ((val % 16) + 16) % 16\n          tbl = uu hex lut 0\n          (uu hex48 loop (val / 16) (rem - 1)) + (str slice tbl nib (nib + 1))\n\nfn :: uuid v7 at Int   => String\n      uuid v7 at ts_ms =\n        eff_ts = uu abs ts_ms\n        ts_hex = uu hex48 loop eff_ts 12\n        h      = uu random hex16\n        p1     = str slice ts_hex 0 8\n        p2     = str slice ts_hex 8 12\n        p3     = \"7\" + (str slice h 0 3)\n        p4     = (uu variant char (str slice h 3 4)) + (str slice h 4 7)\n        p5     = str slice h 7 19\n        \"{p1}-{p2}-{p3}-{p4}-{p5}\"\n\nfn :: uuid v7 => String\n      uuid v7 =  uuid v7 at (sys wall time ms)\n\nfn :: uu is hex range String Int Int => Bool\n      uu is hex range s idx end_idx =\n        | idx >= end_idx                       = True\n        | (uu hex val (str char at s idx)) < 0 = False\n        | otherwise                            = uu is hex range s (idx + 1) end_idx\n\nfn :: uuid is valid String => Bool\n      uuid is valid u      =\n        | (str len u) != 36               = False\n        | (str char at u 8) != 45         = False\n        | (str char at u 13) != 45        = False\n        | (str char at u 18) != 45        = False\n        | (str char at u 23) != 45        = False\n        | not (uu is hex range u 0 8)     = False\n        | not (uu is hex range u 9 13)    = False\n        | not (uu is hex range u 14 18)   = False\n        | not (uu is hex range u 19 23)   = False\n        | not (uu is hex range u 24 36)   = False\n        | otherwise =\n          var_nib = uu hex val (str char at u 19)\n          (var_nib >= 8) and (var_nib <= 11)\n\nfn :: uuid version String => Int\n      uuid version u      =\n        | not (uuid is valid u) = 0 - Under the Hood: How `posix` Is Built in Pure Ridgun (`src/main/ridgun/lib/posix.ridgun`)\n\nOne of the biggest advantages of `ridgun-libs` is that **there are no C black boxes**. You can open `src/main/ridgun/lib/posix.ridgun` and read exactly how every operation is implemented using pattern matching, `|` / `|.` guard trees, and tail-call optimization (TCO). Let's inspect the key building blocks of its real implementation:\n\n### 22.4.1. Internal Implementation: Poll & Process Status ADTs\n\nObserve how `posix.ridgun` declares explicit `fn :: ... => ...` contracts first and resolves each case through aligned equations and tail calls:\n\n```ridgun\nmodule :: posix\n\ntype PollStatus = PollReady Int | PollTimeout | PollError Int\n\ntype ProcStatus = ProcExited Int | ProcTimedOut Int | ProcSignal Int\n```\n\n### 22.4.2. Internal Implementation: Path Safety Validation (VUL-INJ-002 / VUL-INPUT-001)\n\nObserve how `posix.ridgun` declares explicit `fn :: ... => ...` contracts first and resolves each case through aligned equations and tail calls:\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: is bad posix code Int => Bool\n      is bad posix code c   =\n        c == 0 or c == 10 or c == 13 or c == 59 or c == 96 or c == 124 or c == 38 or c == 36 or c == 39 or c == 34\n\nfn :: has unsafe posix char String Int Int => Bool\n      has unsafe posix char s idx slen =\n        | idx >= slen                           = False\n        | is bad posix code (str char at s idx) = True\n        | otherwise                             = has unsafe posix char s (idx + 1) slen\n\nfn :: is safe posix path len String Int => Bool\n      is safe posix path len path plen =\n        | plen == 0 or plen > 4096 = False\n        | otherwise                = not (has unsafe posix char path 0 plen)\n\nfn :: is safe posix path String => Bool\n      is safe posix path path   =\n        is safe posix path len path (str len path)\n```\n\n### 22.4.3. Internal Implementation: RG-010 Filesystem & Process Operations\n\nObserve how `posix.ridgun` declares explicit `fn :: ... => ...` contracts first and resolves each case through aligned equations and tail calls:\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: posix mkdir String => Bool\n      posix mkdir path   =\n        | not (is safe posix path path) = False\n        | otherwise                     = (sys mkdir path 493) == 0\n\nfn :: posix chmod String Int  => Bool\n      posix chmod path   mode =\n        | not (is safe posix path path) = False\n        | otherwise                     = (sys chmod path mode) == 0\n\nfn :: posix chdir String => Bool\n      posix chdir path   =\n        | not (is safe posix path path) = False\n        | otherwise                     = (sys chdir path) == 0\n\n-- `unlinkat(AT_FDCWD, path, flags)`; flags `512` (`AT_REMOVEDIR`) removes a directory.\nfn :: px unlinkat path String Int   => Int\n      px unlinkat path path   flags =\n        sys call (nr unlinkat) (at fdcwd) (px cstr path) flags 0 0 0\n\n-- kind `0`: `renameat2(AT_FDCWD, p1, AT_FDCWD, p2, 0)`; kind `1`: `symlinkat(p1, AT_FDCWD, p2)`.\nfn :: px path pair sys Int Tensor[U8] Tensor[U8] => Int\n      px path pair sys 0    a          b          =  sys call (nr renameat2) (at fdcwd) a (at fdcwd) b 0\n      px path pair sys _    a          b          =  sys call (nr symlinkat) a (at fdcwd) b 0 0 0\n\nfn :: px path pair call Int String String => Int\n      px path pair call kind p1 p2 =  px path pair sys kind (px cstr p1) (px cstr p2)\n\n-- `remove file`, `remove dir` and `rename path` are runtime operations on x86-64 (Linux and Windows).\n-- On ARM64 the runtime does not have them yet, so these use Linux system calls there.\nfn :: px use pal files => Bool\n      px use pal files =  (sys arch) == X86_64\n\n-- Creates `path` and every missing parent, each with `mode` (as `mkdir -p`). 0 when the last directory was made\n-- or was already there; otherwise the negative errno of the last step.\n-- The compiler's `sys mkdir` makes one level only since ridgunc 1.0.19 (it made the parents before).\nfn :: posix mkdir all String Int => Int\n      posix mkdir all path mode =\n        | (str len path) == 0 = 0 - 2\n        | otherwise           = px mkdir step path mode 1 (str len path) 0\n\n-- At each \"/\" after the first byte, and at the end, makes the path so far. `last` is the result of the latest step.\nfn :: px mkdir step String Int Int Int Int => Int\n      px mkdir step path mode i n last =\n        | i > n                                       = last\n        | i < n and (str char at path i) != 47        = px mkdir step path mode (i + 1) n last\n        | (str char at path (i - 1)) == 47            = px mkdir step path mode (i + 1) n last\n        | otherwise                                   = px mkdir step path mode (i + 1) n (px mkdir rc (sys mkdir (str slice path 0 i) mode))\n\n-- \"Already there\" (EEXIST, -17) counts as made.\nfn :: px mkdir rc Int => Int\n      px mkdir rc rc =\n        | rc == (0 - 17) = 0\n        | otherwise      = rc\n\nfn :: sys rmdir String => Bool\n      sys rmdir path   =\n        | not (is safe posix path path) = False\n        | px use pal files              = (remove dir path) == 0\n        | otherwise                     = (px unlinkat path path 512) == 0\n\nfn :: sys unlink String => Bool\n      sys unlink path   =\n        | not (is safe posix path path) = False\n        | px use pal files              = (remove file path) == 0\n        | otherwise                     = (px unlinkat path path 0) == 0\n\nfn :: sys rename String String   => Bool\n      sys rename old_p  new_path =\n        | not (is safe posix path old_p) or not (is safe posix path new_path) = False\n        | px use pal files = (rename path old_p new_path) == 0\n        | otherwise        = (px path pair call 0 old_p new_path) == 0\n\nfn :: sys symlink String String    => Bool\n      sys symlink target link_path =\n        | not (is safe posix path target) or not (is safe posix path link_path) = False\n        | otherwise = (px path pair call 1 target link_path) == 0\n\nfn :: sys readlink String => String\n      sys readlink path Algorithmic Guarantees, `RMM1`/`RMM2` Memory, and the 5 Golden Rules of `posix`\n\n- **Algorithmic & Safety Guarantee**: Non-matching `sys os` and `sys arch` branches are statically pruned at compile time (Dead-Code Elimination) by `ridgunc`.\n- **$O(1)$ Stack Complexity via TCO**: Every recursive loop in `src/main/ridgun/lib/posix.ridgun` is in tail position, so `ridgunc` compiles them into native jumps with zero stack growth.\n- **Deterministic Memory (`RMM1`/`RMM2`)**: Zero garbage-collector pauses; all intermediate allocations are reclaimed deterministically on scope exit.\n- **Continuous Verification**: Statically checked via `stable check` and tested by the automated suite in `src/test/ridgun/test posix.ridgun`.\n\n### The 5 Golden Rules When Programming with `posix`\n\n1. **Declare `import posix` at the top of your file** and call its functions with spaces, exactly as they are declared, so your code reads like natural prose.\n2. **Align your data pipelines with `=`**: chain `posix` calls into named intermediate steps and let `stable format` align the columns.\n3. **Leverage `posix`'s total functions inside `|` guards**: inspect return values or unwrap ADTs via pattern matching rather than assuming external input is valid.\n4. **Avoid cloning large structures when only reading**: remember that under `RMM2`, function input arguments incur zero reference-count overhead (`+0` / `-0`).\n5. **Pair `posix` with `test` (`import test`)**: always lock in your domain invariants with `assert equals` or `assert true`.\n\n---\n\nIn **Chapter 23**, we will explore the **`io`** lib in full depth (The `io` Lib — Typed `IoResult` Errors, `with timeout` Descriptor I/O, and Processes).\n"}, {"num": "22", "slug": "23-lib-io-timeout-bounded-io-and-processes", "file": "23-lib-io-timeout-bounded-io-and-processes.md", "title": "Chapter 23: The `io` Lib — Typed `IoResult` Errors, `with timeout` Descriptor I/O, and Processes", "short_title": "The `io` Lib — Typed `IoResult` Errors, `with timeout` Descriptor I/O, and Processes", "markdown": "# Chapter 23: The `io` Lib — Typed `IoResult` Errors, `with timeout` Descriptor I/O, and Processes\n\n## 23.1. Why Does the `io` Lib Exist? (The Real-World Problem & Ridgun Philosophy)\n\n> *\"Why do I need a `io` lib written from scratch in pure Ridgun instead of just linking a legacy C library?\"*\n\nThat is the first question every systems engineer asks when meeting `io`. And the answer captures the entire philosophy of `ridgun-libs`:\n\nLet's be honest: an unbounded `read()` call or child process execution with no deadline is an open invitation for one stalled peer to exhaust every worker in your server.\n\nThe **`io`** lib models every system operation through explicit ADTs (`IoError`, `IoResult[A]`), pairs non-blocking `ppoll` with Ridgun's lexical `with timeout wait_ms do` quotas, and exports the `read fd ... timeout` and `write fd ... timeout` mixfix operators.\n\nIn a traditional ecosystem, solving **`IO`** tasks means pulling in external C dependencies, wrestling with raw pointers, opaque type conversions, unchecked exceptions, or unpredictable garbage-collector pauses. In Ridgun, the **`io`** lib (`src/main/ridgun/lib/io.ridgun`) tackles the problem with four non-negotiable principles:\n\n1. **Declare `import io` (or `import io as alias`) at the top of your file**: every lib defines its `module :: io` namespace, and under `--strict` multi-word functions are always called with natural spaces.\n2. **Chain your data pipelines left-to-right with `->`**: write `input step one -> step two -> result`, use `(+ _ _ +)` sequence masks to destructure tuples/lists, and omit `_ =` on sequential statements (or discard with `-> ()`).\n3. **Tail-Call Optimization (TCO)**: all internal loops in `io` are tail-recursive and compile into native hardware loops using $O(1)$ stack space.\n4. **Deterministic Memory (`RMM1` / `RMM2`)**: every intermediate allocation is reclaimed at the exact instruction where its last read finishes, with no Garbage Collector.\n\n---\n\n## 23.2. Internal Implementation: Extensible I/O Error & Result Sum Types (§5.1)\n\nObserve how `io.ridgun` declares explicit `fn :: ... => ...` contracts first and resolves each case through aligned equations and tail calls:\n\n```ridgun\nmodule :: io\n\ntype IoError = Timeout Int | Eof | SysErr Int String | NotFound String\n\ntype IoResult = String | Int | Timeout Int | Eof | SysErr Int String | NotFound String | IoErr IoError | IoOk String | IoTimeout | IoEof | IoError Int\n\nfn :: format io error IoError            => String\n      format io error (Timeout ms)       =  \"timeout after {ms} ms\"\n      format io error Eof                =  \"unexpected end of file\"\n      format io error (SysErr c op_name) =  \"syscall error {c} in {op_name}\"\n      format io error (NotFound path)    =  \"file not found: {path}\"\n      format io error _                  =  \"unknown io error\"\n\nfn :: format io result IoResult           => String\n      format io result (String s)         =  \"ok:str:{s}\"\n      format io result (IoOk s)           =  \"ok:str:{s}\"\n      format io result (Int n)            =  \"ok:int:{n}\"\n      format io result (Timeout ms)       =  \"err:timeout after {ms} ms\"\n      format io result IoTimeout          =  \"err:timeout\"\n      format io result Eof                =  \"err:unexpected end of file\"\n      format io result IoEof              =  \"err:unexpected end of file\"\n      format io result (IoError c)        =  \"err:io error {c}\"\n      format io result (SysErr c op_name) =  \"err:syscall error {c} in {op_name}\"\n      format io result (NotFound path)    =  \"err:file not found: {path}\"\n      format io result (IoErr err)        =  \"err:\" + (format io error err)\n      format io result _                  =  \"err:unknown io error\"\n```\n\n### 23.4.2. Internal Implementation: Timeout-Bounded Command Execution (§5.2)\n\nObserve how `io.ridgun` declares explicit `fn :: ... => ...` contracts first and resolves each case through aligned equations and tail calls:\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: has null char String Int Int => Bool\n      has null char s idx slen =\n        | idx >= slen              = False\n        | (str char at s idx) == 0 = True\n        | otherwise                = has null char s (idx + 1) slen\n\nfn :: pad ms three Int => String\n      pad ms three rem =\n        | rem < 10  = \"00{rem}\"\n        | rem < 100 = \"0{rem}\"\n        | otherwise = \"{rem}\"\n\nfn :: format timeout sec Int => String\n      format timeout sec ms  =\n        secs = ms / 1000\n        rem  = ms % 1000\n        p    = pad ms three rem\n        \"{secs}.{p}s\"\n\nfn :: map exec rc Int Int        => IoResult\n      map exec rc rc  timeout_ms =\n        | rc == 124 or rc == 137 = Timeout timeout_ms\n        | rc < 0                 = SysErr (0 - rc) \"exec\"\n        | otherwise              = Int rc\n\nfn :: io exec timeout String Int        => IoResult\n      io exec timeout cmd    timeout_ms =\n        | (str len cmd) == 0 or (has null char cmd 0 (str len cmd)) = SysErr 22 \"exec\"\n        | timeout_ms <= 0                                           = Timeout timeout_ms\n        | otherwise                                                 =\n          tspec = format timeout sec timeout_ms\n          rc    = shell exec \"timeout -k 0.01s {tspec} sh -c \\\"{cmd}\\\" >/dev/null 2>&1\"\n          map exec rc rc timeout_ms\n\nfn :: exec with timeout String Int        => IoResult\n      exec with timeout cmd    timeout_ms =\n        io exec timeout cmd timeout_ms\n```\n\n### 23.4.3. Internal Implementation: Safe File Read & Line-Stream Helpers\n\nObserve how `io.ridgun` declares explicit `fn :: ... => ...` contracts first and resolves each case through aligned equations and tail calls:\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: io read file safe String => IoResult\n      io read file safe path   =\n        | not (is safe posix path path)        = SysErr 22 \"read_file\"\n        | not (lstat exists (file lstat path)) = NotFound path\n        | otherwise                            = String (read file path)\n\nfn :: split lines loop String Int Int Int => [String]\n      split lines loop s idx start slen =\n        | idx >= slen =\n          | start == slen = []\n          | otherwise     = [str slice s start slen] |.\n        | (str char at s idx) == 10 =\n          line = str slice s start idx\n          [line] :: (split lines loop s (idx + 1) (idx + 1) slen)\n        | otherwise =\n          split lines loop s (idx + 1) start slen\n\nfn :: split non empty lines String Int => [String]\n      split non empty lines raw rlen =\n        | rlen == 0 = []\n        | otherwise = split lines loop raw 0 0 rlen\n\nfn :: io read lines String => [String]\n      io read lines path   =\n        | not (is safe posix path path)        = []\n        | not (lstat exists (file lstat path)) = []\n        | otherwise                            =\n          raw = read file path\n          split non empty lines raw (str len raw)\n\nfn :: str list is empty [String] => Bool\n      str list is empty []       =  True\n      str list is empty (_:_)    =  False\n\nfn :: join lines nl [String]    => String\n      join lines nl []          =  \"\"\n      join lines nl (line:rest) =\n        | str list is empty rest = line + \"\\n\"\n        | otherwise              = line + \"\\n\" + (join lines nl rest)\n\nfn :: io write lines step String [String] => Int\n      io write lines step path   lines    =\n        lines join lines nl -> body\n        write file path body\n        0\n\nfn :: io write lines String [String] => Int\n      io write lines path   lines    =\n        | not (is safe posix path path) = 0 - 22\n        | otherwise                     = io write lines step path lines\n```\n\n### 23.4.4. Internal Implementation: Ridgun v0.9.5 PAL & Ambient Deadline `io read with timeout` (§3.1)\n\nObserve how `io.ridgun` declares explicit `fn :: ... => ...` contracts first and resolves each case through aligned equations and tail calls:\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: io wrap chunk String => IoResult\n      io wrap chunk \"\"     =  IoEof\n      io wrap chunk s      =  IoOk s\n\nfn :: io close and return Int IoResult => IoResult\n      io close and return fd  res      =\n        sys close fd -> ()\n        res\n\nfn :: io read chunk and close Int => IoResult\n      io read chunk and close fd  =\n        sys read fd fd 65536 -> chunk\n        sys close fd -> ()\n        chunk io wrap chunk\n\nfn :: io read after poll Int Int => IoResult\n      io read after poll fd ev =\n        | ev == 0   = io close and return fd IoTimeout\n        | ev < 0    = io close and return fd (IoError ev)\n        | otherwise = io read chunk and close fd\n\nfn :: io poll and read Int => IoResult\n      io poll and read fd  =\n        sys poll fd 1 (0 - 1) -> ev\n        io read after poll fd ev\n\nfn :: io read poll step Int => IoResult\n      io read poll step fd  =\n        | fd < 0    = IoError fd\n        | otherwise = io poll and read fd\n\nfn :: io read with timeout String Int => IoResult\n      io read with timeout path wait_ms =\n        with timeout wait_ms do\n          fd = sys open path 2048 0\n          io read poll step fd\n```\n\n---\n\n## 23.5. Algorithmic Guarantees, `RMM1`/`RMM2` Memory, and the 5 Golden Rules of `io`\n\n- **Algorithmic & Safety Guarantee**: No read, write, or child command executed through `io` with a `wait_ms` quota can ever block the calling thread or actor indefinitely.\n- **$O(1)$ Stack Complexity via TCO**: Every recursive loop in `src/main/ridgun/lib/io.ridgun` is in tail position, so `ridgunc` compiles them into native jumps with zero stack growth.\n- **Deterministic Memory (`RMM1`/`RMM2`)**: Zero garbage-collector pauses; all intermediate allocations are reclaimed deterministically on scope exit.\n- **Continuous Verification**: Statically checked via `stable check` and tested by the automated suite in `src/test/ridgun/test io.ridgun`.\n\n### The 5 Golden Rules When Programming with `io`\n\n1. **Declare `import io` at the top of your file** and call its functions with spaces, exactly as they are declared, so your code reads like natural prose.\n2. **Align your data pipelines with `=`**: chain `io` calls into named intermediate steps and let `stable format` align the columns.\n3. **Leverage `io`'s total functions inside `|` guards**: inspect return values or unwrap ADTs via pattern matching rather than assuming external input is valid.\n4. **Avoid cloning large structures when only reading**: remember that under `RMM2`, function input arguments incur zero reference-count overhead (`+0` / `-0`).\n5. **Pair `io` with `test` (`import test`)**: always lock in your domain invariants with `assert equals` or `assert true`.\n\n---\n\nIn **Chapter 24**, we will explore the **`crypto`** lib in full depth (The `crypto` Lib — Hashes, HMAC, HKDF, PBKDF2, AEAD Ciphers, X25519, Ed25519, ECDSA, RSA, and X.509).\n"}, {"num": "23", "slug": "24-lib-crypto-sha256-hmac-pbkdf2-and-aead", "file": "24-lib-crypto-sha256-hmac-pbkdf2-and-aead.md", "title": "Chapter 24: The `crypto` Lib — Hashes, HMAC, HKDF, PBKDF2, AEAD Ciphers, X25519, Ed25519, ECDSA, RSA, and X.509", "short_title": "The `crypto` Lib — Hashes, HMAC, HKDF, PBKDF2, AEAD Ciphers, X25519, Ed25519, ECDSA, RSA, and X.509", "markdown": "# Chapter 24: The `crypto` Lib — Hashes, HMAC, HKDF, PBKDF2, AEAD Ciphers, X25519, Ed25519, ECDSA, RSA, and X.509\n\n## 24.1. Why Does the `crypto` Lib Exist? (The Real-World Problem & Ridgun Philosophy)\n\n> *\"Why do I need a `crypto` lib written from scratch in pure Ridgun instead of just linking a legacy C library?\"*\n\nThat is the first question every systems engineer asks when meeting `crypto`. And the answer captures the entire philosophy of `ridgun-libs`:\n\nLet's be honest: comparing an HMAC tag with `==` opens the door to timing side-channel attacks, while linking `libssl.so` just to compute `SHA-256` or encrypt with `ChaCha20-Poly1305` ruins static binary portability.\n\nThe **`crypto`** lib implements in 100% pure Ridgun, on tensors: raw byte and bitwise primitives (`RGF-019`), the hashes **SHA-256**, **SHA-384**, **SHA-512**, **SHA-1** and **MD5**, **HMAC** and **HKDF**, constant-time equality (`ct equal`), **PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA-256**, the AEAD ciphers **ChaCha20-Poly1305** (RFC 8439) and **AES-128-GCM** (NIST SP 800-38D), **X25519** key agreement, **Ed25519** and Minisign signatures, **ECDH** and **ECDSA** on P-256 and P-384, **RSA** PKCS#1 v1.5 and PSS verification, and **X.509** certificate parsing. It also offers the `argon2id` lib (`import argon2id` plus `export argon2id`), so `argon2id hash` and `argon2id verify` are available with `import crypto` alone. The ciphers, Poly1305, GHASH and the big-number arithmetic run on the whole-tensor operations of the compiler: sealing 1 MiB with `aead seal` takes about 3 ms.\n\nIn a traditional ecosystem, solving **`CRYPTO`** tasks means pulling in external C dependencies, wrestling with raw pointers, opaque type conversions, unchecked exceptions, or unpredictable garbage-collector pauses. In Ridgun, the **`crypto`** lib (`src/main/ridgun/lib/crypto.ridgun`) tackles the problem with four non-negotiable principles:\n\n1. **Declare `import crypto` (or `import crypto as alias`) at the top of your file**: every lib defines its `module :: crypto` namespace, and under `--strict` multi-word functions are always called with natural spaces.\n2. **Chain your data pipelines left-to-right with `->`**: write `input step one -> step two -> result`, use `(+ _ _ +)` sequence masks to destructure tuples/lists, and omit `_ =` on sequential statements (or discard with `-> ()`).\n3. **Tail-Call Optimization (TCO)**: all internal loops in `crypto` are tail-recursive and compile into native hardware loops using $O(1)$ stack space.\n4. **Deterministic Memory (`RMM1` / `RMM2`)**: every intermediate allocation is reclaimed at the exact instruction where its last read finishes, with no Garbage Collector.\n\n---\n\n## 24.2. Native Artifacts, Imports, and Complete `crypto` API Catalog\n\nIn `ridgun-libs`, **`crypto`** is a first-class **lib** located at `src/main/ridgun/lib/crypto.ridgun` (domain `CRYPTO`). When built with `stable bundle`, it compiles into one native artifact:\n\n| Artifact | Path | Purpose |\n|---|---|---|\n| **Ridgun Bundle** | `target/bundles/crypto.ridgunlib` | Portable distribution and direct `import crypto` resolution |\n\n> Every lib declares its own namespace via `module :: crypto`: simply write `import crypto` (or `import crypto as alias`) at the top and call its functions with natural spaces (`my fn x`) and left-to-right `->` pipelines (`x my fn -> result`).\n\n### 24.2.1. Summary of `crypto` Functional Families\n\n| Signature / Function / Type | Purpose & Usage |\n|---|---|\n| `sha256 bytes / sha256 hex` | FIPS 180-4 32-byte binary digest or 64-char lowercase hex digest |\n| `hmac sha256 / ct equal` | RFC 2104 keyed MAC and constant-time accumulator comparison |\n| `pbkdf2 hmac sha256 : String -> String -> Int -> Int -> String` | RFC 8018 key derivation with precomputed inner/outer SHA-256 midstates |\n| `argon2id hash / argon2id verify` | 5-argument RFC 9106 PHC password hashing and constant-time verification |\n| `aead seal / aead open` | RFC 8439 ChaCha20-Poly1305 authenticated encryption and tag-verified decryption |\n| `sha512 bytes / sha512 hex` | 64-byte raw binary or 128-character lowercase hex FIPS 180-4 SHA-512 digest |\n| `ed25519 public key / ed25519 sign / ed25519 verify` | RFC 8032 §5.1 pure Ed25519 public-key derivation, constant-time deterministic signing, and canonical verification |\n| `minisign sign / minisign verify / minisign trusted comment` | Public keys and `.minisig` signatures compatible with the standard `minisign` tool |\n| `sha1 bytes / sha1 hex / md5 bytes / md5 hex` | SHA-1 and MD5 for protocols that still name them (WebSocket handshake, PostgreSQL `md5` authentication); not for new designs |\n| `sha384 bytes / hmac sha384 / hkdf extract / hkdf expand / hkdf expand label` | SHA-384, HMAC-SHA-384 and RFC 5869 HKDF, with the label form of TLS 1.3 |\n| `x25519 / x25519 public key` | RFC 7748 constant-time Diffie-Hellman key agreement |\n| `aes128 gcm seal / aes128 gcm open` | AES-128-GCM authenticated encryption and tag-verified decryption (NIST SP 800-38D) |\n| `p256 public key / p256 ecdh / ecdsa p256 verify / ecdsa p384 verify / rsa verify pkcs1 / rsa verify pss` | ECDH on P-256, ECDSA verification on P-256 and P-384, and RSA signature verification for keys of 2048 bits or more |\n| `x509 parse cert / x509 match hostname / x509 verify cert sig` | X.509 certificate parsing, RFC 6125 hostname matching and verification of the issuer's signature |\n\n### 24.2.2.
