Deep Dive into `crypto`: Step-by-Step Examples for Every Feature\n\nA signature table alone is never enough: let's explore **every capability** of the `crypto` lib through progressive, runnable Ridgun examples. We will start with two everyday tabular recipes and then walk through every functional scenario, transformation, and boundary condition verified in `src/test/ridgun/test crypto.ridgun`.\n\n### 24.3.1. Example 1: Core Tabular Workflow with `crypto`\n\nNotice how in Ridgun the `=` signs and transformation steps using `crypto` align into a clean, scannable table without unnecessary mutable variables or hidden side effects:\n\n```ridgun\nimport crypto\n\nfn :: cifrar mensaje sesion String String => Int String\n      cifrar mensaje sesion secreto texto =\n        secreto sha256 raw -> key32\n        \"0123456789ab\" -> nonce12\n        \"canal-autenticado\" -> aad\n        aead seal key32 nonce12 aad texto -> sellado\n        aead open key32 nonce12 aad sellado\n```\n\n### 24.3.2. Example 2: Safe Composition and Boundary Handling\n\nEvery function in the `crypto` lib is designed to compose cleanly with boolean guards `|` and with the rest of the 38 libs in `ridgun-libs`:\n\n```ridgun\nimport crypto\n\nfn :: verificar firma webhook String String String => Bool\n      verificar firma webhook clave cuerpo firma_hex =\n        hmac sha256 clave cuerpo -> esperada\n        ct equal esperada firma_hex\n```\n\n### 24.3.3. Example 3: Raw Byte `0..255` Manipulation (`byte str`, `bytes from list`, `bytes to list`) and 32-Bit Unsigned Bitwise Ops (`band`, `bor`, `bxor`, `shl`, `shr`)\n\nIn this hands-on walkthrough we thoroughly exercise how `crypto` behaves across this functional area, covering standard inputs, parameter combinations, and corner cases:\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: test rgf019 bytes and bitops => ()\n      test rgf019 bytes and bitops =\n        -- 1. Raw byte_str lengths, wraparound normalization, and full 0..255 round-trip\n        str len (byte str 0) -> assert int equals 1 \"len byte_str 0\"\n        str len (byte str 127) -> assert int equals 1 \"len byte_str 127\"\n        str len (byte str 128) -> assert int equals 1 \"len byte_str 128\"\n        str len (byte str 255) -> assert int equals 1 \"len byte_str 255\"\n        byte str (0 - 1) -> assert str eq (byte str 255) \"byte_str -1 wraps to 255\"\n        byte str 256 -> assert str eq (byte str 0) \"byte_str 256 wraps to 0\"\n        b5   = bytes from list [0, 1, 127, 128, 255]\n        str len b5 -> assert int equals 5 \"len b5 == 5\"\n        rt   = bytes to list b5\n        nth of rt 0 -> assert int equals 0 \"rt 0\"\n        nth of rt 1 -> assert int equals 1 \"rt 1\"\n        nth of rt 2 -> assert int equals 127 \"rt 2\"\n        nth of rt 3 -> assert int equals 128 \"rt 3\"\n        nth of rt 4 -> assert int equals 255 \"rt 4\"\n        b256 = bytes from list (range bytes 0 255)\n        str len b256 -> assert int equals 256 \"len b256 == 256\"\n        r256 = bytes to list b256\n        int count r256 -> assert int equals 256 \"r256 list len == 256\"\n        nth of r256 0 -> assert int equals 0 \"r256[0] == 0\"\n        nth of r256 128 -> assert int equals 128 \"r256[128] == 128\"\n        nth of r256 255 -> assert int equals 255 \"r256[255] == 255\"\n        same ints r256 (range bytes 0 255) -> assert true \"bytes to list (bytes from list 0..255) == 0..255\"\n\n        -- ADR-0010: bytes are built on Tensor[U8]; values outside 0..255 are taken modulo 256\n        hi7  = [0, 7, 128, 200, 255, 192, 245]\n        b7   = bytes from list hi7\n        str len b7 -> assert int equals 7 \"len bytes from list hi7 == 7\"\n        same ints (bytes to list b7) hi7 -> assert true \"bytes from list [0, 7, 128, 200, 255, 192, 245] round-trips\"\n        all byte str len one 0 -> assert true \"str len (byte str n) == 1 for all n in 0..255\"\n        bytes from list [256, 0 - 1, 300, 0 - 256] -> assert str eq (bytes from list [0, 255, 44, 0]) \"bytes from list wraps modulo 256\"\n        bytes from list [] -> assert str eq \"\" \"bytes from list [] is empty\"\n        bytes to hex str (bytes from list hi7) -> assert str eq \"000780c8ffc0f5\" \"bytes to hex str\"\n        bytes list to hex (hex str to bytes \"000780c8ffc0f5\") -> assert str eq \"000780c8ffc0f5\" \"hex str to bytes Tensor[U8] round-trip\"\n        bytes to hex str (bitxor byte strings (hex to byte str \"ff00f0\") (hex to byte str \"0f0fff\")) -> assert str eq \"f00f0f\" \"bitxor byte strings\"\n        bytes to hex str (byte slice b7 2 5) -> assert str eq \"80c8ff\" \"byte slice keeps high bytes\"\n\n        -- 2. RGF-019 32-bit unsigned bitwise operations and boundary shifts\n        band 4294967295 255 -> assert int equals 255 \"band\"\n        band 305419896 0 -> assert int equals 0 \"band with 0\"\n        bor 240 15 -> assert int equals 255 \"bor\"\n        bor 305419896 0 -> assert int equals 305419896 \"bor with 0\"\n        bxor 305419896 4294967295 -> assert int equals 3989547399 \"bxor\"\n        bxor 305419896 305419896 -> assert int equals 0 \"bxor self == 0\"\n        shl 1 0 -> assert int equals 1 \"shl 0\"\n        shl 1 (0 - 1) -> assert int equals 0 \"shl negative shift\"\n        shl 1 31 -> assert int equals 2147483648 \"shl 31\"\n        shl 1 32 -> assert int equals 0 \"shl 32\"\n        shr 2147483648 0 -> assert int equals 2147483648 \"shr 0\"\n        shr 2147483648 (0 - 1) -> assert int equals 0 \"shr negative shift\"\n        shr 2147483648 31 -> assert int equals 1 \"shr 31\"\n        shr 2147483648 32 -> assert int equals 0 \"shr 32\"\n        ()\n```\n\n### 24.3.4. Example 4: Official Vectors for SHA-256 (FIPS 180-4), HMAC-SHA-256 (RFC 4231), Constant-Time Equality (`ct equal`), and PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA-256 (RFC 6070)\n\nIn this hands-on walkthrough we thoroughly exercise how `crypto` behaves across this functional area, covering standard inputs, parameter combinations, and corner cases:\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: test sha256 hmac and pbkdf2 => ()\n      test sha256 hmac and pbkdf2 =\n        -- 1. SHA-256 (empty string \"\" and \"abc\" -> FIPS 180-4 vectors)\n        h_emp = sha256 hex \"\"\n        h_emp -> assert str eq \"e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855\" \"sha256_hex empty\"\n        h_hex = sha256 hex \"abc\"\n        h_hex -> assert str eq \"ba7816bf8f01cfea414140de5dae2223b00361a396177a9cb410ff61f20015ad\" \"sha256_hex abc\"\n        h_raw = sha256 bytes \"abc\"\n        str len h_raw -> assert eq 32\n        bytes to hex str h_raw -> assert str eq h_hex \"sha256_bytes matches sha256_hex\"\n\n        -- 2. HMAC-SHA-256 (RFC 4231 Test Case 2 and >64-byte key reduction)\n        mac   = hmac sha256 \"Jefe\" \"what do ya want for nothing?\"\n        str len mac -> assert eq 32\n        bytes to hex str mac -> assert str eq \"5bdcc146bf60754e6a042426089575c75a003f089d2739839dec58b964ec3843\" \"RFC 4231 Test Case 2\"\n        long_k = \"0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef_extra_key_bytes\"\n        mac_lk = hmac sha256 long_k \"message\"\n        str len mac_lk -> assert eq 32\n        ct equal mac_lk (hmac sha256 (sha256 bytes long_k) \"message\") -> assert true \"HMAC >64B key hashed to 32B\"\n\n        -- 3. Constant-time comparison (`ct_equal`)\n        ct equal \"\" \"\" -> assert true \"ct_equal empty strings\"\n        ct equal mac mac -> assert true \"ct_equal identical\"\n        ct equal mac (sha256 bytes \"abc\") -> assert false \"ct_equal different 32B\"\n        ct equal \"short\" \"longer\" -> assert false \"ct_equal different lengths\"\n\n        -- 4. PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA-256 (RFC 6070 c=1, c=2, multi-block dk_len=64, sub-block dk_len=16, invalid args)\n        dk1   = pbkdf2 hmac sha256 \"password\" \"salt\" 1 32\n        str len dk1 -> assert eq 32\n        bytes to hex str dk1 -> assert str eq \"120fb6cffcf8b32c43e7225256c4f837a86548c92ccc35480805987cb70be17b\" \"RFC 6070 PBKDF2 c=1\"\n        dk2   = pbkdf2 hmac sha256 \"password\" \"salt\" 2 32\n        bytes to hex str dk2 -> assert str eq \"ae4d0c95af6b46d32d0adff928f06dd02a303f8ef3c251dfd6e2d85a95474c43\" \"RFC 6070 PBKDF2 c=2\"\n        dk16  = pbkdf2 hmac sha256 \"password\" \"salt\" 1 16\n        str len dk16 -> assert eq 16\n        bytes to hex str dk16 -> assert str eq \"120fb6cffcf8b32c43e7225256c4f837\" \"PBKDF2 16-byte prefix\"\n        dk64  = pbkdf2 hmac sha256 \"password\" \"salt\" 1 64\n        str len dk64 -> assert eq 64\n        byte slice dk64 0 32 -> assert str eq dk1 \"PBKDF2 64-byte block 1 matches dk1\"\n        pbkdf2 hmac sha256 \"password\" \"salt\" 0 32 -> assert str eq \"\" \"PBKDF2 iterations=0 rejected\"\n        pbkdf2 hmac sha256 \"password\" \"salt\" 1 0 -> assert str eq \"\" \"PBKDF2 dk_len=0 rejected\"\n        ()\n```\n\n### 24.3.5. Example 5: 5-Argument Argon2id Password Hashing (`argon2id hash`, `argon2id verify`) and Memory-Hard Verification (RFC 9106)\n\nIn this hands-on walkthrough we thoroughly exercise how `crypto` behaves across this functional area, covering standard inputs, parameter combinations, and corner cases:\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: test argon2id five arg and perf => ()\n      test argon2id five arg and perf =\n        phc = argon2id hash \"correct horse battery staple\" \"0123456789abcdef\" 64 2 1\n        str starts with phc \"$argon2id$v=19$m=64,t=2,p=1$\" -> assert true \"PHC header format\"\n        argon2id verify \"correct horse battery staple\" phc -> assert true \"argon2id_verify matching (pwd, phc)\"\n        argon2id verify \"wrong password\" phc -> assert false \"argon2id_verify wrong password\"\n        argon2id verify \"correct horse battery staple\" \"$argon2id$v=19$m=64,t=2,p=1$bad$bad\" -> assert false \"argon2id_verify bad PHC\"\n\n        -- Negative parameter guards for 5-arg argon2id_hash\n        argon2id hash \"password\" \"short\" 64 2 1 -> assert str eq \"\" \"salt < 8 bytes rejected\"\n        argon2id hash \"password\" \"0123456789abcdef\" 4 2 1 -> assert str eq \"\" \"m_cost < 8*p rejected\"\n        argon2id hash \"password\" \"0123456789abcdef\" 64 0 1 -> assert str eq \"\" \"t_cost < 1 rejected\"\n        argon2id hash \"password\" \"0123456789abcdef\" 64 2 0 -> assert str eq \"\" \"p_cost < 1 rejected\"\n\n        -- RG-050 / RG-051: Verify 100% in-process pure-Ridgun Argon2id and PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256\n        -- (OpenSSL 3.5 / RFC 9106 vectors + 4096-iteration PBKDF2 vector)\n        phc_s       = argon2id hash \"correct horse\" \"saltsaltsaltsalt\" 64 2 1\n        argon_exact = phc_s == \"$argon2id$v=19$m=64,t=2,p=1$c2FsdHNhbHRzYWx0c2FsdA$5jdMIzWoFbzSOl6k3wai9uU3f8LD+HmGXQgo1uhHQPI\"\n        ok_s        = argon2id verify \"correct horse\" phc_s\n        bad_s       = argon2id verify \"wrong horse\" phc_s\n        bad_empty   = argon2id verify \"correct horse\" \"$argon2id$v=19$m=64,t=2,p=1$c2FsdHNhbHRzYWx0c2FsdA$\"\n        phc_ok      = str starts with phc_s \"$argon2id$v=19$m=64,t=2,p=1$\"\n        pb4k        = bytes to hex str (pbkdf2 hmac sha256 \"correct horse battery staple\" \"0123456789abcdef\" 4096 32)\n        ok_s -> assert true \"Solstice RGF-015 argon_ok\"\n        bad_s -> assert false \"Solstice RGF-015 argon_bad\"\n        bad_empty -> assert false \"RG-051 reject PHC with empty tag\"\n        phc_ok -> assert true \"Solstice RGF-015 phc prefix\"\n        argon_exact -> assert true \"Solstice RGF-015 exact OpenSSL 3.5 / libsodium PHC\"\n        pb4k -> assert str eq \"b87f4b27148d3b05ad7985e3df997f0d9afa6e768e6384555bab71ba10f0c1a5\" \"Solstice RGF-015 PBKDF2 4096\"\n\n        -- RG-043: PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 600,000 iterations must match Python hashlib and run in < 3500 ms on one core (down from 32,600 ms)\n        t_pbk0      = sys monotonic ms\n        pb600k      = bytes to hex str (pbkdf2 hmac sha256 \"correct horse battery staple\" \"0123456789abcdef\" 600000 32)\n        dt_pbk      = (sys monotonic ms) - t_pbk0\n        echo (\"  [BENCH] PBKDF2 600,000 iterations: \" + (int to str dt_pbk) + \" ms\")\n        pb600k -> assert str eq \"6c4a646aad10d067add5fb79d9078a16da83d50f81670a8e7593b249e6d94936\" \"RG-043: PBKDF2 600,000 iterations matches Python hashlib\"\n        dt_pbk < 3500 -> assert true (\"RG-043: PBKDF2 600,000 iterations must complete in < 3500 ms (took \" + (int to str dt_pbk) + \" ms)\")\n\n        -- RG-060: Argon2id OWASP m=19456 KiB, t=2, p=1 must match OpenSSL 3.5.7 and run in < 14500 ms on one core\n echo (\"  [BENCH] Argon2id m=19456, t=2, p=1: \" + (int to str dt_a2) + \" ms\")\n        phc_19m -> assert str eq \"$argon2id$v=19$m=19456,t=2,p=1$MDEyMzQ1Njc4OWFiY2RlZg$gy5SuVm5Z7Vw7keB9se9p87QGcomaseB/S2U1OhTsM0\" \"RG-060: Argon2id m=19456,t=2,p=1 matches OpenSSL 3.5.7\"\n        dt_a2 < 14500 -> assert true (\"RG-060: Argon2id m=19456, t=2, p=1 must complete in < 14500 ms (took \" + (int to str dt_a2) + \" ms)\")\n        ()\n```\n\n### 24.3.6. Example 6: ChaCha20 Stream Cipher, Poly1305 Authenticator, and RFC 8439 ChaCha20-Poly1305 AEAD Seal & Open\n\nIn this hands-on walkthrough we thoroughly exercise how `crypto` behaves across this functional area, covering standard inputs, parameter combinations, and corner cases:\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: test rfc8439 chacha20 poly1305 aead => ()\n      test rfc8439 chacha20 poly1305 aead =\n        key   = bytes from list (range bytes 128 159)\n        nonce = bytes from list [7, 0, 0, 0, 64, 65, 66, 67, 68, 69, 70, 71]\n        aad   = bytes from list [80, 81, 82, 83, 192, 193, 194, 195, 196, 197, 198, 199]\n        pt    = \"Ladies and Gentlemen of the class of '99: If I could offer you only one tip for the future, sunscreen would be it.\"\n\n        sealed = aead seal key nonce aad pt\n str (byte slice sealed 0 16)\n        tag_hex       = bytes to hex str (byte slice sealed 114 130)\n        ct_prefix_hex -> assert str eq \"d31a8d34648e60db7b86afbc53ef7ec2\" \"RFC 8439 §2.8.2 ciphertext prefix\"\n        tag_hex -> assert str eq \"1ae10b594f09e26a7e902ecbd0600691\" \"RFC 8439 §2.8.2 Poly1305 tag\"\n\n        -- Verify aead_open succeeds with (0, pt)\n        res_ok   = aead open key nonce aad sealed\n        aead rc res_ok -> assert eq 0\n        aead pt res_ok -> assert str eq pt \"aead_open decrypted plaintext\"\n\n        -- Verify empty plaintext and empty AAD ciphertext, or modified tag\n        res_aad  = aead open key nonce \"tampered-aad\" sealed\n        aead rc res_aad -> assert eq (0 - 12)\n        aead pt res_aad -> assert str eq \"\" \"tampered AAD returns empty plaintext\"\n\n        bad_nonce = bytes from list [8, 0, 0, 0, 64, 65, 66, 67, 68, 69, 70, 71]\n        res_nonce = aead open key bad_nonce aad sealed\n        aead rc res_nonce -> assert eq (0 - 12)\n        aead pt res_nonce -> assert str eq \"\" \"tampered nonce returns empty plaintext\"\n\n        bad_ct   = (byte str 0) + (byte slice sealed 1 130)\n        res_ct   = aead open key nonce aad bad_ct\n        aead rc res_ct -> assert eq (0 - 12)\n        aead pt res_ct -> assert str eq \"\" \"tampered ciphertext byte returns empty plaintext\"\n\n        bad_seal = (byte slice sealed 0 129) + (byte str 0)\n        res_tag  = aead open key nonce aad bad_seal\n        aead rc res_tag -> assert eq (0 - 12)\n        aead pt res_tag -> assert str eq \"\" \"tampered tag returns empty plaintext\"\n\n        -- Verify invalid key/nonce/ciphertext length returns (-7, \"\") or \"\"\n        aead seal \"short-key\" nonce aad pt -> assert str eq \"\" \"aead_seal invalid key length\"\n        aead seal key \"short-nonce\" aad pt -> assert str eq \"\" \"aead_seal invalid nonce length\"\n        res_inv  = aead open \"short-key\" nonce aad sealed\n        aead rc res_inv -> assert eq (0 - 7)\n        res_ninv = aead open key \"short-nonce\" aad sealed\n        aead rc res_ninv -> assert eq (0 - 7)\n        res_tinv = aead open key nonce aad \"short-tag\"\n        aead rc res_tinv -> assert eq (0 - 7)\n        ()\n```\n\n### 24.3.7. Example 7: FIPS 180-4 SHA-512 (`sha512 bytes`, `sha512 hex`), RFC 8032 §5.1 Ed25519 Signatures (`ed25519 public key`, `ed25519 sign`, `ed25519 verify`) and Minisign Format (`minisign sign`, `minisign verify`)\n\nIn this practical example we verify official FIPS 180-4 SHA-512 test vectors, constant-time Ed25519 key derivation and signing (with strict $S \\ge L$ malleability and non-curve-point rejection), and `.minisig` release manifest signing/verification:\n\n```ridgun\nimport crypto\nimport test\n\nfn :: verificar sha512 ed25519 y minisign => ()\n      verificar sha512 ed25519 y minisign =\n        \"abc\" sha512 hex -> h_abc\n        assert str eq h_abc \"ddaf35a193617abacc417349ae20413112e6fa4e89a97ea20a9eeee64b55d39a2192992a274fc1a836ba3c23a3feebbd454d4423643ce80e2a9ac94fa54ca49f\" \"SHA-512 abc\"\n        \"9d61b19deffd5a60ba844af492ec2cc44449c5697b326919703bac031cae7f60\" hex to byte str -> sk\n        sk ed25519 public key -> pk\n        ed25519 sign sk \"\" -> sig\n        assert true (ed25519 verify pk \"\" sig) \"RFC 8032 Test 1\"\n        assert false (ed25519 verify pk \"tampered\" sig) \"Tampered message rejected\"\n        minisign encode pubkey \"01234567\" pk -> pub_txt\n        \"e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855  ridgun-linux-x86_64.tar.gz\\n\" -> sums\n        minisign sign sk \"01234567\" sums \"ridgun release key\" \"timestamp:1761667200\\tfile:SHA256SUMS\" -> msig\n        assert true (minisign verify pub_txt sums msig) \"Valid Minisign\"\n        assert str eq (minisign trusted comment msig) \"timestamp:1761667200\\tfile:SHA256SUMS\" \"Authenticated trusted comment\" -> ()\n```\n\n### 24.3.8. \"abcdbcdecdefdefgefghfghighijhijkijkljklmklmnlmnomnopnopq\") \"84983e441c3bd26ebaae4aa1f95129e5e54670f1\" \"SHA-1 448-bit\" -> ()\n        assert str eq (sha1 hex \"4916d6bdb7f78e6803698cab32d1586ea457dfc8\" \"SHA-1 bytes 0..255\" -> ()\n        assert str eq (sha1 hex \"The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog\") \"2fd4e1c67a2d28fced849ee1bb76e7391b93eb12\" \"SHA-1 quick brown fox\" -> ()\n\n        -- One million \"a\" characters\n        t0   = sys monotonic ms\n        h1m  = sha1 hex (make a1m)\n        dt1m = (sys monotonic ms) - t0\n        echo (\"  [BENCH] SHA-1 1,000,000 x 'a': \" + (int to str dt1m) + \" ms\") -> ()\n        assert str eq h1m \"34aa973cd4c4daa4f61eeb2bdbad27316534016f\" \"SHA-1 1,000,000 'a'\" -> ()\n```\n\n### 24.3.9. One million \"a\" characters\n        t0    = sys monotonic ms\n        h1m   = sha512 hex (make a1m)\n        dt1m  = (sys monotonic ms) - t0\n        echo (\"  [BENCH] SHA-512 1,000,000 x 'a': \" + (int to str dt1m) + \" ms\") -> ()\n        assert str eq h1m \"e718483d0ce769644e2e42c7bc15b4638e1f98b13b2044285632a803afa973ebde0ff244877ea60a4cb0432ce577c31beb009c5c2c49aa2e4eadb217ad8cc09b\" \"SHA-512 1,000,000 'a'\" -> ()\n```\n\n### 24.3.10. Example 11: Minisign Public Keys and Signatures: Round Trip and Tamper Detection\n\nIn this hands-on walkthrough we thoroughly exercise how `crypto` behaves across this functional area, covering standard inputs, parameter combinations, and corner cases:\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: test minisign roundtrip and tamper => ()\n      test minisign roundtrip and tamper =\n        seed   = hex to byte str \"9d61b19deffd5a60ba844af492ec2cc44449c5697b326919703bac031cae7f60\"\n        pk     = ed25519 public key seed\n        kid    = \"01234567\"\n        pk_b64 = minisign encode pubkey kid pk\n        assert true ((str len pk_b64) == 56) \"minisign encoded pubkey is 56 chars\" -> ()\n\n        dec1   = minisign decode pubkey pk_b64\n        assert str eq (ms kid dec1) kid \"minisign decode 1-line key_id\" -> ()\n        assert str eq (ms pk dec1) pk \"minisign decode 1-line pubkey\" -> ()\n\n        pub_2l = \"untrusted comment: ridgun release key\\n\" + pk_b64 + \"\\n\"\n        dec2   = minisign decode pubkey pub_2l\n        assert str eq (ms kid dec2) kid \"minisign decode 2-line key_id\" -> ()\n        assert str eq (ms pk dec2) pk \"minisign decode 2-line pubkey\" -> ()\n\n        msg    = \"e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855  ridgun-v0.9.21-linux-x86_64.tar.gz\\n\"\n        tc     = \"timestamp:1761667200\\tfile:SHA256SUMS\"\n        msig   = minisign sign seed kid msg \"signature from ridgun secret key\" tc\n        assert str eq (minisign trusted comment msig) tc \"minisign trusted comment extracted\" -> ()\n        assert true (minisign verify pub_2l msg msig) \"minisign verify valid signature\" -> ()\n        assert true (minisign verify pk_b64 msg msig) \"minisign verify valid with 1-line pubkey\" -> ()\n\n        -- Tampered payload rejected\n        assert false (minisign verify pub_2l (msg + \"x\") msig) \"minisign verify rejects tampered payload\" -> ()\n\n        -- Tampered trusted comment rejected even though payload signature is intact\n        msig_bad_tc = minisign sign seed kid msg \"signature from ridgun secret key\" \"timestamp:9999999999\\tfile:EVIL\"\n        lines_good  = c split lines msig\n        lines_bad   = c split lines msig_bad_tc\n        forged_msig = (c nth str lines_good 0) + \"\\n\" + (c nth str lines_good 1) + \"\\n\" + (c nth str lines_bad 2) + \"\\n\" + (c nth str lines_good 3) + \"\\n\"\n        assert false (minisign verify pub_2l msg forged_msig) \"minisign verify rejects tampered trusted comment\" -> ()\n\n        -- Wrong key_id rejected\n        other_pub = minisign encode pubkey \"76543210\" pk\n        assert false (minisign verify other_pub msg msig) \"minisign verify rejects mismatched key_id\" -> ()\n```\n\n### 24.3.12. Example 12: HMAC-SHA-384, HKDF (RFC 5869), X25519 (RFC 7748), and AES-128-GCM (NIST SP 800-38D)\n\nIn this hands-on walkthrough we thoroughly exercise how `crypto` behaves across this functional area, covering standard inputs, parameter combinations, and corner cases:\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: test sha384 hkdf x25519 aes128gcm => ()\n      test sha384 hkdf x25519 aes128gcm =\n        -- 1. SHA-384 & HMAC-SHA-384 (FIPS 180-4 & RFC 4231 TC2)\n        h384_emp = sha384 hex \"\"\n        assert str eq h384_emp \"38b060a751ac96384cd9327eb1b1e36a21fdb71114be07434c0cc7bf63f6e1da274edebfe76f65fbd51ad2f14898b95b\" \"SHA-384 empty\" -> ()\n        h384_abc = sha384 hex \"abc\"\n        assert str eq h384_abc \"cb00753f45a35e8bb5a03d699ac65007272c32ab0eded1631a8b605a43ff5bed8086072ba1e7cc2358baeca134c825a7\" \"SHA-384 abc\" -> ()\n        assert eq (str len (sha384 bytes \"abc\")) 48 -> ()\n        mac384   = hmac sha384 \"Jefe\" \"what do ya want for nothing?\"\n        assert str eq (bytes to hex str mac384) \"af45d2e376484031617f78d2b58a6b1b9c7ef464f5a01b47e42ec3736322445e8e2240ca5e69e2c78b3239ecfab21649\" \"RFC 4231 TC2 HMAC-SHA-384\" -> ()\n\n        -- 2. HKDF-SHA-256 (RFC 5869 Appendix A Test Case 1) & TLS 1.3 Derive-Secret (RFC 8448 §3)\n        ikm1 = hex to byte str \"0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b\"\n        slt1 = hex to byte str \"000102030405060708090a0b0c\"\n        inf1 = hex to byte str \"f0f1f2f3f4f5f6f7f8f9\"\n        prk1 = hkdf extract slt1 ikm1\n        okm1 = hkdf expand prk1 inf1 42\n        assert str eq (bytes to hex str prk1) \"077709362c2e32df0ddc3f0dc47bba6390b6c73bb50f9c3122ec844ad7c2b3e5\" \"RFC 5869 TC1 PRK\" -> ()\n        assert str eq (bytes to hex str okm1) \"3cb25f25faacd57a90434f64d0362f2a2d2d0a90cf1a5a4c5db02d56ecc4c5bf34007208d5b887185865\" \"RFC 5869 TC1 OKM\" -> ()\n        early_sec = hkdf extract \"\" (c repeat byte 0 32)\n        assert str eq (bytes to hex str early_sec) \"33ad0a1c607ec03b09e6cd9893680ce210adf300aa1f2660e1b22e10f170f92a\" \"RFC 8448 Early Secret\" -> ()\n        derived_s = derive secret early_sec \"derived\" \"\"\n        assert str eq (bytes to hex str derived_s) \"6f2615a108c702c5678f54fc9dbab69716c076189c48250cebeac3576c3611ba\" \"RFC 8448 Derived Secret\" -> ()\n\n        -- 3. RFC 7748 X25519 Test Vectors (§5.2 and §6.1 Alice/Bob DH)\n        x_sc1  = hex to byte str \"a546e36bf0527c9d3b16154b82465edd62144c0ac1fc5a18506a2244ba449ac4\"\n        x_u1   = hex to byte str \"e6db6867583030db3594c1a424b15f7c726624ec26b3353b10a903a6d0ab1c4c\"\n        x_out1 = x25519 x_sc1 x_u1\n        assert str eq (bytes to hex str x_out1) \"c3da55379de9c6908e94ea4df28d084f32eccf03491c71f754b4075577a28552\" \"RFC 7748 §5.2 vector 1\" -> ()\n        a_priv = hex to byte str \"77076d0a7318a57d3c16c17251b26645df4c2f87ebc0992ab177fba51db92c2a\"\n        a_pub  = x25519 public key a_priv\n        b_priv = hex to byte str \"5dab087e624a8a4b79e17f8b83800ee66f3bb1292618b6fd1c2f8b27ff88e0eb\"\n        b_pub  = x25519 public key b_priv\n        assert str eq (bytes to hex str a_pub) \"8520f0098930a754748b7ddcb43ef75a0dbf3a0d26381af4eba4a98eaa9b4e6a\" \"RFC 7748 §6.1 Alice pubkey\" -> ()\n        assert str eq (bytes to hex str b_pub) \"de9edb7d7b7dc1b4d35b61c2ece435373f8343c85b78674dadfc7e146f882b4f\" \"RFC 7748 §6.1 Bob pubkey\" -> ()\n        sh_ab  = x25519 a_priv b_pub\n        sh_ba  = x25519 b_priv a_pub\n        assert str eq (bytes to hex str sh_ab) \"4a5d9d5ba4ce2de1728e3bf480350f25e07e21c947d19e3376f09b3c1e161742\" \"RFC 7748 §6.1 shared secret\" -> ()\n        assert str eq sh_ab sh_ba \"X25519 Alice == Bob\" -> ()\n        assert str eq (x25519 a_priv (c repeat byte 0 32)) \"\" \"X25519 rejects all-zero low-order point\" -> ()\n\n        -- 4. FIPS 197 AES-128 & NIST SP 800-38D AES-128-GCM\n        aes_k   = hex to byte str \"2b7e151628aed2a6abf7158809cf4f3c\"\n        aes_pt  = hex to byte str \"3243f6a8885a308d313198a2e0370734\"\n        aes_ct  = aes128 block aes_k aes_pt\n        assert str eq (bytes to hex str aes_ct) \"3925841d02dc09fbdc118597196a0b32\" \"FIPS 197 Appendix B AES-128 block\" -> ()\n\n        gk1     = c repeat byte 0 16\n        gn1     = c repeat byte 0 12\n        g_seal1 = aes128 gcm seal gk1 gn1 \"\" \"\"\n        assert str eq (bytes to hex str g_seal1) \"58e2fccefa7e3061367f1d57a4e7455a\" \"NIST GCM Test Case 1 empty PT/AAD\" -> ()\n        g_seal2 = aes128 gcm seal gk1 gn1 \"\" (c repeat byte 0 16)\n        assert str eq (bytes to hex str g_seal2) \"0388dace60b6a392f328c2b971b2fe78ab6e47d42cec13bdf53a67b21257bddf\" \"NIST GCM Test Case 2 16B zero PT\" -> ()\n        g_open2 = aes128 gcm open gk1 gn1 \"\" g_seal2\n        assert eq (aead rc g_open2) 0 -> ()\n        assert str eq (aead pt g_open2) (c repeat byte 0 16) \"AES-128-GCM open TC2\" -> ()\n\n        -- Tampered tag / AAD rejected with (-12, \"\")\n        g_bad_aad = aes128 gcm open gk1 gn1 \"wrong-aad\" g_seal2\n        assert eq (aead rc g_bad_aad) (0 - 12) -> ()\n        assert str eq (aead pt g_bad_aad) \"\" \"AES-128-GCM tampered AAD returns empty\" -> ()\n        g_bad_tag = aes128 gcm open gk1 gn1 \"\" ((byte slice g_seal2 0 31) + (byte str 0))\n        assert eq (aead rc g_bad_tag) (0 - 12) -> ()\n```\n\n### 24.3.13. Example 15: RFC 1321 MD5 Vectors (`md5 bytes`, `md5 hex`) for Protocols That Still Name It\n\nIn this hands-on walkthrough we thoroughly exercise how `crypto` behaves across this functional area, covering standard inputs, parameter combinations, and corner cases:\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: test md5 rfc1321 vectors => ()\n      test md5 rfc1321 vectors =\n        md5 hex \"\" -> assert str eq \"d41d8cd98f00b204e9800998ecf8427e\" \"MD5 empty\"\n        md5 hex \"a\" -> assert str eq \"0cc175b9c0f1b6a831c399e269772661\" \"MD5 a\"\n        md5 hex \"abc\" -> assert str eq \"900150983cd24fb0d6963f7d28e17f72\" \"MD5 abc\"\n        md5 hex \"message digest\" -> assert str eq \"f96b697d7cb7938d525a2f31aaf161d0\" \"MD5 message digest\"\n        md5 hex \"abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz\" -> assert str eq \"c3fcd3d76192e4007dfb496cca67e13b\" \"MD5 alphabet\"\n        md5 hex \"ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz0123456789\" -> assert str eq \"d174ab98d277d9f5a5611c2c9f419d9f\" \"MD5 62 characters (two blocks)\"\n        md5 hex \"12345678901234567890123456789012345678901234567890123456789012345678901234567890\" -> assert str eq \"57edf4a22be3c955ac49da2e2107b67a\" \"MD5 80 digits\"\n        bytes to hex str (md5 bytes \"abc\") -> assert str eq (md5 hex \"abc\") \"md5 bytes matches md5 hex\"\n```\n\n---\n\n## 24.4. Under the Hood: How `crypto` Is Built in Pure Ridgun (`src/main/ridgun/lib/crypto.ridgun`)\n\nOne of the biggest advantages of `ridgun-libs` is that **there are no C black boxes**. You can open `src/main/ridgun/lib/crypto.ridgun` and read exactly how every operation is implemented using pattern matching, `|` / `|.` guard trees, and tail-call optimization (TCO). Let's inspect the key building blocks of its real implementation:\n\n### 24.4.1. Internal Implementation: RGF-019 Raw Byte Manipulation (`byte_str`, `bytes_from_list`, `bytes_to_list`)\n\nObserve how `crypto.ridgun` declares explicit `fn :: ... => ...` contracts first and resolves each case through aligned equations and tail calls:\n\n```ridgun\nmodule :: crypto\n\nfn :: norm byte mod Int => Int\n      norm byte mod m   =\n        | m < 0     = m + 256\n        | otherwise = m\n\nfn :: norm byte Int => Int\n      norm byte b   =  norm byte mod (b % 256)\n\nfn :: byte str norm Int => String\n      byte str norm ub  =\n        t     = Tensor[U8 * 1]\n        t_(0) = ub and 255\n        tensor to str t\n\nfn :: byte str Int => String\n      byte str n   =\n        byte str norm (norm byte n)\n\nfn :: c sb append3 String String => String String String String\n      c sb append3 n2     c3     =\n        | (str len n2) < 65536 = (\"\", \"\", n2, c3)\n        | otherwise            = (\"\", \"\", \"\", c3 + n2)\n\nfn :: c sb append2 String String String => String String String String\n      c sb append2 n1 c2 c3 =\n        | (str len n1) < 8192 = (\"\", n1, c2, c3)\n        | otherwise           = c sb append3 (c2 + n1) c3\n\nfn :: c sb append1 String String String String => String String String String\n      c sb append1 n0 c1 c2 c3 =\n        | (str len n0) < 512 = (n0, c1, c2, c3)\n        | otherwise          = c sb append2 (c1 + n0) c2 c3\n\nfn :: c sb append String String String String String => String String String String\n      c sb append chunk c0 c1 c2 c3 =\n        c sb append1 (c0 + chunk) c1 c2 c3\n\nfn :: c sb finish String String String String => String\n      c sb finish c0 c1 c2 c3 = ((c3 + c2) + c1) + c0\n\n-- The tensor is bound to a name: with `_` ridgunc 0.9.49 binds a wrong `n`.\nfn :: c u8 len Tensor[U8]          => Int\n      c u8 len (Tensor[U8 * n] bs) =  n\n\nfn :: c copy loop Tensor[U8] Int Tensor[U8] Int Int Int => Int\n      c copy loop dst doff src soff i n =\n        | i >= n    = doff + n\n        | otherwise =\n          dst_(doff + i) = src_(soff + i)\n          c copy loop dst doff src soff (i + 1) n\n\n-- Copies `n` bytes of `src` from `soff` into `dst` at `doff`; returns `doff + n`.\nfn :: c copy bytes Tensor[U8] Int Tensor[U8] Int Int => Int\n      c copy bytes dst doff src soff n =  c copy loop dst doff src soff 0 n\n\n-- Writes `w` as 4 little-endian bytes at `off`; returns `off + 4`.\nfn :: c put le32 Tensor[U8] Int Int => Int\n      c put le32 t          off w   =\n        uw          = w and 0xFFFFFFFF\n        t_(off)     = uw and 255\n        t_(off + 1) = (uw shr 8) and 255\n        t_(off + 2) = (uw shr 16) and 255\n        t_(off + 3) = (uw shr 24) and 255\n        off + 4\n\nfn :: bytes from list loop Tensor[U8] [Int]    Int => Tensor[U8]\n      bytes from list loop t          []       _   =  t\n      bytes from list loop t          (b:rest) i   =\n        t_(i) = b and 255\n        bytes from list loop t rest (i + 1)\n\n-- Values outside 0..255 are taken modulo 256 (`norm byte`).\nfn :: bytes from list [Int] => String\n      bytes from list []    =  \"\"\n      bytes from list bs    =\n        n = c list len bs\n        t = Tensor[U8 * n]\n        tensor to str (bytes from list loop t bs 0)\n\nfn :: bytes to list String => [Int]\n      bytes to list s      =\n        tensor to list (tensor from str s)\n```\n\n### 24.4.2. 1)\n```\n\n---\n\n## 24.5. Algorithmic Guarantees, `RMM1`/`RMM2` Memory, and the 5 Golden Rules of `crypto`\n\n- **Algorithmic & Safety Guarantee**: `aead open` verifies the 16-byte Poly1305 authentication tag in constant time before releasing a single byte of plaintext (returning `(-1, \"\")` on tamper).\n- **$O(1)$ Stack Complexity via TCO**: Every recursive loop in `src/main/ridgun/lib/crypto.ridgun` is in tail position, so `ridgunc` compiles them into native jumps with zero stack growth.\n- **Deterministic Memory (`RMM1`/`RMM2`)**: Zero garbage-collector pauses; all intermediate allocations are reclaimed deterministically on scope exit.\n- **Continuous Verification**: Statically checked via `stable check` and tested by the automated suite in `src/test/ridgun/test crypto.ridgun`.\n\n### The 5 Golden Rules When Programming with `crypto`\n\n1. **Declare `import crypto` at the top of your file** and call its functions with spaces, exactly as they are declared, so your code reads like natural prose.\n2. **Align your data pipelines with `=`**: chain `crypto` calls into named intermediate steps and let `stable format` align the columns.\n3. **Leverage `crypto`'s total functions inside `|` guards**: inspect return values or unwrap ADTs via pattern matching rather than assuming external input is valid.\n4. **Avoid cloning large structures when only reading**: remember that under `RMM2`, function input arguments incur zero reference-count overhead (`+0` / `-0`).\n5. **Pair `crypto` with `test` (`import test`)**: always lock in your domain invariants with `assert equals` or `assert true`.\n\n---\n\nIn **Chapter 25**, we will explore the **`argon2id`** lib in full depth (The `argon2id` Lib — RFC 9106 Argon2id on `Tensor[U64 * 128]`, Blake2b, and OWASP Presets).\n"}, {"num": "24", "slug": "25-lib-argon2id-rfc9106-password-hashing", "file": "25-lib-argon2id-rfc9106-password-hashing.md", "title": "Chapter 25: The `argon2id` Lib — RFC 9106 Argon2id on `Tensor[U64 * 128]`, Blake2b, and OWASP Presets", "short_title": "The `argon2id` Lib — RFC 9106 Argon2id on `Tensor[U64 * 128]`, Blake2b, and OWASP Presets", "markdown": "# Chapter 25: The `argon2id` Lib — RFC 9106 Argon2id on `Tensor[U64 * 128]`, Blake2b, and OWASP Presets\n\n## 25.1. Why Does the `argon2id` Lib Exist? (The Real-World Problem & Ridgun Philosophy)\n\n> *\"Why do I need a `argon2id` lib written from scratch in pure Ridgun instead of just linking a legacy C library?\"*\n\nThat is the first question every systems engineer asks when meeting `argon2id`. And the answer captures the entire philosophy of `ridgun-libs`:\n\nLet's be honest: hashing passwords with plain SHA-256 lets a modern GPU brute-force billions of guesses per second, yet linking external C libraries for Argon2id often brings FFI and build headaches.\n\nThe **`argon2id`** lib implements **RFC 9106 Argon2id** and **RFC 7693 Blake2b-512** in 100% pure Ridgun directly over native `Tensor[U64 * 128]` blocks (1,024 contiguous bytes per block in RMM2 memory), complete with **PHC** string formatting (`$argon2id$v=19$m=...,t=...,p=...$`), **OWASP** presets (`default argon2 params`, `argon2 moderate params`), secret pepper/associated-data context (`argon2id hash ctx`), raw key derivation (`argon2id derive key`), and parameter upgrade detection (`argon2id needs rehash`).\n\nIn a traditional ecosystem, solving **`CRYPTO`** tasks means pulling in external C dependencies, wrestling with raw pointers, opaque type conversions, unchecked exceptions, or unpredictable garbage-collector pauses. In Ridgun, the **`argon2id`** lib (`src/main/ridgun/lib/argon2id.ridgun`) tackles the problem with four non-negotiable principles:\n\n1. **Declare `import argon2id` (or `import argon2id as alias`) at the top of your file**: every lib defines its `module :: argon2id` namespace, and under `--strict` multi-word functions are always called with natural spaces.\n2. **Chain your data pipelines left-to-right with `->`**: write `input step one -> step two -> result`, use `(+ _ _ +)` sequence masks to destructure tuples/lists, and omit `_ =` on sequential statements (or discard with `-> ()`).\n3. **Tail-Call Optimization (TCO)**: all internal loops in `argon2id` are tail-recursive and compile into native hardware loops using $O(1)$ stack space.\n4. **Deterministic Memory (`RMM1` / `RMM2`)**: every intermediate allocation is reclaimed at the exact instruction where its last read finishes, with no Garbage Collector.\n\n---\n\n## 25.2. Native Artifacts, Imports, and Complete `argon2id` API Catalog\n\nIn `ridgun-libs`, **`argon2id`** is a first-class **lib** located at `src/main/ridgun/lib/argon2id.ridgun` (domain `CRYPTO`). When built with `stable bundle`, it compiles into one native artifact:\n\n| Artifact | Path | Purpose |\n|---|---|---|\n| **Ridgun Bundle** | `target/bundles/argon2id.ridgunlib` | Portable distribution and direct `import argon2id` resolution |\n\n> Every lib declares its own namespace via `module :: argon2id`: simply write `import argon2id` (or `import argon2id as alias`) at the top and call its functions with natural spaces (`my fn x`) and left-to-right `->` pipelines (`x my fn -> result`).\n\n### 25.2.1. Summary of `argon2id` Functional Families\n\n| Signature / Function / Type | Purpose & Usage |\n|---|---|\n| `argon2id hash / argon2id verify` | 5-argument RFC 9106 PHC password hashing (`pwd, salt, m_kib, t, p`) and constant-time verification |\n| `default argon2 params / argon2 interactive params / argon2 moderate params / argon2 sensitive params / argon2 params` | Parameter presets (19 MiB OWASP minimum, 46 MiB, 64 MiB) and custom parameters (`m_cost` in KiB, `t_cost`, `lanes`, `tag_len`) |\n| `argon2id hash ctx / argon2id verify ctx` | RFC 9106 hashing with secret `pepper` ($K$) and associated data ($X$) |\n| `argon2id derive key / argon2id needs rehash` | Raw binary key derivation and policy-upgrade detection on stored PHC strings |\n| `blake2b` | General-purpose RFC 7693 Blake2b cryptographic digest (`1..64` bytes) |\n\n### 25.2.2. Under the Hood: How `argon2id` Is Built in Pure Ridgun (`src/main/ridgun/lib/argon2id.ridgun`)\n\nOne of the biggest advantages of `ridgun-libs` is that **there are no C black boxes**. You can open `src/main/ridgun/lib/argon2id.ridgun` and read exactly how every operation is implemented using pattern matching, `|` / `|.` guard trees, and tail-call optimization (TCO). Let's inspect the key building blocks of its real implementation:\n\n### 25.4.1. Internal Implementation: Byte (Tensor[U8], ADR-0010), String & 32/64-bit Modular Arithmetic Helpers (Internal)\n\nObserve how `argon2id.ridgun` declares explicit `fn :: ... => ...` contracts first and resolves each case through aligned equations and tail calls:\n\n```ridgun\nmodule :: argon2id\n\nfn :: a2 str list len [String] => Int\n      a2 str list len []       =  0\n      a2 str list len (_:rest) =  1 + (a2 str list len rest)\n\nfn :: a2 nth str [String] Int => String\n      a2 nth str []       _   =  \"\"\n      a2 nth str (x:rest) idx =\n        | idx <= 0  = x\n        | otherwise = a2 nth str rest (idx - 1)\n\n-- The tensor is bound to a name: with `_` ridgunc 0.9.49 binds a wrong `n`.\nfn :: a2 u8 len Tensor[U8]          => Int\n      a2 u8 len (Tensor[U8 * n] bs) =  n\n\nfn :: a2 copy loop Tensor[U8] Int Tensor[U8] Int Int Int => Int\n      a2 copy loop dst doff src soff i n =\n        | i >= n    = doff + n\n        | otherwise =\n          dst_(doff + i) = src_(soff + i)\n          a2 copy loop dst doff src soff (i + 1) n\n\n-- Copies `n` bytes of `src` from `soff` into `dst` at `doff`; returns `doff + n`.\nfn :: a2 copy bytes Tensor[U8] Int Tensor[U8] Int Int => Int\n      a2 copy bytes dst doff src soff n =  a2 copy loop dst doff src soff 0 n\n\n-- Writes `w` as 4 little-endian bytes at `off`; returns `off + 4`.\nfn :: a2 put u32 Tensor[U8] Int Int => Int\n      a2 put u32 t off w =\n        uw          = w and 0xFFFFFFFF\n        t_(off)     = uw and 255\n        t_(off + 1) = (uw shr 8) and 255\n        t_(off + 2) = (uw shr 16) and 255\n        t_(off + 3) = (uw shr 24) and 255\n        off + 4\n\n-- Writes `le32(len src) || src` at `off` (RFC 9106 H0 field); Argon2Params 19456 2 1 32 19\n\nfn :: argon2 moderate params => Argon2Params\n      argon2 moderate params =  Argon2Params 47104 3 1 32 19\n\nfn :: argon2 sensitive params => Argon2Params\n tag_len 19\n\nfn :: clamp salt len Int => Int\n      clamp salt len n   =\n        | n < 16    = 16\n        | n > 64    = 64\n        | otherwise = n\n\nfn :: a2 random next Tensor[U8] Int Int Tensor[U8] Int => Int\n      a2 random next buf        off n   tmp        rc  =\n        | rc == (0 - 4) = a2 random fill buf off n\n        | rc <= 0       = rc\n        | otherwise     = a2 random fill buf (a2 copy bytes buf off tmp 0 rc) n\n\n-- Fills `buf[off..n)` from getrandom(2); retries on EINTR and on short reads.\nfn :: a2 random fill Tensor[U8] Int Int => Int\n      a2 random fill buf 0 0)\n\nfn :: argon2id generate salt Int => String\n      argon2id generate salt n   =\n        eff_n = clamp salt len n\n        buf   = Tensor[U8 * eff_n]\n        a2 random fill buf 0 eff_n\n => Argon2KeyRes\n      finish derive key checked tag_raw exp_len =\n        | (a2 u8 len tag_raw) != exp_len = Argon2KeyErr \"tag derivation failed\"\n        | otherwise                      = Argon2KeyOk tag_raw\n\nfn :: finish derive key String Tensor[U8] Argon2Params String => Argon2KeyRes\n      finish derive key pwd salt_bytes params err =\n        | (str len err) > 0 = Argon2KeyErr err\n        | otherwise         =\n          tag_raw = derive raw tag (tensor from str pwd) salt_bytes params\n          finish derive key checked tag_raw (tag_len params)\n\nfn :: argon2id derive params params salt_bytes)\n\nfn :: key res to hex Argon2KeyRes       => Argon2Res\n      key res to hex (Argon2KeyErr err) =  Argon2Err err\n      key res to hex (Argon2KeyOk bytes) = Argon2Ok (bytes to hex bytes)\n\nfn :: argon2id derive key hex String String Argon2Params => Argon2Res\n      argon2id derive key hex pwd salt params = key res to hex (argon2id derive key pwd salt params)\n\nfn :: failed\"\n        | otherwise =\n          salt_b64 = b64 encode nopad salt_bytes\n          tag_b64  = b64 encode nopad tag_raw\n          m        = m_cost params\n          t        = t_cost String => Argon2Res\n      finish argon2id hash ctx pwd salt_bytes secret ad params err =\n        | (str len err) > 0 = Argon2Err err\n        | otherwise =\n          pwd_raw = tensor from str pwd\n Argon2Res\n      argon2id hash ctx pwd salt secret ad params =\n        salt_bytes = tensor from str salt\n        finish argon2id hash ctx pwd salt_bytes secret ad params (validate argon2 params params salt_bytes)\n\nfn :: argon2id hash bytes String Tensor[U8] Argon2Params => Argon2Res\n      argon2id hash bytes pwd salt_bytes params =\n        finish argon2id hash ctx pwd salt_bytes \"\" (tensor from str salt) params\n\nfn :: argon2id hash password String Argon2Params => Argon2Res\n      argon2id hash password pwd    params       =  argon2id hash params pwd (argon2id generate salt 16) params\n\nfn :: ct diff loop Tensor[U8] Tensor[U8] Int Int Int => Int\n      ct diff loop a          b          i   n   acc =\n        | i >= n    = acc\n        | otherwise = ct diff loop a b (i + 1) n (acc or (byte bitxor a_(i) b_(i)))\n\n-- Compares every byte of the common prefix without early exit; equal only when lengths match too.\nfn :: constant time bytes eq Tensor[U8] Tensor[U8] => Bool\n diff loop a b 0 n 0\n        (la == lb) and (diff == 0)\n\nfn :: constant time eq String String => Bool\n      constant time eq a      b      =  constant time bytes eq (tensor from str a) (tensor from idx) == ch = [(str slice s start idx)] :: (split str loop s ch (idx + 1) (idx + 1) len)\n        | otherwise                 = split str loop s ch start (idx + 1) len\n\nfn :: a2 is digits loop String Int Int => Bool\n      a2 is digits loop s idx len =\n        | idx >= len                                           = True\n        | (str char at s idx) < 48 or (str char at s idx) > 57 = False\n in PHC string\"\n        | not (is valid b64 nopad t_b64) = Argon2PhcErr \"invalid Base64 tag in PHC string\"\n        | otherwise =\n          salt_bytes = b64 decode nopad s_b64\n          tag_bytes phc mtp Int Int Int [String] => Argon2PhcRes\n      parse phc mtp m t p parts =\n        | m < 8 or t < 1 or p < 1 = Argon2PhcErr \"invalid m, t, or p in PHC string\"\n        | otherwise (Argon2Ok phc) =  phc\n      unwrap phc res (Argon2Err _)  =  \"\"\n\nfn :: argon2id hash String String Int Int Int => String\n      argon2id hash pwd salt m_kib t_iters p_lanes =\n        argon2id hash params pwd salt (Argon2Params m_kib t_iters p_lanes 32 19) -> unwrap phc res\n\nfn :: argon2id hash phc String String Int Int Int => String\n      argon2id hash phc pwd salt m_kib t_iters p_lanes Algorithmic Guarantees, `RMM1`/`RMM2` Memory, and the 5 Golden Rules of `argon2id`\n\n- **Algorithmic & Safety Guarantee**: Byte-for-byte match with official RFC 9106 §5.3 and OpenSSL 3.5 test vectors, operating on native `Tensor[U64 * 128]` blocks without a single line of C.\n- **$O(1)$ Stack Complexity via TCO**: Every recursive loop in `src/main/ridgun/lib/argon2id.ridgun` is in tail position, so `ridgunc` compiles them into native jumps with zero stack growth.\n- **Deterministic Memory (`RMM1`/`RMM2`)**: Zero garbage-collector pauses; all intermediate allocations are reclaimed deterministically on scope exit.\n- **Continuous Verification**: Statically checked via `stable check` and tested by the automated suite in `src/test/ridgun/test argon2id.ridgun`.\n\n### The 5 Golden Rules When Programming with `argon2id`\n\n1. **Declare `import argon2id` at the top of your file** and call its functions with spaces, exactly as they are declared, so your code reads like natural prose.\n2. **Align your data pipelines with `=`**: chain `argon2id` calls into named intermediate steps and let `stable format` align the columns.\n3. **Leverage `argon2id`'s total functions inside `|` guards**: inspect return values or unwrap ADTs via pattern matching rather than assuming external input is valid.\n4. **Avoid cloning large structures when only reading**: remember that under `RMM2`, function input arguments incur zero reference-count overhead (`+0` / `-0`).\n5. **Pair `argon2id` with `test` (`import test`)**: always lock in your domain invariants with `assert equals` or `assert true`.\n\n---\n\nIn **Chapter 26**, we will explore the **`jwt`** lib in full depth (The `jwt` Lib — RFC 7519 `HS256` JSON Web Tokens and ChaCha20-Poly1305 Encrypted Tokens).\n"}, {"num": "25", "slug": "26-lib-jwt-rfc7519-and-encrypted-tokens", "file": "26-lib-jwt-rfc7519-and-encrypted-tokens.md", "title": "Chapter 26: The `jwt` Lib — RFC 7519 `HS256` JSON Web Tokens and ChaCha20-Poly1305 Encrypted Tokens", "short_title": "The `jwt` Lib — RFC 7519 `HS256` JSON Web Tokens and ChaCha20-Poly1305 Encrypted Tokens", "markdown": "# Chapter 26: The `jwt` Lib — RFC 7519 `HS256` JSON Web Tokens and ChaCha20-Poly1305 Encrypted Tokens\n\n## 26.1. Why Does the `jwt` Lib Exist? (The Real-World Problem & Ridgun Philosophy)\n\n> *\"Why do I need a `jwt` lib written from scratch in pure Ridgun instead of just linking a legacy C library?\"*\n\nThat is the first question every systems engineer asks when meeting `jwt`. And the answer captures the entire philosophy of `ridgun-libs`:\n\nLet's be honest: the JWT ecosystem is notorious for `\"alg\":\"none\"` signature-bypass bugs and for developers stuffing confidential data into a standard JWT while forgetting that its payload is merely Base64url-encoded, not encrypted.\n\nThe **`jwt`** lib solves both needs: it signs and verifies **RFC 7519 (`HS256`) JWTs** while strictly enforcing `alg == \"HS256\"`, constant-time MAC comparison, and `exp`/`nbf` windows, and it also provides **`jwt seal aead` / `jwt open aead`** for opaque tokens encrypted with **ChaCha20-Poly1305 AEAD**.\n\nIn a traditional ecosystem, solving **`JWT`** tasks means pulling in external C dependencies, wrestling with raw pointers, opaque type conversions, unchecked exceptions, or unpredictable garbage-collector pauses. In Ridgun, the **`jwt`** lib (`src/main/ridgun/lib/jwt.ridgun`) tackles the problem with four non-negotiable principles:\n\n1. **Declare `import jwt` (or `import jwt as alias`) at the top of your file**: every lib defines its `module :: jwt` namespace, and under `--strict` multi-word functions are always called with natural spaces.\n2. **Chain your data pipelines left-to-right with `->`**: write `input step one -> step two -> result`, use `(+ _ _ +)` sequence masks to destructure tuples/lists, and omit `_ =` on sequential statements (or discard with `-> ()`).\n3. **Tail-Call Optimization (TCO)**: all internal loops in `jwt` are tail-recursive and compile into native hardware loops using $O(1)$ stack space.\n4. **Deterministic Memory (`RMM1` / `RMM2`)**: every intermediate allocation is reclaimed at the exact instruction where its last read finishes, with no Garbage Collector.\n\n---\n\n## 26.2. Native Artifacts, Imports, and Complete `jwt` API Catalog\n\nIn `ridgun-libs`, **`jwt`** is a first-class **lib** located at `src/main/ridgun/lib/jwt.ridgun` (domain `JWT`). When built with `stable bundle`, it compiles into one native artifact:\n\n| Artifact | Path | Purpose |\n|---|---|---|\n| **Ridgun Bundle** | `target/bundles/jwt.ridgunlib` | Portable distribution and direct `import jwt` resolution |\n\n> Every lib declares its own namespace via `module :: jwt`: simply write `import jwt` (or `import jwt as alias`) at the top and call its functions with natural spaces (`my fn x`) and left-to-right `->` pipelines (`x my fn -> result`).\n\n### 26.2.1. Deep Dive into `jwt`: Step-by-Step Examples for Every Feature\n\nA signature table alone is never enough: let's explore **every capability** of the `jwt` lib through progressive, runnable Ridgun examples. We will start with two everyday tabular recipes and then walk through every functional scenario, transformation, and boundary condition verified in `src/test/ridgun/test jwt.ridgun`.\n\n### 26.3.1. Example 1: Core Tabular Workflow with `jwt`\n\nNotice how in Ridgun the `=` signs and transformation steps using `jwt` align into a clean, scannable table without unnecessary mutable variables or hidden side effects:\n\n```ridgun\nimport jwt\n\nfn :: sujeto de JwtClaimsRes     => String\n      sujeto de (JwtClaimsOk c)  =  subject c\n      sujeto de (JwtClaimsErr e) =  \"error: \" + e\n\nfn :: emitir y verificar sesion String => String String\n      emitir y verificar sesion secreto =\n        jwt sign claims (JwtClaims \"solstice\" \"user-42\" 1700003600 0 \"{}\") secreto -> tok\n        jwt verify claims tok secreto 1700001000 -> res\n        (tok, sujeto de res)\n```\n\n### 26.3.2. Example 2: Safe Composition and Boundary Handling\n\nEvery function in the `jwt` lib is designed to compose cleanly with boolean guards `|` and with the rest of the 38 libs in `ridgun-libs`:\n\n```ridgun\nimport jwt\n\nfn :: abrir sobre JwtRes       String String => JwtRes\n      abrir sobre (JwtOk tok)  clave  nonce  =  jwt open aead clave nonce tok\n      abrir sobre (JwtErr e)   _      _      =  JwtErr e\n\nfn :: sellar token confidencial String => JwtRes\n      sellar token confidencial clave =\n        jwt seal aead clave \"nonce-12byte\" \"{\\\"rol\\\":\\\"root\\\",\\\"pin\\\":\\\"9988\\\"}\" -> sobre\n        abrir sobre sobre clave \"nonce-12byte\"\n```\n\n### 26.3.3. Example 3: JWT HS256 Signing & Verification (`jwt sign hs256`, `jwt verify hs256`), `alg: none` Attack Rejection, and Tamper Detection\n\nIn this hands-on walkthrough we thoroughly exercise how `jwt` behaves across this functional area, covering standard inputs, parameter combinations, and corner cases:\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: test jwt hs256 sign verify and tamper => ()\n      test jwt hs256 sign verify and tamper =\n        payload = '{\"sub\":\"user-42\",\"role\":\"admin\"}'\n        secret = \"super-secret-hmac-key-2026\"\n        tok = jwt sign hs256 payload secret\n\n        dec = jwt decode payload tok\n        is jwt ok dec -> assert true \"AC1: jwt decode payload succeeds\"\n        unwrap jwt dec -> assert str eq payload \"AC1: decoded payload matches input\"\n\n        ver = jwt verify hs256 tok secret\n        is jwt ok ver -> assert true \"AC2: jwt verify hs256 accepts valid signature\"\n        unwrap jwt ver -> assert str eq payload \"AC2: verified payload matches input\"\n\n        wrong_sec = jwt verify hs256 tok \"wrong-secret\"\n        is jwt ok wrong_sec -> assert false \"AC2: jwt verify hs256 rejects wrong secret\"\n        is jwt ok (jwt verify hs256 tok \"\") -> assert false \"AC2: jwt verify hs256 rejects empty secret\"\n\n        tampered = tok + \"x\"\n        is jwt ok (jwt verify hs256 tampered secret) -> assert false \"AC2: jwt verify hs256 Internal Implementation: Constant-Time Equality\n\nObserve how `jwt.ridgun` declares explicit `fn :: ... => ...` contracts first and resolves each case through aligned equations and tail calls:\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: jwt byte bxor Int Int => Int\n      jwt byte bxor a b = (jwt u8 a) xor (jwt u8 b)\n\nfn :: jwt ct diff String String Int Int Int => Int\n      jwt ct diff a b idx len acc =\n        | idx >= len = acc\n        | otherwise = jwt ct diff a b (idx + 1) len (acc or (jwt byte bxor (str char at a idx) (str char at b idx)))\n\nfn :: jwt ct eq String String => Bool\n      jwt ct eq a b =\n        | (str len a) != (str len b) = False\n        | otherwise = (jwt ct diff a b 0 (str len a) 0) == 0\n```\n\n### 26.4.3. Internal Implementation: Structured Claims Signing & Temporal Validation\n\nObserve how `jwt.ridgun` declares explicit `fn :: ... => ...` contracts first and resolves each case through aligned equations and tail calls:\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: jwt sign claims JwtClaims String => String\n      jwt sign claims c secret =\n        JsonObj [JsonField \"iss\" (JsonStr (issuer c)), JsonField \"sub\" (JsonStr (subject c)), JsonField \"exp\" (JsonInt (expires_at c)), JsonField \"nbf\" (JsonInt (not_before_at c)), JsonField \"custom\" (JsonStr (custom_json c))] -> base_obj\n        jwt sign hs256 (json stringify base_obj) secret\n\nfn :: jwt verify claims String String Int => JwtClaimsRes\n      jwt verify claims token secret now =\n        jwt verify hs256 token secret -> vres\n        jwt validate verified payload vres now\n\nfn :: jwt validate verified payload JwtRes Int => JwtClaimsRes\n      jwt validate verified payload (JwtErr msg) _ = JwtClaimsErr msg\n      jwt validate verified payload (JwtOk pay_str) now = jwt validate parsed claims (json parse pay_str) now\n\nfn :: jwt validate parsed claims JsonRes Int => JwtClaimsRes\n      jwt validate parsed claims (JsonErr msg) _ = JwtClaimsErr (\"invalid claims JSON: \" + msg)\n      jwt validate parsed claims (JsonOk node) now =\n        json get str node \"iss\" \"\" -> iss\n        json get str node \"sub\" \"\" -> sub\n        json get int node \"exp\" 0 -> exp_t\n        json get int node \"nbf\" 0 -> nbf_t\n        json get str node \"custom\" \"\" -> cust\n        jwt check claim times (JwtClaims iss sub exp_t nbf_t cust) now\n\nfn :: jwt check claim times JwtClaims Int => JwtClaimsRes\n      jwt check claim times c now =\n        | (not_before_at c) > 0 and now < (not_before_at c) = JwtClaimsErr \"JWT token not yet valid (nbf)\"\n        | (expires_at c) > 0 and now >= (expires_at c) = JwtClaimsErr \"JWT token expired (exp)\"\n        | otherwise = JwtClaimsOk c\n```\n\n---\n\n## 26.5. Algorithmic Guarantees, `RMM1`/`RMM2` Memory, and the 5 Golden Rules of `jwt`\n\n- **Algorithmic & Safety Guarantee**: Complete immunity to `\"alg\":\"none\"` downgrade attacks (any header where `alg != \"HS256\"` returns `JwtErr`) and constant-time MAC verification.\n- **$O(1)$ Stack Complexity via TCO**: Every recursive loop in `src/main/ridgun/lib/jwt.ridgun` is in tail position, so `ridgunc` compiles them into native jumps with zero stack growth.\n- **Deterministic Memory (`RMM1`/`RMM2`)**: Zero garbage-collector pauses; all intermediate allocations are reclaimed deterministically on scope exit.\n- **Continuous Verification**: Statically checked via `stable check` and tested by the automated suite in `src/test/ridgun/test jwt.ridgun`.\n\n### The 5 Golden Rules When Programming with `jwt`\n\n1. **Declare `import jwt` at the top of your file** and call its functions with spaces, exactly as they are declared, so your code reads like natural prose.\n2. **Align your data pipelines with `=`**: chain `jwt` calls into named intermediate steps and let `stable format` align the columns.\n3. **Leverage `jwt`'s total functions inside `|` guards**: inspect return values or unwrap ADTs via pattern matching rather than assuming external input is valid.\n4. **Avoid cloning large structures when only reading**: remember that under `RMM2`, function input arguments incur zero reference-count overhead (`+0` / `-0`).\n5. **Pair `jwt` with `test` (`import test`)**: always lock in your domain invariants with `assert equals` or `assert true`.\n\n---\n\nIn **Chapter 27**, we will explore the **`socket`** lib in full depth (The `socket` Lib — TCP, UDP, AF_UNIX, Framing, DNS, and `RGF-001` Kernel Sockets).\n"}, {"num": "26", "slug": "27-lib-socket-tcp-udp-dns-and-kernel-sockets", "file": "27-lib-socket-tcp-udp-dns-and-kernel-sockets.md", "title": "Chapter 27: The `socket` Lib — TCP, UDP, AF_UNIX, Framing, DNS, and `RGF-001` Kernel Sockets", "short_title": "The `socket` Lib — TCP, UDP, AF_UNIX, Framing, DNS, and `RGF-001` Kernel Sockets", "markdown": "# Chapter 27: The `socket` Lib — TCP, UDP, AF_UNIX, Framing, DNS, and `RGF-001` Kernel Sockets\n\n## 27.1. Why Does the `socket` Lib Exist? (The Real-World Problem & Ridgun Philosophy)\n\n> *\"Why do I need a `socket` lib written from scratch in pure Ridgun instead of just linking a legacy C library?\"*\n\nThat is the first question every systems engineer asks when meeting `socket`. And the answer captures the entire philosophy of `ridgun-libs`:\n\nLet's be honest: programming BSD sockets in C with `struct sockaddr_in`, `htons`, `inet_pton`, and `getaddrinfo` (which drags in `glibc`'s dynamic `libnss` plugins) is an arcane 1980s ritual.\n\nThe **`socket`** lib provides two complementary zero-C layers: (1) the **`RGF-001`** kernel descriptor API built for production servers like **Solstice** (`sys tcp listen`, `sys tcp listen reuseport`, `sys accept`, `sys tcp connect`, `sys send`, `sys recv`, `sys resolve ipv4` via `/etc/hosts` + RFC 1035 UDP port 53 DNS wire packets) and (2) the immutable functional `Socket` state machine with length-prefixed framing, CRLF line I/O, and CIDR matching.\n\nIn a traditional ecosystem, solving **`SOCK`** tasks means pulling in external C dependencies, wrestling with raw pointers, opaque type conversions, unchecked exceptions, or unpredictable garbage-collector pauses. In Ridgun, the **`socket`** lib (`src/main/ridgun/lib/socket.ridgun`) tackles the problem with four non-negotiable principles:\n\n1. **Declare `import socket` (or `import socket as alias`) at the top of your file**: every lib defines its `module :: socket` namespace, and under `--strict` multi-word functions are always called with natural spaces.\n2. **Chain your data pipelines left-to-right with `->`**: write `input step one -> step two -> result`, use `(+ _ _ +)` sequence masks to destructure tuples/lists, and omit `_ =` on sequential statements (or discard with `-> ()`).\n3. **Tail-Call Optimization (TCO)**: all internal loops in `socket` are tail-recursive and compile into native hardware loops using $O(1)$ stack space.\n4. **Deterministic Memory (`RMM1` / `RMM2`)**: every intermediate allocation is reclaimed at the exact instruction where its last read finishes, with no Garbage Collector.\n\n---\n\n## 27.2. Native Artifacts, Imports, and Complete `socket` API Catalog\n\nIn `ridgun-libs`, **`socket`** is a first-class **lib** located at `src/main/ridgun/lib/socket.ridgun` (domain `SOCK`). We will start with two everyday tabular recipes and then walk through every functional scenario, transformation, and boundary condition verified in `src/test/ridgun/test socket.ridgun`.\n\n### 27.3.1. Example 1: Core Tabular Workflow with `socket`\n\nNotice how in Ridgun the `=` signs and transformation steps using `socket` align into a clean, scannable table without unnecessary mutable variables or hidden side effects:\n\n```ridgun\nimport socket\n\nfn :: eco tcp local => String\n      eco tcp local =\n        sys tcp listen \"127.0.0.1\" 0 16 -> (_ +) -> lfd\n        lfd sys local port -> port\n        sys tcp connect \"127.0.0.1\" port 1000 -> (_ +) -> cfd\n        sys accept lfd 1000 -> a_res\n        a_res sock accept fd -> sfd\n        sys send cfd \"hola-solstice\" 1000 -> ()\n        sys recv sfd 64 1000 -> r_res\n        r_res sock recv data -> datos\n        sys close cfd -> ()\n        sys close sfd -> ()\n        sys close lfd -> ()\n        datos\n```\n\n### 27.3.2. Example 2: Safe Composition and Boundary Handling\n\nEvery function in the `socket` lib is designed to compose cleanly with boolean guards `|` and with the rest of the 38 libs in `ridgun-libs`:\n\n```ridgun\nimport socket\n\nfn :: verificar ip interna String => Bool\n      verificar ip interna ip =\n        ip in cidr ip \"10.0.0.0/8\"\n```\n\n### 27.3.3. Example 3: Typed Addresses (`IPv4`, `IPv6`, `Unix`), Port Validation, and Full Socket Lifecycle (`sock listen`, `accept`, `connect`, `close`)\n\nIn this hands-on walkthrough we thoroughly exercise how `socket` behaves across this functional area, covering standard inputs, parameter combinations, and corner cases:\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: test sock address and lifecycle => ()\n      test sock address and 7) \"sys_resolve_ipv4 invalid hostname -> -7\"\n        dns_q  = sk build dns query \"example.com\"\n        str len dns_q -> assert int equals 29 \"RFC 1035 DNS query length for example.com == 29\"\n        -- Construct an RFC 1035 DNS response packet with 1 A record (93.184.216.34) using 0xC00C name compression\n        dns_hd = (sk raw byte 18) + (sk raw byte 52) + (sk raw byte 129) + (sk raw byte 128) + (sk raw byte 0) + (sk raw byte 1) + (sk raw byte 0) + (sk raw byte 1) + (sk raw byte 0) + (sk raw byte 0) + (sk raw byte 0) + (sk raw byte 0)\n        dns_qn = sk encode qname [\"example\", \"com\"]\n        dns_qt = (sk raw byte 0) + (sk raw byte 1) + (sk raw byte 0) + (sk raw byte 1)\n        dns_an = (sk raw byte 192) + (sk raw byte 12) + (sk raw byte 0) + (sk raw byte 1) + (sk raw byte 0) + (sk raw byte 1) + (sk raw byte 0) + (sk raw byte 0) + (sk raw byte 0) + (sk raw byte 60) + (sk raw byte 0) + (sk raw byte 4) + (sk raw byte 93) + (sk raw byte 184) + (sk raw byte 216) + (sk raw byte 34)\n        dns_ip = sk extract dns ipv4 (dns_hd + dns_qn + dns_qt + dns_an)\n        dns_ip -> assert str eq \"93.184.216.34\" \"sk_extract_dns_ipv4 parses RFC 1035 A record (93.184.216.34)\"\n        c_host = sys tcp connect \"localhost\" lport 500\n        tup2 fst c_host -> assert int equals 0 \"sys_tcp_connect via hostname localhost ok\"\n        a_host = sys accept lfd 500\n        tup3 rc a_host -> assert int equals 0 \"sys_accept from hostname connect ok\"\n        sys close (tup2 snd c_host) -> assert int equals 0 \"close c_host\"\n        sys close (tup3 fd a_host) -> assert int equals 0 \"close a_host\"\n\n        -- 2. Under the Hood: How `socket` Is Built in Pure Ridgun (`src/main/ridgun/lib/socket.ridgun`)\n\nOne of the biggest advantages of `ridgun-libs` is that **there are no C black boxes**. Let's inspect the key building blocks of its real implementation:\n\n### 27.4.1. And the answer captures the entire philosophy of `ridgun-libs`:\n\nLet's be honest: failing to strip `\\r\\n` from HTTP header values invites CRLF header-injection attacks, while linking `libcurl` just to make a clean HTTP/1.1 `GET` or `POST` call is massive overkill.\n\nThe **`http`** lib implements **RFC 3986 URI** parsing, **RFC 9112 HTTP/1.1** request/response wire formatting and parsing with automatic CRLF sanitization (`VUL-INJ-002`) and `Content-Length` injection, `Bearer` token extraction, and a **live kernel-TCP HTTP/1.1 client** (`http get`, `http post`, `http request tcp`).\n\nIn a traditional ecosystem, solving **`HTTP`** tasks means pulling in external C dependencies, wrestling with raw pointers, opaque type conversions, unchecked exceptions, or unpredictable garbage-collector pauses. In Ridgun, the **`http`** lib (`src/main/ridgun/lib/http.ridgun`) tackles the problem with four non-negotiable principles:\n\n1. **Declare `import http` (or `import http as alias`) at the top of your file**: every lib defines its `module :: http` namespace, and under `--strict` multi-word functions are always called with natural spaces.\n2. **Chain your data pipelines left-to-right with `->`**: write `input step one -> step two -> result`, use `(+ _ _ +)` sequence masks to destructure tuples/lists, and omit `_ =` on sequential statements (or discard with `-> ()`).\n3. **Tail-Call Optimization (TCO)**: all internal loops in `http` are tail-recursive and compile into native hardware loops using $O(1)$ stack space.\n4. **Deterministic Memory (`RMM1` / `RMM2`)**: every intermediate allocation is reclaimed at the exact instruction where its last read finishes, with no Garbage Collector.\n\n---\n\n## 28.2. Algorithmic Guarantees, `RMM1`/`RMM2` Memory, and the 5 Golden Rules of `http`\n\n- **Algorithmic & Safety Guarantee**: Automatic stripping of `\\r` and `\\n` across all header keys and values (`http build request`) to prevent HTTP response-splitting attacks.\n- **$O(1)$ Stack Complexity via TCO**: Every recursive loop in `src/main/ridgun/lib/http.ridgun` is in tail position, so `ridgunc` compiles them into native jumps with zero stack growth.\n- **Deterministic Memory (`RMM1`/`RMM2`)**: Zero garbage-collector pauses; all intermediate allocations are reclaimed deterministically on scope exit.\n- **Continuous Verification**: Statically checked via `stable check` and tested by the automated suite in `src/test/ridgun/test http.ridgun`.\n\n### The 5 Golden Rules When Programming with `http`\n\n1. **Declare `import http` at the top of your file** and call its functions with spaces, exactly as they are declared, so your code reads like natural prose.\n2. **Align your data pipelines with `=`**: chain `http` calls into named intermediate steps and let `stable format` align the columns.\n3. **Leverage `http`'s total functions inside `|` guards**: inspect return values or unwrap ADTs via pattern matching rather than assuming external input is valid.\n4. **Avoid cloning large structures when only reading**: remember that under `RMM2`, function input arguments incur zero reference-count overhead (`+0` / `-0`).\n5. **Pair `http` with `test` (`import test`)**: always lock in your domain invariants with `assert equals` or `assert true`.\n\n---\n\nIn **Chapter 29**, we will explore the **`ws`** lib in full depth (The `ws` Lib — RFC 6455 WebSocket Handshake, 16/64-Bit Frame Codec, and XOR Masking).\n"}, {"num": "28", "slug": "29-lib-ws-rfc6455-websocket-protocol", "file": "29-lib-ws-rfc6455-websocket-protocol.md", "title": "Chapter 29: The `ws` Lib — RFC 6455 WebSocket Handshake, 16/64-Bit Frame Codec, and XOR Masking", "short_title": "The `ws` Lib — RFC 6455 WebSocket Handshake, 16/64-Bit Frame Codec, and XOR Masking", "markdown": "# Chapter 29: The `ws` Lib — RFC 6455 WebSocket Handshake, 16/64-Bit Frame Codec, and XOR Masking\n\n## 29.1. Why Does the `ws` Lib Exist? (The Real-World Problem & Ridgun Philosophy)\n\n> *\"Why do I need a `ws` lib written from scratch in pure Ridgun instead of just linking a legacy C library?\"*\n\nThat is the first question every systems engineer asks when meeting `ws`. And the answer captures the entire philosophy of `ridgun-libs`:\n\nLet's be honest: the WebSocket protocol (RFC 6455) combines a SHA-1 + Base64 upgrade handshake with variable-length binary framing (7-bit, 16-bit, or 64-bit) and mandatory client-to-server 4-byte XOR payload masking.\n\nThe **`ws`** lib implements full **RFC 6455** in pure Ridgun: `Sec-WebSocket-Accept` derivation (including a self-contained RFC 3174 SHA-1 solely for the handshake GUID), `101 Switching Protocols` HTTP upgrade builders, 7/16/64-bit `WsFrame` wire encoding/decoding, symmetric 4-byte XOR masking, and text/ping/pong/close frame constructors.\n\nIn a traditional ecosystem, solving **`WS`** tasks means pulling in external C dependencies, wrestling with raw pointers, opaque type conversions, unchecked exceptions, or unpredictable garbage-collector pauses. In Ridgun, the **`ws`** lib (`src/main/ridgun/lib/ws.ridgun`) tackles the problem with four non-negotiable principles:\n\n1. **Declare `import ws` (or `import ws as alias`) at the top of your file**: every lib defines its `module :: ws` namespace, and under `--strict` multi-word functions are always called with natural spaces.\n2. **Chain your data pipelines left-to-right with `->`**: write `input step one -> step two -> result`, use `(+ _ _ +)` sequence masks to destructure tuples/lists, and omit `_ =` on sequential statements (or discard with `-> ()`).\n3. **Tail-Call Optimization (TCO)**: all internal loops in `ws` are tail-recursive and compile into native hardware loops using $O(1)$ stack space.\n4. **Deterministic Memory (`RMM1` / `RMM2`)**: every intermediate allocation is reclaimed at the exact instruction where its last read finishes, with no Garbage Collector.\n\n---\n\n## 29.2. frame w_mhello\n        is ws ok r_mhello -> assert true \"AC2: decode RFC 6455 masked 'Hello'\"\n        f_mhello = unwrap ws frame r_mhello\n        is_masked f_mhello -> assert true \"AC2: masked frame is_masked=true\"\n        payload_text f_mhello -> assert str eq \"Hello\" \"AC2: XOR unmasked text matches 'Hello'\"\n        unwrap ws len r_mhello -> assert int equals 11 \"AC2: consumed 11 bytes\"\n\n        -- Empty payload frame (0 bytes)\n        w_empty = ws encode text \"\"\n        r_empty = ws decode frame w_empty\n        is ws ok r_empty -> assert true \"AC2: decode empty text frame\"\n        payload_text (unwrap ws frame r_empty) -> assert str eq \"\" \"AC2: empty payload_text\"\n        unwrap ws len r_empty -> assert int equals 2 \"AC2: 2-byte header for empty unmasked frame\"\n\n        -- Boundary length 125 (max 7-bit length) vs 126 (min 16-bit extended length)\n        msg_125 = ws repeat str \"A\" 125\n        w_125 = ws encode text msg_125\n        r_125 = ws decode frame w_125\n        unwrap ws len r_125 -> assert int equals 127 \"AC2: 125B payload uses 2B header (127 total)\"\n        payload_text (unwrap ws frame r_125) -> assert str eq msg_125 \"AC2: 125B payload round-trips\"\n\n        msg_126 = ws repeat str \"B\" 126\n        w_126 = ws encode masked text msg_126 mask_rfc\n        r_126 = ws decode frame w_126\n        unwrap ws len r_126 -> assert int equals 134 \"AC2: 126B masked payload uses 4B hdr + 4B mask + 126B (134 total)\"\n        payload_text (unwrap ws frame r_126) -> assert str eq msg_126 \"AC2: 126B payload round-trips\"\n\n        -- Control frames: Ping (9), Pong (10), Close (8)\n        w_ping = ws encode ping (ws bytes of [1, 2, 3])\n        f_ping = unwrap ws frame (ws decode frame w_ping)\n        ws_opcode f_ping -> assert int equals 9 \"AC2: ping opcode=9\"\n        ws bytes eq (payload_bytes f_ping) [1, 2, 3] -> assert true \"AC2: ping payload bytes\"\n\n        w_pong = ws encode pong (ws bytes of [4, 5])\n big-endian [0x03, 0xE8]\"\n        ()\n```\n\n### 29.3.5. 29.5. Algorithmic Guarantees, `RMM1`/`RMM2` Memory, and the 5 Golden Rules of `ws`\n\n- **Algorithmic & Safety Guarantee**: Exact match with the official RFC 6455 handshake vector (`\"dGhlIHNhbXBsZSBub25jZQ==\"` $\\rightarrow$ `\"s3pPLMBiTxaQ9kYGzzhZRbK+xOo=\"`) and automatic XOR unmasking in `ws decode frame`.\n- **$O(1)$ Stack Complexity via TCO**: Every recursive loop in `src/main/ridgun/lib/ws.ridgun` is in tail position, so `ridgunc` compiles them into native jumps with zero stack growth.\n- **Deterministic Memory (`RMM1`/`RMM2`)**: Zero garbage-collector pauses; all intermediate allocations are reclaimed deterministically on scope exit.\n- **Continuous Verification**: Statically checked via `stable check` and tested by the automated suite in `src/test/ridgun/test ws.ridgun`.\n\n### The 5 Golden Rules When Programming with `ws`\n\n1. **Declare `import ws` at the top of your file** and call its functions with spaces, exactly as they are declared, so your code reads like natural prose.\n2. **Align your data pipelines with `=`**: chain `ws` calls into named intermediate steps and let `stable format` align the columns.\n3. **Leverage `ws`'s total functions inside `|` guards**: inspect return values or unwrap ADTs via pattern matching rather than assuming external input is valid.\n4. **Avoid cloning large structures when only reading**: remember that under `RMM2`, function input arguments incur zero reference-count overhead (`+0` / `-0`).\n5. **Pair `ws` with `test` (`import test`)**: always lock in your domain invariants with `assert equals` or `assert true`.\n\n---\n\nIn **Chapter 30**, we will explore the **`agent`** lib in full depth (The `agent` Lib — Native Actor Concurrency (`agent`, `send`, `receive`), Request-Reply Combinators, and Counter, Log and Key-Value Agents).\n"}, {"num": "29", "slug": "30-lib-agent-native-actor-concurrency", "file": "30-lib-agent-native-actor-concurrency.md", "title": "Chapter 30: The `agent` Lib — Native Actor Concurrency (`agent`, `send`, `receive`), Request-Reply Combinators, and Counter, Log and Key-Value Agents", "short_title": "The `agent` Lib — Native Actor Concurrency (`agent`, `send`, `receive`), Request-Reply Combinators, and Counter, Log and Key-Value Agents", "markdown": "# Chapter 30: The `agent` Lib — Native Actor Concurrency (`agent`, `send`, `receive`), Request-Reply Combinators, and Counter, Log and Key-Value Agents\n\n## 30.1. Why Does the `agent` Lib Exist? (The Real-World Problem & Ridgun Philosophy)\n\n> *\"Why do I need a `agent` lib written from scratch in pure Ridgun instead of just linking a legacy C library?\"*\n\nThat is the first question every systems engineer asks when meeting `agent`. And the answer captures the entire philosophy of `ridgun-libs`:\n\nLet's be honest: sharing mutable state across threads with `Mutex`, `RwLock`, and condition variables is an endless factory of deadlocks and race conditions.\n\nThe **`agent`** lib builds on Ridgun's **Native Agent Model** (`agent`, `send ... to`, `receive from`, `try receive from`, `stop`) to provide request-reply combinators, blocking, non-blocking or bounded by a timeout (`agent ask`, `agent try ask`, `ask int with timeout`), batch dispatch and draining (`agent send batch`, `agent map batch`, `agent drain ready`), lifecycle inspection (`is agent alive`, `agent status`, `stop agent`), and three ready-made stateful agents: a counter, an append-only log and an in-memory key-value store.\n\nIn a traditional ecosystem, solving **`AGENT`** tasks means pulling in external C dependencies, wrestling with raw pointers, opaque type conversions, unchecked exceptions, or unpredictable garbage-collector pauses. In Ridgun, the **`agent`** lib (`src/main/ridgun/lib/agent.ridgun`) tackles the problem with four non-negotiable principles:\n\n1. **Declare `import agent` (or `import agent as alias`) at the top of your file**: every lib defines its `module :: agent` namespace, and under `--strict` multi-word functions are always called with natural spaces.\n2. **Chain your data pipelines left-to-right with `->`**: write `input step one -> step two -> result`, use `(+ _ _ +)` sequence masks to destructure tuples/lists, and omit `_ =` on sequential statements (or discard with `-> ()`).\n3. **Tail-Call Optimization (TCO)**: all internal loops in `agent` are tail-recursive and compile into native hardware loops using $O(1)$ stack space.\n4. **Deterministic Memory (`RMM1` / `RMM2`)**: every intermediate allocation is reclaimed at the exact instruction where its last read finishes, with no Garbage Collector.\n\n---\n\n## 30.2. Native Artifacts, Imports, and Complete `agent` API Catalog\n\nIn `ridgun-libs`, **`agent`** is a first-class **lib** located at `src/main/ridgun/lib/agent.ridgun` (domain `AGENT`). When built with `stable bundle`, it compiles into one native artifact:\n\n| Artifact | Path | Purpose |\n|---|---|---|\n| **Ridgun Bundle** | `target/bundles/agent.ridgunlib` | Portable distribution and direct `import agent` resolution |\n\n> Every lib declares its own namespace via `module :: agent`: simply write `import agent` (or `import agent as alias`) at the top and call its functions with natural spaces (`my fn x`) and left-to-right `->` pipelines (`x my fn -> result`).\n\n### 30.2.1. Summary of `agent` Functional Families\n\n| Signature / Function / Type | Purpose & Usage |\n|---|---|\n| `agent ask / agent try ask / ask int / ask str / ask int with timeout / ask str with timeout` | Request-reply with an agent: blocking, non-blocking or bounded by a timeout |\n| `agent send batch / agent map batch / agent receive count / agent drain ready / relay int / relay str` | Send a batch of messages, collect the replies and relay a result from one agent to another |\n| `is agent alive / agent status / stop agent / agent stop all` | Lifecycle inspection and orderly stop, with a typed `AgentStatus` |\n| `new counter agent / counter add / counter get / counter reset` | A counter kept inside an agent |\n| `new log agent / log append / log read / log clear` | An append-only log kept inside an agent |\n| `new kv agent / agent kv put / agent kv get / agent kv delete / agent kv has / agent kv count / agent kv keys / agent kv clear` | An in-memory key-value store kept inside an agent |\n\n### 30.2.2. Algorithmic Guarantees, `RMM1`/`RMM2` Memory, and the 5 Golden Rules of `agent`\n\n- **Algorithmic & Safety Guarantee**: Zero shared mutable memory across actors: every message is transferred by value / Copy-on-Write and `stop` deterministically reclaims the actor's region.\n- **$O(1)$ Stack Complexity via TCO**: Every recursive loop in `src/main/ridgun/lib/agent.ridgun` is in tail position, so `ridgunc` compiles them into native jumps with zero stack growth.\n- **Deterministic Memory (`RMM1`/`RMM2`)**: Zero garbage-collector pauses;
