Why Does the `pool` Lib Exist? (The Real-World Problem & Ridgun Philosophy)\n\n> *\"Why do I need a `pool` lib written from scratch in pure Ridgun instead of just linking a legacy C library?\"*\n\nThat is the first question every systems engineer asks when meeting `pool`. And the answer captures the entire philosophy of `ridgun-libs`:\n\nLet's be honest: when every request for the same user or the same key must reach the same worker, and now and then one message must reach all of them, writing that routing and the orderly stop by hand in every program is repetitive and easy to get wrong.\n\nThe **`pool`** lib groups a fixed number of agents into an `AgentPool`: `pool ask shard` sends each request to the agent chosen by its key, so the same key always reaches the same agent; `pool broadcast` sends one message to every agent; `pool drain all` collects, without blocking, the replies that are ready; and `pool shutdown` stops all of them.\n\nIn a traditional ecosystem, solving **`AGENT`** tasks means pulling in external C dependencies, wrestling with raw pointers, opaque type conversions, unchecked exceptions, or unpredictable garbage-collector pauses. In Ridgun, the **`pool`** lib (`src/main/ridgun/lib/pool.ridgun`) tackles the problem with four non-negotiable principles:\n\n1. **Declare `import pool` (or `import pool as alias`) at the top of your file**: every lib defines its `module :: pool` namespace, and under `--strict` multi-word functions are always called with natural spaces.\n2. **Chain your data pipelines left-to-right with `->`**: write `input step one -> step two -> result`, use `(+ _ _ +)` sequence masks to destructure tuples/lists, and omit `_ =` on sequential statements (or discard with `-> ()`).\n3. **Tail-Call Optimization (TCO)**: all internal loops in `pool` are tail-recursive and compile into native hardware loops using $O(1)$ stack space.\n4. **Deterministic Memory (`RMM1` / `RMM2`)**: every intermediate allocation is reclaimed at the exact instruction where its last read finishes, with no Garbage Collector.\n\n---\n\n## 31.2. Under the Hood: How `pool` Is Built in Pure Ridgun (`src/main/ridgun/lib/pool.ridgun`)\n\nOne of the biggest advantages of `ridgun-libs` is that **there are no C black boxes**. You can open `src/main/ridgun/lib/pool.ridgun` and read exactly how every operation is implemented using pattern matching, `|` / `|.` guard trees, and tail-call optimization (TCO). Let's inspect the key building blocks of its real implementation:\n\n### 31.4.1. Internal Implementation: Pool Size, Agent Selection, and Request-Reply by Key\n\nObserve how `pool.ridgun` declares explicit `fn :: ... => ...` contracts first and resolves each case through aligned equations and tail calls:\n\n```ridgun\nmodule :: pool\n\ntype AgentPool = Pool Int [Agent]\n\nfn :: pool size AgentPool   => Int\n      pool size (Pool sz _) =  sz\n\nfn :: pool agents AgentPool    => [Agent]\n      pool agents (Pool _ ags) =  ags\n\n-- Look up the i-th agent in a pool (0-indexed)\nfn :: pool get agent [Agent]  Int => Agent\n      pool get agent (ag:_)   0   =  ag\n      pool get agent (_:rest) idx =  pool get agent rest (idx - 1)\n\nfn :: pool abs Int => Int\n      pool abs x\n        | x < 0     = 0 - x\n        | otherwise = x\n\n-- Route a message to a deterministic shard `key_hash % size` and return the reply via `ask`\nfn :: pool ask shard AgentPool Int A => B\n      pool ask shard (Pool size agents) key_hash msg =\n        (pool abs key_hash) % size -> shard_idx\n        pool get agent agents shard_idx -> target_ag\n        ask target_ag msg\n```\n\n### 31.4.2. Internal Implementation: Broadcast, Non-Blocking Drain, and Shutdown\n\nObserve how `pool.ridgun` declares explicit `fn :: ... => ...` contracts first and resolves each case through aligned equations and tail calls:\n\n```ridgun\n-- Broadcast a message to every agent in the pool (e.g. configuration reload or tick)\nfn :: pool broadcast AgentPool       A   => ()\n      pool broadcast (Pool _ agents) msg =  pool broadcast list agents msg\n\nfn :: pool send one Agent A => ()\n      pool send one ag    m =\n        send m to ag\n\nfn :: pool broadcast list [Agent]   A   => ()\n      pool broadcast list []        _   =  ()\n      pool broadcast list (ag:rest) msg =\n        pool send one ag msg -> ()\n        pool broadcast list rest msg\n\nfn :: pool drain ready Agent => [B]\n      pool drain ready ag    =  pool drain ready loop ag []\n\nfn :: pool drain ready loop Agent [B] => [B]\n      pool drain ready loop ag acc =\n        pool drain step ag (try receive from ag) acc\n\nfn :: pool drain step Agent Option [B] => [B]\n      pool drain step _ None acc = acc\n      pool drain step ag (Some r) acc = pool drain ready loop ag (acc :: [r])\n\n-- Drain all ready responses across all shards in the pool (non-blocking)\nfn :: pool drain all AgentPool       => [B]\n      pool drain all (Pool _ agents) =  pool drain list agents []\n\nfn :: pool drain list [Agent]   [B] => [B]\n      pool drain list []        acc =  acc\n      pool drain list (ag:rest) acc =\n        ag pool drain ready -> ready\n        pool drain list rest (acc :: ready)\n\nfn :: pool stop list [Agent]   => ()\n      pool stop list []        =  ()\n      pool stop list (ag:rest) =\n        stop ag\n        pool stop list rest\n\n-- Stop all agents in the pool and reclaim their isolated state\nfn :: pool shutdown AgentPool       => ()\n      pool shutdown (Pool _ agents) =  pool stop list agents\n```\n\n---\n\n## 31.5. Algorithmic Guarantees, `RMM1`/`RMM2` Memory, and the 5 Golden Rules of `pool`\n\n- **Algorithmic & Safety Guarantee**: The number of agents is fixed when the pool is built, so the memory of the pool is bounded, and routing by `abs(key) % size` is deterministic: the same key always reaches the same agent.\n- **$O(1)$ Stack Complexity via TCO**: Every recursive loop in `src/main/ridgun/lib/pool.ridgun` is in tail position, so `ridgunc` compiles them into native jumps with zero stack growth.\n- **Deterministic Memory (`RMM1`/`RMM2`)**: Zero garbage-collector pauses; all intermediate allocations are reclaimed deterministically on scope exit.\n- **Continuous Verification**: Statically checked via `stable check` and tested by the automated suite in `src/test/ridgun/test pool.ridgun`.\n\n### The 5 Golden Rules When Programming with `pool`\n\n1. **Declare `import pool` at the top of your file** and call its functions with spaces, exactly as they are declared, so your code reads like natural prose.\n2. **Align your data pipelines with `=`**: chain `pool` calls into named intermediate steps and let `stable format` align the columns.\n3. **Leverage `pool`'s total functions inside `|` guards**: inspect return values or unwrap ADTs via pattern matching rather than assuming external input is valid.\n4. **Avoid cloning large structures when only reading**: remember that under `RMM2`, function input arguments incur zero reference-count overhead (`+0` / `-0`).\n5. **Pair `pool` with `test` (`import test`)**: always lock in your domain invariants with `assert equals` or `assert true`.\n\n---\n\nIn **Chapter 32**, we will explore the **`net_agent`** lib in full depth (The `net_agent` Lib — One Agent per Connection: Non-Blocking Polling and Reactor Sweep).\n"}, {"num": "31", "slug": "32-lib-net-agent-one-agent-per-connection-and-reactor", "file": "32-lib-net-agent-one-agent-per-connection-and-reactor.md", "title": "Chapter 32: The `net_agent` Lib — One Agent per Connection: Non-Blocking Polling and Reactor Sweep", "short_title": "The `net_agent` Lib — One Agent per Connection: Non-Blocking Polling and Reactor Sweep", "markdown": "# Chapter 32: The `net_agent` Lib — One Agent per Connection: Non-Blocking Polling and Reactor Sweep\n\n## 32.1. Why Does the `net_agent` Lib Exist? (The Real-World Problem & Ridgun Philosophy)\n\n> *\"Why do I need a `net_agent` lib written from scratch in pure Ridgun instead of just linking a legacy C library?\"*\n\nThat is the first question every systems engineer asks when meeting `net_agent`. And the answer captures the entire philosophy of `ridgun-libs`:\n\nLet's be honest: in a server, accepting TCP connections is the easy part; the hard part is keeping the state of each connection apart, reading and writing without blocking the others, and closing every descriptor and stopping every agent when a connection ends.\n\nThe **`net_agent`** lib closes the loop of `ridgun-libs` by uniting **`posix`**, **`socket`**, and **`agent`**: a `ConnSlot` pairs a connection descriptor with the agent that holds its state; `conn poll step` polls the descriptor without blocking, passes what arrives to the agent and writes its reply back; `reactor sweep` does that for a whole table of connections and drops the closed ones; and `reactor shutdown` closes every descriptor and stops every agent.\n\nIn a traditional ecosystem, solving **`AGENT`** tasks means pulling in external C dependencies, wrestling with raw pointers, opaque type conversions, unchecked exceptions, or unpredictable garbage-collector pauses. In Ridgun, the **`net_agent`** lib (`src/main/ridgun/lib/net_agent.ridgun`) tackles the problem with four non-negotiable principles:\n\n1. **Declare `import net_agent` (or `import net_agent as alias`) at the top of your file**: every lib defines its `module :: net agent` namespace, and under `--strict` multi-word functions are always called with natural spaces.\n2. **Chain your data pipelines left-to-right with `->`**: write `input step one -> step two -> result`, use `(+ _ _ +)` sequence masks to destructure tuples/lists, and omit `_ =` on sequential statements (or discard with `-> ()`).\n3. **Tail-Call Optimization (TCO)**: all internal loops in `net_agent` are tail-recursive and compile into native hardware loops using $O(1)$ stack space.\n4. **Deterministic Memory (`RMM1` / `RMM2`)**: every intermediate allocation is reclaimed at the exact instruction where its last read finishes, with no Garbage Collector.\n\n---\n\n## 32.2. Native Artifacts, Imports, and Complete `net_agent` API Catalog\n\nIn `ridgun-libs`, **`net_agent`** is a first-class **lib** located at `src/main/ridgun/lib/net_agent.ridgun` (domain `AGENT`). When built with `stable bundle`, it compiles into one native artifact:\n\n| Artifact | Path | Purpose |\n|---|---|---|\n| **Ridgun Bundle** | `target/bundles/net_agent.ridgunlib` | Portable distribution and direct `import net_agent` resolution |\n\n> Every lib declares its own namespace via `module :: net agent`: simply write `import net_agent` (or `import net_agent as alias`) at the top and call its functions with natural spaces (`my fn x`) and left-to-right `->` pipelines (`x my fn -> result`).\n\n### 32.2.1. Summary of `net_agent` Functional Families\n\n| Signature / Function / Type | Purpose & Usage |\n|---|---|\n| `ConnSlot / StepOutcome` | A connection descriptor with its agent, and the result of one step: `ConnKeep` or `ConnClosed` |\n| `conn poll step` | Poll one connection without blocking, pass what arrives to its agent and send the reply |\n| `reactor sweep` | One step over every connection of a table; the closed ones leave it |\n| `reactor shutdown` | Close every descriptor and stop every agent |\n\n### 32.2.2. 2) \"no data: the client receives nothing\"\n\n        s1 = sys send cfd \"ping\" 500\n        sock rc s1 -> assert int equals 0 \"client sends ping\"\n        step until reply slot cfd 50 -> assert str eq \"keep:echo:1:ping\" \"the data reaches the agent and its reply is written\"\n        sock recv data (sys recv cfd 64 500) -> assert str eq \"echo:1:ping\" \"the client reads the reply\"\n\n        s2 = sys send cfd \"pong\" 500\n        sock rc s2 -> assert int equals 0 \"client sends pong\"\n        step until reply slot cfd 50 -> assert str eq \"keep:echo:2:pong\" \"the agent keeps the state of its connection\"\n        sock recv data (sys recv cfd 64 500) -> assert str eq \"echo:2:pong\" \"the client reads the second reply\"\n\n        agent list len (reactor sweep [slot]) 0 -> assert int equals 1 \"reactor sweep keeps a live connection\"\n        is agent alive ag -> assert true \"the agent of a live connection is running\"\n\n        sys close cfd\n        sys poll sfd 1 500 -> closed_ev\n        agent list len (reactor sweep [slot]) 0 -> assert int equals 0 \"reactor sweep drops a connection closed by the peer\"\n        is agent alive ag -> assert false \"the agent stops when its connection closes\"\n        sys close lfd\n        ()\n```\n\n### 32.3.8. t0\n        took < 5000 -> assert true \"the step returns after the write timeout instead of blocking\"\n        is agent alive ag2 -> assert false \"the agent of the closed connection is stopped\"\n        agent list len (reactor sweep []) 0 -> assert int equals 0 \"an empty table stays empty\"\n        sys close c2\n        sys close lfd\n        ()\n```\n\n---\n\n## 32.4. Under the Hood: How `net_agent` Is Built in Pure Ridgun (`src/main/ridgun/lib/net_agent.ridgun`)\n\nOne of the biggest advantages of `ridgun-libs` is that **there are no C black boxes**. You can open `src/main/ridgun/lib/net_agent.ridgun` and read exactly how every operation is implemented using pattern matching, `|` / `|.` guard trees, and tail-call optimization (TCO). Let's inspect the key building blocks of its real implementation:\n\n### 32.4.1. Internal Implementation: One Step of a Connection: Poll, Pass to the Agent, Write the Reply\n\nObserve how `net_agent.ridgun` declares explicit `fn :: ... => ...` contracts first and resolves each case through aligned equations and tail calls:\n\n```ridgun\nmodule :: net_agent\n\ntype ConnSlot = ConnSlot Int Agent\n\ntype StepOutcome = ConnKeep ConnSlot String | ConnClosed\n\n-- Poll a single connection fd (non-blocking, timeout = 0) and route incoming data to its Agent\nfn :: conn poll step ConnSlot         => StepOutcome\n      conn poll step (ConnSlot fd ag) =\n        sys poll fd 1 0 -> ev\n        conn handle event fd ag ev\n\nfn :: conn handle event Int Agent Int => StepOutcome\n      conn handle event fd ag ev\n        | ev < 0 =\n          -- Poll error: close descriptor and stop agent\n          sys close fd\n          stop ag\n          ConnClosed\n        | ev >= 8 =\n          -- POLLERR (8) or POLLHUP (16): peer disconnected\n          sys close fd\n          stop ag\n          ConnClosed\n        | ev == 0 =\n          -- No new bytes to read; check if the agent has a queued async reply\n      conn drain outbound fd ag (try receive from ag)\n        | otherwise =\n          -- POLLIN (1): read frame and forward to the connection's stateful agent\n          payload = sys read fd fd 65536\n          conn feed payload fd ag payload\n\nfn :: conn feed payload Int Agent String => StepOutcome\n      conn feed payload fd ag \"\" =\n        -- EOF on socket: close descriptor and stop agent deterministically\n        sys close fd -> ()\n        stop ag\n        ConnClosed\n      conn feed payload fd ag data =\n        send data to ag\n        conn drain outbound fd ag (try receive from ag)\n\nfn :: conn cast str A => String\n      conn cast str x =  x\n\n-- The longest a step waits for a peer to take a reply (milliseconds).\nfn :: conn write timeout ms => Int\n      conn write timeout ms =  1000\n\nfn :: conn drain outbound Int Agent Option => StepOutcome\n      conn drain outbound fd ag None = ConnKeep (ConnSlot fd ag) \"\"\n      conn drain outbound fd ag (Some resp) =\n        resp conn cast str -> s\n        conn after write fd ag s (sys send fd s (conn write timeout ms))\n\n-- The reply is written whole or the connection is closed: a peer that does not read\n-- cannot hold the reactor longer than `conn write timeout ms`, and never gets a cut reply.\nfn :: conn after write Int Agent String (Int Int) => StepOutcome\n      conn after write fd ag s (rc, sent) =\n        | rc == 0 and sent == (str len s) = ConnKeep (ConnSlot fd ag) s\n        | otherwise =\n          sys close fd -> ()\n          stop ag\n          ConnClosed\n```\n\n### 32.4.2. Internal Implementation: Reactor Sweep and Shutdown\n\nObserve how `net_agent.ridgun` declares explicit `fn :: ... => ...` contracts first and resolves each case through aligned equations and tail calls:\n\n```ridgun\n-- Sweep an entire connection table, pruning closed connections and keeping active ones\nfn :: reactor sweep [ConnSlot]  => [ConnSlot]\n      reactor sweep []          =  []\n      reactor sweep (slot:rest) =\n        slot conn poll step -> outcome\n        rest reactor sweep -> kept\n        reactor sweep next outcome kept\n\nfn :: reactor sweep next StepOutcome       [ConnSlot] => [ConnSlot]\n      reactor sweep next ConnClosed        kept       =  kept\n      reactor sweep next (ConnKeep slot _) kept       =  [slot] :: kept\n\n-- Gracefully close all sockets and stop all connection agents on server shutdown\nfn :: reactor shutdown [ConnSlot] => ()\n      reactor shutdown []         =  ()\n      reactor shutdown ((ConnSlot fd ag):rest) =\n        sys close fd -> ()\n        stop ag\n        reactor shutdown rest\n```\n\n---\n\n## 32.5. Algorithmic Guarantees, `RMM1`/`RMM2` Memory, and the 5 Golden Rules of `net_agent`\n\n- **Algorithmic & Safety Guarantee**: A connection that is closed or fails leaves the table on the sweep that sees it, with its descriptor closed and its agent stopped, and `reactor shutdown` does the same for all the rest, so no descriptor and no agent is leaked.\n- **$O(1)$ Stack Complexity via TCO**: Every recursive loop in `src/main/ridgun/lib/net_agent.ridgun` is in tail position, so `ridgunc` compiles them into native jumps with zero stack growth.\n- **Deterministic Memory (`RMM1`/`RMM2`)**: Zero garbage-collector pauses; all intermediate allocations are reclaimed deterministically on scope exit.\n- **Continuous Verification**: Statically checked via `stable check` and tested by the automated suite in `src/test/ridgun/test net_agent.ridgun`.\n\n### The 5 Golden Rules When Programming with `net_agent`\n\n1. **Declare `import net_agent` at the top of your file** and call its functions with spaces, exactly as they are declared, so your code reads like natural prose.\n2. **Align your data pipelines with `=`**: chain `net_agent` calls into named intermediate steps and let `stable format` align the columns.\n3. **Leverage `net_agent`'s total functions inside `|` guards**: inspect return values or unwrap ADTs via pattern matching rather than assuming external input is valid.\n4. **Avoid cloning large structures when only reading**: remember that under `RMM2`, function input arguments incur zero reference-count overhead (`+0` / `-0`).\n5. **Pair `net_agent` with `test` (`import test`)**: always lock in your domain invariants with `assert equals` or `assert true`.\n\n---\n\nIn **Chapter 33**, we will explore the **`ai`** lib in full depth (The `ai` lib — AI Agents, Tool Calling, SSE Streaming, Bounded ReAct, Guardrails, Mini-RAG & MCP).\n"}, {"num": "32", "slug": "33-lib-ai-ai-agents-tools-streaming-rag-and-mcp", "file": "33-lib-ai-ai-agents-tools-streaming-rag-and-mcp.md", "title": "Chapter 33: The `ai` lib — AI Agents, Tool Calling, SSE Streaming, Bounded ReAct, Guardrails, Mini-RAG & MCP", "short_title": "The `ai` lib — AI Agents, Tool Calling, SSE Streaming, Bounded ReAct, Guardrails, Mini-RAG & MCP", "markdown": "# Chapter 33: The `ai` lib — AI Agents, Tool Calling, SSE Streaming, Bounded ReAct, Guardrails, Mini-RAG & MCP\n\n## 33.1. (Real-World AI Engineering in Pure Ridgun)\n\nIn Ridgun, `agent` is the language-level actor concurrency primitive, whereas **`ai`** (`src/main/ridgun/lib/ai.ridgun`, domain `AI`) provides the complete, 100% pure-Ridgun cognitive and protocol layer for building **production AI Agents**:\n\n1. **Immutable Conversations, `...` Separation & Context Compaction (`ai compact conv`)**: reasoning models (*DeepSeek-R1*, *Qwen-QwQ*, *Claude Thinking*) emit `` blocks that should be separated from visible replies and stripped from subsequent turns (`ai split thinking`, `ai strip thinking`, `ai trim context`, `ai compact conv`).\n2. **Declarative Tool Schemas (`AiTool`) & Multi-Provider Codecs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Ollama & XML ``)**: define tools once with `ai tool` and `ai param`, validate tool call arguments before execution with `ai validate tool call`, and encode/decode OpenAI, Anthropic, Ollama, and local XML `` payloads.\n3. **Incremental SSE Streaming (`AiStreamAcc`) & Structured Output Self-Repair (`ai extract json`, `ai build repair prompt`)**: parse Server-Sent Events (`data:` lines and `[DONE]`), reassemble streamed text/reasoning/tool-call deltas, extract balanced JSON from dirty Markdown fences, and generate self-repair prompts on schema failure.\n4. **Bounded ReAct State Machine (`AiPolicy`, `ai step`), Deterministic Replay Cache (`ai replay lookup`), Security Guardrails (`ai wrap untrusted`, `ai has injection pattern`, `ai scrub secrets`), In-Memory Mini-RAG (`ai retrieve top k`), Multi-Agent Handoff & MCP JSON-RPC 2.0 (`ai mcp tools call req`)**.\n\n---\n\n## 33.2. Int, au_completion: Int, au_total: Int\ntype AiConv         = ac_system: String, ac_msgs: [AiMsg], ac_steps: Int, ac_usage: AiUsage\ntype AiParam        = ap_name: String, ap_type: String, ap_desc: String, ap_req: Bool\ntype AiTool         = at_name: String, at_desc: String, at_params: [AiParam]\ntype AiToolCall     = atc_id: String, atc_name: String, atc_args: String\ntype AiTurn         = String, asa_done: Bool\ntype AiPolicy       = apol_max_steps: Int, apol_max_tokens: Int, apol_allowed: [String]\ntype AiStepDecision = AiDecisionDone String | AiDecisionRunTools [AiToolCall] |     ai split thinking \"Let me analyze the bounds.The answer is 42.\" -> sp\n        assert str eq (fst str sp) \"Let me analyze the bounds.\" \"AC1: extracted  reasoning block\"\n        assert str eq (snd str sp) \"The answer is 42.\" \"AC1: extracted clean visible reply\"\n        assert str eq (ai strip thinking \"internalVisible out\") \"Visible out\" \"AC1: ai strip thinking removes reasoning block\"\n\n        ai estimate tokens \"12345678\" -> tok8\n        assert true (tok8 > 0) \"AC1: token estimation positive for non-empty text\"\n        assert equals (ai estimate tokens \"\") 0 \"AC1: token estimation 0 for empty text\"\n\n        ai conv tokens c4 -> total_conv_tok\n        assert true (total_conv_tok > 10) \"AC1: conversation token budget includes system and messages\"\n\n        ai trim context c4 18 -> c_trimmed\n        assert str eq (ac_system c_trimmed) \"You are a strict coding agent.\" \"AC1: trim context preserves system prompt\"\n        assert true ((count msgs (ac_msgs c_trimmed) 0) < 4) \"AC1: trim context drops oldest messages to fit budget\"\n\n        ai compact conv c4 \"User asked for a parser and tool 1 succeeded.\" 1 -> assert true ((ai find sub (am_content sum_msg) \"\" 0) >= 0) \"AC1: compacted message contains \"\n        ()\n```\n\n### 33.3.2. step_over_tok\n        assert true (dec is abort (step dec step_over_tok)) \"AC6: exceeding max_tokens aborts ReAct loop\"\n        assert str eq (dec text (step dec step_over_tok)) \"max_tokens budget exceeded\" \"AC6: max_tokens diagnostic\"\n\n        AiReply \"quietClean final answer\" (AiUsage 10 15 25) -> turn_done\n        ai step c0 turn_done pol -> step_done\n        assert true (dec Why does the `locale` lib exist? (Pure-Ridgun CLDR Internationalization)\n\nIn systems programming, C's `setlocale()` mutates process-wide global state across threads, while linking `libicu` adds tens of megabytes of C++ dependencies. The **`locale`** lib (`src/main/ridgun/lib/locale.ridgun`, domain `LOCALE`) brings deterministic **Unicode CLDR 46** rules and Howard Hinnant's $O(1)$ civil calendar directly into pure Ridgun:\n\n1. **Dual-Mode CLDR Cardinal Plural Rules (`.po`-compatible 2-form default + strict CLDR 46 `\"many\"`)**: `plural category`, `plural categories`, and `plural index` provide the 2-form `[\"one\", \"other\"]` mode expected by Gettext `.po` catalogs for Western European locales (`es`, `ca`, `gl`, `eu`, `en`, `pt`, `sv`, `it`, `de`, `nl`), French `0/1 -> \"one\"`, 3-form Slavic rules (`ru`, `uk`, `pl`), 6-form Arabic rules (`ar`), and invariant East Asian rules (`ja`, `zh`, `ko`), while `plural category cldr` and `plural categories cldr` expose strict CLDR 46 `\"many\"` for exact millions (`1000000`, `2000000`...) in `es`, `ca`, `pt`, `it`, and `fr`.\n2. **UTC Date & Datetime Formatting (`format date`, `format datetime`, `month name`, `weekday name`)**: converts Unix epoch seconds in $O(1)$ into `short`, `medium`, `long`, and `full` locale patterns.\n3. **Locale-Aware Integer & Decimal Formatting (`format int`, `format decimal`)**: thousands grouping and half-away-from-zero decimal rounding.\n4. **Native Language Autonyms (`language name`) & BCP-47 / POSIX Tag Normalization (`normalize locale`)** with deterministic fallback to `\"en\"`.\n\n---\n\n## 34.2. Algorithmic Guarantees and `RMM1`/`RMM2` Memory\n\n- **Algorithmic & safety guarantee**: 100% pure functions with zero global mutable locale state, $O(1)$ proleptic Gregorian UTC calendar conversion, and deterministic fallback to `\"en\"`.\n- **Continuous verification**: Verified by `src/test/ridgun/test locale.ridgun`.\n\n---\n\nIn **Chapter 35**, we will explore the **`hash`** lib in full depth (The `hash` Lib — SipHash-1-3 Keyed Hashing for Hash Tables).\n"}, {"num": "34", "slug": "35-lib-hash-siphash-keyed-hashing", "file": "35-lib-hash-siphash-keyed-hashing.md", "title": "Chapter 35: The `hash` Lib — SipHash-1-3 Keyed Hashing for Hash Tables", "short_title": "The `hash` Lib — SipHash-1-3 Keyed Hashing for Hash Tables", "markdown": "# Chapter 35: The `hash` Lib — SipHash-1-3 Keyed Hashing for Hash Tables\n\n## 35.1. Why Does the `hash` Lib Exist? (The Real-World Problem & Ridgun Philosophy)\n\n> *\"Why do I need a `hash` lib written from scratch in pure Ridgun instead of just linking a legacy C library?\"*\n\nThat is the first question every systems engineer asks when meeting `hash`. And the answer captures the entire philosophy of `ridgun-libs`:\n\nLet's be honest: when the hash function of a hash table is public, whoever controls the keys can send thousands that land in the same slot, and one request then costs what a million should (hash flooding).\n\nThe **`hash`** lib implements **SipHash-1-3** (Aumasson & Bernstein) with a 128-bit key and a 64-bit result. `siphash13` hashes a whole string; the compiler's native operations `siphash13 range` and `siphash13 range low` (ridgunc 1.0.44) hash a range of bytes in some tens of nanoseconds; `siphash13 reference` is the same hash written in plain Ridgun, to read and to test against; and `siphash new key` draws a random 16-byte key from the system.\n\nIn a traditional ecosystem, solving **`HASH`** tasks means pulling in external C dependencies, wrestling with raw pointers, opaque type conversions, unchecked exceptions, or unpredictable garbage-collector pauses. In Ridgun, the **`hash`** lib (`src/main/ridgun/lib/hash.ridgun`) tackles the problem with four non-negotiable principles:\n\n1. **Declare `import hash` (or `import hash as alias`) at the top of your file**: every lib defines its `module :: hash` namespace, and under `--strict` multi-word functions are always called with natural spaces.\n2. **Chain your data pipelines left-to-right with `->`**: write `input step one -> step two -> result`, use `(+ _ _ +)` sequence masks to destructure tuples/lists, and omit `_ =` on sequential statements (or discard with `-> ()`).\n3. **Tail-Call Optimization (TCO)**: all internal loops in `hash` are tail-recursive and compile into native hardware loops using $O(1)$ stack space.\n4. **Deterministic Memory (`RMM1` / `RMM2`)**: every intermediate allocation is reclaimed at the exact instruction where its last read finishes, with no Garbage Collector.\n\n---\n\n## 35.2. Native Artifacts, Imports, and Complete `hash` API Catalog\n\nIn `ridgun-libs`, **`hash`** is a first-class **lib** located at `src/main/ridgun/lib/hash.ridgun` (domain `HASH`). When built with `stable bundle`, it compiles into one native artifact:\n\n| Artifact | Path | Purpose |\n|---|---|---|\n| **Ridgun Bundle** | `target/bundles/hash.ridgunlib` | Portable distribution and direct `import hash` resolution |\n\n> Every lib declares its own namespace via `module :: hash`: simply write `import hash` (or `import hash as alias`) at the top and call its functions with natural spaces (`my fn x`) and left-to-right `->` pipelines (`x my fn -> result`).\n\n### 35.2.1. Summary of `hash` Functional Families\n\n| Signature / Function / Type | Purpose & Usage |\n|---|---|\n| `siphash13` | SipHash-1-3 of a whole string under a 16-byte key, as a 64-bit `Int` |\n| `siphash13 range / siphash13 range low` | Native operations of the compiler: the 64 bits, or the low 32 bits, of the hash of a range of bytes |\n| `siphash13 reference` | The same hash in plain Ridgun, on 32-bit halves: the definition the native operation is tested against |\n| `siphash new key` | A random 16-byte key from the system random source (`\"\"` when it cannot be read) |\n\n### 35.2.2. Let's inspect the key building blocks of its real implementation:\n\n### 35.4.1. Internal Implementation: SipRound on 32-Bit Halves: One Message Word per Turn\n\nObserve how `hash.ridgun` declares explicit `fn :: ... => ...` contracts first and resolves each case through aligned equations and tail calls:\n\n```ridgun\n-- The byte at `i` as 0..255.\nfn :: hs byte String Int => Int\n      hs byte s i =  (str char at s i) and 255\n\n-- The byte at `i`, or 0 at or after `to`.\nfn :: hs tail String Int Int => Int\n      hs tail s i to =\n        | i >= to   = 0\n        | otherwise = (str char at s i) and 255\n\nfn :: hs pick Int Int Int => Int\n      hs pick want hi lo =\n        | want == 0 = lo\n        | otherwise = (hi shl 32) or lo\n\n-- Little-endian 32-bit word of the key at `off`.\nfn :: hs key word String Int => Int\n      hs key word k off =  (hs byte k off) or ((hs byte k (off + 1)) shl 8) or ((hs byte k (off + 2)) shl 16) or ((hs byte k (off + 3)) shl 24)\n\n-- One message word per turn: v3 ^= m, 1 round(s), v0 ^= m. The 8 state values are the halves of v0..v3.\nfn :: siphash13 loop String Int Int Int Int Int Int Int Int Int Int Int Int Int => Int\n      siphash13 loop s off full to n want a0 b0 a1 b1 a2 b2 a3 b3 =\n        | off >= full = siphash13 last s off to n want a0 b0 a1 b1 a2 b2 a3 b3\n        | otherwise   =\n          t1 = (hs byte s off) or ((hs byte s (off + 1)) shl 8) or ((hs byte s (off + 2)) shl 16) or ((hs byte s (off + 3)) shl 24)\n          t2 = (hs byte s (off + 4)) or ((hs byte s (off + 5)) shl 8) or ((hs byte s (off + 6)) shl 16) or ((hs byte s (off + 7)) shl 24)\n          t3 = a3 xor t2\n          t4 = b3 xor t1\n          t5 = b0 + b1\n          t6 = ((a0 + a1) + (t5 shr 32)) and 0xFFFFFFFF\n          t7 = t5 and 0xFFFFFFFF\n          t8 = ((a1 shl 13) or (b1 shr 19)) and 0xFFFFFFFF\n          t9 = ((b1 shl 13) or (a1 shr 19)) and 0xFFFFFFFF\n          t10 = t8 xor t6\n          t11 = t9 xor t7\n          t12 = b2 + t4\n          t13 = ((a2 + t3) + (t12 shr 32)) and 0xFFFFFFFF\n          t14 = t12 and 0xFFFFFFFF\n          t15 = ((t3 shl 16) or (t4 shr 16)) and 0xFFFFFFFF\n          t16 = ((t4 shl 16) or (t3 shr 16)) and 0xFFFFFFFF\n          t17 = t15 xor t13\n          t18 = t16 xor t14\n          t19 = t6 + t18\n          t20 = ((t7 + t17) + (t19 shr 32)) and 0xFFFFFFFF\n          t21 = t19 and 0xFFFFFFFF\n          t22 = ((t17 shl 21) or (t18 shr 11)) and 0xFFFFFFFF\n          t23 = ((t18 shl 21) or (t17 shr 11)) and 0xFFFFFFFF\n          t24 = t22 xor t20\n          t25 = t23 xor t21\n          t26 = t14 + t11\n          t27 = ((t13 + t10) + (t26 shr 32)) and 0xFFFFFFFF\n          t28 = t26 and 0xFFFFFFFF\n          t29 = ((t10 shl 17) or (t11 shr 15)) and 0xFFFFFFFF\n          t30 = ((t11 shl 17) or (t10 shr 15)) and 0xFFFFFFFF\n          t31 = t29 xor t27\n          t32 = t30 xor t28\n          t33 = t20 xor t2\n          t34 = t21 xor t1\n          siphash13 loop s (off + 8) full to n want t33 t34 t31 t32 t28 t27 t24 t25\n```\n\n### 35.4.2. Internal Implementation: Public API: `siphash13`, the Plain-Ridgun Reference, and Random Keys\n\nObserve how `hash.ridgun` declares explicit `fn :: ... => ...` contracts first and resolves each case through aligned equations and tail calls:\n\n```ridgun\n-- v0..v3 from the key (k0 = bytes 0-7, k1 = bytes 8-15, little-endian) and the constants \"somepseudorandomlygeneratedbytes\".\nfn :: siphash13 start String String Int Int Int => Int\n      siphash13 start key s from to want =\n        k0l = hs key word key 0\n        k0h = hs key word key 4\n        k1l = hs key word key 8\n        k1h = hs key word key 12\n        n   = to - from\n        siphash13 loop s from (from + ((n shr 3) shl 3)) to n want (k0h xor 0x736f6d65) (k0l xor 0x70736575) (k1h xor 0x646f7261) (k1l xor 0x6e646f6d) (k0h xor 0x6c796765) (k0l xor 0x6e657261) (k1h xor 0x74656462) (k1l xor 0x79746573)\n\n-- `siphash13 range key data from to` (64 bits) and `siphash13 range low key data from to` (the low 32 bits)\n-- are operations of the compiler since ridgunc 1.0.44: native, some tens of ns for a short key. They take\n-- a 16-byte key and the bytes `from` (included) to `to` (excluded) of `data`; a key of another length or a\n-- range outside `data` gives 0. This lib does not define them, so that the native ones are used.\n\n-- SipHash-1-3 of the whole of `data`.\nfn :: siphash13 String String => Int\n      siphash13 key data =  siphash13 range key data 0 (str len data)\n\n-- The same hash written in plain Ridgun (about 2 µs for a 25-byte key): the definition the native operation\n-- is tested against, and the one to read. `want` 0 gives the low 32 bits, anything else the 64 bits.\nfn :: siphash13 reference String String Int Int Int => Int\n      siphash13 reference key data from to want =\n        | (str len key) != 16 or from < 0 or to < from or to > (str len data) = 0\n        | otherwise = siphash13 start key data from to want\n\n-- A new random 16-byte key (from the system random source). \"\" when it cannot be read.\nfn :: siphash new key => String\n      siphash new key =  hs key of (sys random bytes 16)\n\nfn :: hs key of (Int String) => String\n      hs key of (rc, k) =\n        | rc == 0 and (str len k) == 16 = k\n        | otherwise                     = \"\"\n```\n\n---\n\n## 35.5. Algorithmic Guarantees, `RMM1`/`RMM2` Memory, and the 5 Golden Rules of `hash`\n\n- **Algorithmic & Safety Guarantee**: A key of another length, or a range outside the data, gives `0` instead of reading out of bounds, and the native operation returns the same 64 bits as the plain-Ridgun reference for every length and offset tested.\n- **$O(1)$ Stack Complexity via TCO**: Every recursive loop in `src/main/ridgun/lib/hash.ridgun` is in tail position, so `ridgunc` compiles them into native jumps with zero stack growth.\n- **Deterministic Memory (`RMM1`/`RMM2`)**: Zero garbage-collector pauses; all intermediate allocations are reclaimed deterministically on scope exit.\n- **Continuous Verification**: Statically checked via `stable check` and tested by the automated suite in `src/test/ridgun/test hash.ridgun`.\n\n### The 5 Golden Rules When Programming with `hash`\n\n1. **Declare `import hash` at the top of your file** and call its functions with spaces, exactly as they are declared, so your code reads like natural prose.\n2. **Align your data pipelines with `=`**: chain `hash` calls into named intermediate steps and let `stable format` align the columns.\n3. **Leverage `hash`'s total functions inside `|` guards**: inspect return values or unwrap ADTs via pattern matching rather than assuming external input is valid.\n4. **Avoid cloning large structures when only reading**: remember that under `RMM2`, function input arguments incur zero reference-count overhead (`+0` / `-0`).\n5. **Pair `hash` with `test` (`import test`)**: always lock in your domain invariants with `assert equals` or `assert true`.\n\n---\n\nIn **Chapter 36**, we will explore the **`hashmap`** lib in full depth (The `hashmap` Lib — A Hash Map from `String` Keys to Any Value, on Tensors and Seeded with SipHash).\n"}, {"num": "35", "slug": "36-lib-hashmap-string-keyed-hash-map-on-tensors", "file": "36-lib-hashmap-string-keyed-hash-map-on-tensors.md", "title": "Chapter 36: The `hashmap` Lib — A Hash Map from `String` Keys to Any Value, on Tensors and Seeded with SipHash", "short_title": "The `hashmap` Lib — A Hash Map from `String` Keys to Any Value, on Tensors and Seeded with SipHash", "markdown": "# Chapter 36: The `hashmap` Lib — A Hash Map from `String` Keys to Any Value, on Tensors and Seeded with SipHash\n\n## 36.1. Why Does the `hashmap` Lib Exist? (The Real-World Problem & Ridgun Philosophy)\n\n> *\"Why do I need a `hashmap` lib written from scratch in pure Ridgun instead of just linking a legacy C library?\"*\n\nThat is the first question every systems engineer asks when meeting `hashmap`. And the answer captures the entire philosophy of `ridgun-libs`:\n\nLet's be honest: counting words or grouping a hundred thousand records with an association list is quadratic, and an ordered tree pays a logarithm and an allocation on every insert when all you need is to find a key.\n\nThe **`hashmap`** lib implements `HashMap V`, a map from `String` keys to values of any type, built on tensors: a slot table with open addressing and linear probing, at most half full, points into dense key and value tensors kept in insertion order. Keys are hashed with SipHash-1-3 (the `hash` lib) under a random seed per map; `hashmap put`, `hashmap add`, `hashmap get` and `hashmap has` take constant expected time, and `hashmap pairs` returns the entries in insertion order.\n\nIn a traditional ecosystem, solving **`HASHMAP`** tasks means pulling in external C dependencies, wrestling with raw pointers, opaque type conversions, unchecked exceptions, or unpredictable garbage-collector pauses. In Ridgun, the **`hashmap`** lib (`src/main/ridgun/lib/hashmap.ridgun`) tackles the problem with four non-negotiable principles:\n\n1. **Declare `import hashmap` (or `import hashmap as alias`) at the top of your file**: every lib defines its `module :: hashmap` namespace, and under `--strict` multi-word functions are always called with natural spaces.\n2. **Chain your data pipelines left-to-right with `->`**: write `input step one -> step two -> result`, use `(+ _ _ +)` sequence masks to destructure tuples/lists, and omit `_ =` on sequential statements (or discard with `-> ()`).\n3. **Tail-Call Optimization (TCO)**: all internal loops in `hashmap` are tail-recursive and compile into native hardware loops using $O(1)$ stack space.\n4. **Deterministic Memory (`RMM1` / `RMM2`)**: every intermediate allocation is reclaimed at the exact instruction where its last read finishes, with no Garbage Collector.\n\n---\n\n## 36.2. Example 2: Safe Composition and Boundary Handling\n\nEvery function in the `hashmap` lib is designed to compose cleanly with boolean guards `|` and with the rest of the 38 libs in `ridgun-libs`:\n\n```ridgun\nimport hashmap\n\nfn :: visitas de (HashMap Int) String => Int\n      visitas de m ruta =\n        | hashmap has m ruta = hashmap get m ruta 0\n        | otherwise          = 0\n```\n\n### 36.3.3. Example 3: The Empty Map, `hashmap put`, Replacement, `hashmap get` with a Default, and `hashmap pairs`\n\nIn this hands-on walkthrough we thoroughly exercise how `hashmap` behaves across this functional area, covering standard inputs, parameter combinations, and corner cases:\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: test hashmap basics => ()\n      test hashmap basics =\n        e = hashmap empty\n        hashmap get e \"a\" 7 -> assert int equals 7 \"AC1: get on empty gives the default\"\n        hashmap has e \"a\" -> assert false \"AC1: has on empty\"\n        hashmap size e -> assert int equals 0 \"AC1: size of empty\"\n        hashmap pairs e -> assert eq []\n\n        m = hashmap put (hashmap put (hashmap put hashmap empty \"b\" 2) \"a\" 1) \"c\" 3\n        m2 = hashmap put m \"a\" 10\n        hashmap get m2 \"a\" 0 -> assert int equals 10 \"AC1: put replaces the value\"\n        hashmap get m2 \"b\" 0 -> assert int equals 2 \"AC1: get b\"\n        hashmap get m2 \"zz\" (0 - 1) -> assert int equals (0 - 1) \"AC1: missing key gives the default\"\n        hashmap has m2 \"c\" -> assert true \"AC1: has c\"\n        hashmap has m2 \"zz\" -> assert false \"AC1: has missing\"\n        hashmap size m2 -> assert int equals 3 \"AC1: replacing does not add a key\"\n        hashmap pairs m2 -> assert eq [(\"b\", 2), (\"a\", 10), (\"c\", 3)]\n        ()\n```\n\n### 36.3.4. Example 4: Counters with `hashmap add`: Sums, Missing Keys, and Reaching Zero\n\nIn this hands-on walkthrough we thoroughly exercise how `hashmap` behaves across this functional area, covering standard inputs, parameter combinations, and corner cases:\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: test hashmap add => ()\n      test hashmap add =\n        m = hashmap add (hashmap add (hashmap add hashmap empty \"x\" 2) \"y\" 5) \"x\" 3\n        hashmap get m \"x\" 0 -> assert int equals 5 \"AC2: add sums\"\n        hashmap get m \"y\" 0 -> assert int equals 5 \"AC2: a missing key starts at 0\"\n        m2 = hashmap add m \"y\" (0 - 5)\n        hashmap get m2 \"y\" 99 -> assert int equals 0 \"AC2: add can reach 0 and the key stays\"\n        hashmap has m2 \"y\" -> assert true \"AC2: has after reaching 0\"\n        hashmap pairs m2 -> assert eq [(\"x\", 5), (\"y\", 0)]\n        ()\n```\n\n### 36.3.5. Example 5: Unusual Keys: the Empty String, Bytes above 127, and 10 KB Keys That Differ in the Last Byte\n\nIn this hands-on walkthrough we thoroughly exercise how `hashmap` behaves across this functional area, covering standard inputs, parameter combinations, and corner cases:\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: test hashmap unusual keys => ()\n      test hashmap unusual keys =\n        hi = (char from code 200) + (char from code 255)\n        la = kb10 \"a\"\n        lb = kb10 \"b\"\n        m = hashmap put (hashmap put (hashmap put (hashmap put hashmap empty \"\" 1) hi 2) la 3) lb 4\n        hashmap get m \"\" 0 -> assert int equals 1 \"AC3: empty key\"\n        hashmap get m hi 0 -> assert int equals 2 \"AC3: bytes >= 128\"\n        hashmap get m la 0 -> assert int equals 3 \"AC3: 10 KB key\"\n        hashmap get m lb 0 -> assert int equals 4 \"AC3: 10 KB key differing in the last byte\"\n        hashmap has m (kb10 \"c\") -> assert false \"AC3: another 10 KB key is missing\"\n        hashmap has m (char from code 200) -> assert false \"AC3: prefix of a key is missing\"\n        hashmap size m -> assert int equals 4 \"AC3: four keys\"\n        ()\n```\n\n### 36.3.6. Example 6: Record Values: a `HashMap` of User-Defined Records\n\nIn this hands-on walkthrough we thoroughly exercise how `hashmap` behaves across this functional area, covering standard inputs, parameter combinations, and corner cases:\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: test hashmap record values => ()\n      test hashmap record values =\n        m = hashmap put (hashmap put (hashmap put hashmap empty \"/a\" (Visit \"/a\" 3)) \"/b\" (Visit \"/b\" 7)) \"/a\" (Visit \"/a\" 4)\n        hashmap get m \"/a\" (Visit \"\" 0) -> assert eq (Visit \"/a\" 4)\n        hashmap get m \"/b\" (Visit \"\" 0) -> assert eq (Visit \"/b\" 7)\n        hashmap get m \"/c\" (Visit \"\" 0) -> assert eq (Visit \"\" 0)\n        hits (hashmap get m \"/a\" (Visit \"\" 0)) -> assert int equals 4 \"AC4: record field\"\n        ()\n```\n\n### 36.3.7. Example 7: Growth: 20,000 Keys, Every Key Found, and Insertion Order Preserved\n\nIn this hands-on walkthrough we thoroughly exercise how `hashmap` behaves across this functional area, covering standard inputs, parameter combinations, and corner cases:\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: test hashmap growth => ()\n      test hashmap growth =\n        n = 20000\n        m = put many hashmap empty 0 n\n        hashmap size m -> assert int equals n \"AC1: 20000 keys after growing\"\n        all found m 0 n -> assert true \"AC1: every key found after growing\"\n        ps = hashmap pairs m\n        sum values ps 0 -> assert int equals (n * (n - 1) / 2) \"AC1: pairs hold every value\"\n        first keys ps 3 [] -> assert eq [\"key 0\", \"key 1\", \"key 2\"]\n        fill 1 + count [] + str len seed -> assert int equals 7 \"Program functions named like fields still work\"\n        ()\n```\n\n---\n\n## 36.4. Under the Hood: How `hashmap` Is Built in Pure Ridgun (`src/main/ridgun/lib/hashmap.ridgun`)\n\nOne of the biggest advantages of `ridgun-libs` is that **there are no C black boxes**. You can open `src/main/ridgun/lib/hashmap.ridgun` and read exactly how every operation is implemented using pattern matching, `|` / `|.` guard trees, and tail-call optimization (TCO). Let's inspect the key building blocks of its real implementation:\n\n### 36.4.1. Internal Implementation: Hash\n\nObserve how `hashmap.ridgun` declares explicit `fn :: ... => ...` contracts first and resolves each case through aligned equations and tail calls:\n\n```ridgun\n-- 31 bits of SipHash-1-3 of the key, with the map's 16-byte seed as the hash key (the compiler's native\n-- `siphash13 range low`, ridgunc 1.0.44), plus 1 so a used slot is never 0.\n-- Keys are always compared when the hashes match.\n-- The per-map random seed stops chosen keys from colliding on purpose.\nfn :: hm hash String String => Int\n      hm hash seed key =  ((siphash13 range low seed key 0 (str len key)) % 2147483648) + 1\n\n-- Exactly 16 bytes: SipHash takes a 128-bit key.\nfn :: hm seed16 String => String\n      hm seed16 s =\n        | (str len s) == 16 = s\n        | otherwise         = str slice (s + \"ridgun-hashmap-0\") 0 16\n\nfn :: hm read seed Int => String\n      hm read seed fd =\n        | fd < 0    = hm seed16 (int to str (sys time ms))\n        | otherwise =\n          s = sys read fd fd 16\n          sys close fd -> ()\n          hm seed16 s\n\nfn :: hm new seed => String\n      hm new seed = hm read seed (sys open mode \"/dev/urandom\" \"r\")\n```\n\n### 36.4.2. Internal Implementation: Slots\n\nObserve how `hashmap.ridgun` declares explicit `fn :: ... => ...` contracts first and resolves each case through aligned equations and tail calls:\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: hm slot hash Int => Int\n      hm slot hash s = s / 2147483648\n\n-- Slot of key k with hash h: the slot that holds it, or the free slot where it goes.\n-- Hot path: the slot is decoded inline (each call costs about 20 ns).\nfn :: hm probe Tensor[Int * n] Tensor[String * m] Int String Int Int => Int\n      hm probe slots keys cap k h i =\n        | slots_(i) == 0                          = i\n        | slots_(i) / 2147483648 != h             = hm probe slots keys cap k h ((i + 1) % cap)\n        | keys_(slots_(i) % 2147483648) == k      = i\n        | otherwise                               = hm probe slots keys cap k h ((i + 1) % cap)\n\n-- First free slot from i; for rehashing, where every key is known to be new.\nfn :: hm free Tensor[Int * n] Int Int => Int\n      hm free slots cap i =\n        | slots_(i) == 0 = i\n        | otherwise      = hm free slots cap ((i + 1) % cap)\n```\n\n### 36.4.3. Internal Implementation: Table\n\nObserve how `hashmap.ridgun` declares explicit `fn :: ... => ...` contracts first and resolves each case through aligned equations and tail calls:\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: hashmap empty => HashMap V\n      hashmap empty = HashMap [] [] (Tensor[Int * 16]) (Tensor[String * 8]) 16 8 (Tensor[Int * 1]) (hm new seed)\n\nfn :: hm size (HashMap V) => Int\n      hm size m = (count m)_(0)\n\nfn :: hm bump Tensor[Int * k] => ()\n      hm bump t =\n        t_(0) = t_(0) + 1\n\nfn :: hm vt [Tensor[V * n]] => Tensor[V * n]\n      hm vt (t:_) = t\n\n-- Copies every used slot to the new table, by its stored hash. Int only.\nfn :: hm rehash Tensor[Int * n] Tensor[Int * m] Int Int Int => ()\n      hm rehash old new i ocap ncap =\n        | i >= ocap     = ()\n        | old_(i) == 0  = hm rehash old new (i + 1) ocap ncap\n        | otherwise     =\n          s = old_(i)\n          new_(hm free new ncap ((hm slot hash s) % ncap)) = s\n          hm rehash old new (i + 1) ocap ncap\n\nfn :: hm grow slots (HashMap V) => HashMap V\n      hm grow slots m =\n        ncap = 2 * (cap m)\n        ns   = Tensor[Int * ncap]\n        hm rehash (slots m) ns 0 (cap m) ncap\n        m with slots = ns, cap = ncap\n\nfn :: hm copy Tensor[String * n] Tensor[V * n] Tensor[String * m] Tensor[V * m] Int Int => ()\n      hm copy ok ov nk nv i n =\n        | i >= n    = ()\n        | otherwise =\n          nk_(i) = ok_(i)\n          nv_(i) = ov_(i)\n          hm copy ok ov nk nv (i + 1) n\n\nfn :: hm grow dense (HashMap V) [V] => HashMap V\n      hm grow dense m (d:_) =\n        nr = 2 * (room m)\n table at most half full and room for one more key.\nfn :: hm make room (HashMap V) => HashMap V\n      hm make room m = hm room dense (hm room slots m)\n\nfn :: hm room slots (HashMap V) => HashMap V\n      hm room slots m =\n        | 2 * ((hm size m) + 1) > cap m = hm grow slots m\n        | otherwise                      = m\n\nfn :: hm room dense (HashMap V) => HashMap V\n      hm room dense m =\n        | (hm size m) + 1 > room m = hm grow dense m (fill m)\n        | otherwise                  = m\n\n-- The first insert supplies the fill value for the value tensor.\nfn :: hm ensure vals (HashMap V) V => HashMap V\n      hm ensure vals m v = m with fill = [v], vals = [Tensor[V * (room m)] with v]\n\n-- Puts a new key at the next position and points slot i at it.\nfn :: hm insert otherwise = hm add at m vt st kt cnt k d (hm hash seed k) cap\n\nfn :: hm add at (HashMap Int) Tensor[Int * n] Tensor[Int * c] Tensor[String * r] Tensor[Int * k] String Int Int Int => HashMap Int\n Tensor[Int * k] String Int Int Int => HashMap Int\n      hm add slot m vt st kt cnt k d h i =\n        | st_(i) == 0 =\n          hm insert vt st kt cnt i h k d\n          m\n        | otherwise =\n For counting.\nfn :: hashmap add (HashMap Int) String Int => HashMap Int\n      hashmap add m k d = hm add go m m k d\n\n-- Slot content for k: 0 when k is missing, otherwise hash * 2^31 + position.\nfn :: hm lookup Tensor[Int * c] Tensor[String * r] Int String Int => Int\n      hm lookup st kt cap k h = st_(hm probe st kt cap k h (h % cap))\n\nfn :: hm get at Tensor[V * n] Int V => V\n      hm get at vt s d =\n        | s == 0    = d\n        | otherwise = vt_(s % 2147483648)\n\n-- The value of k, or d when k is missing.\nfn :: hashmap get (HashMap V) String V => V\n      hashmap get (HashMap _ []     _  _  _   _ _   _   ) k d = d\n      hashmap get (HashMap _ (vt:_) st kt cap _ _   seed) k d = hm get at vt (hm lookup st kt cap k (hm hash seed k)) d\n\nfn :: hashmap has (HashMap V) String => Bool\n      hashmap has (HashMap _ []     _  _  _   _ _ _   ) k = False\n      hashmap has (HashMap _ (vt:_) st kt cap _ _ seed) k = hm lookup st kt cap k (hm hash seed k) != 0\n\nfn :: hashmap size (HashMap V) => Int\n      hashmap size m = hm size m\n\nfn :: hm pairs loop Tensor[String * n] Tensor[V * n] Int [String V] => [String V]\n      hm pairs loop ks vt i acc =\n        | i < 0     = acc\n        | otherwise = hm pairs loop ks vt (i - 1) ([(ks_(i), vt_(i))] :: acc)\n\n-- Every (key, value) pair, in the order the keys were first inserted.\nfn :: hashmap pairs (HashMap V) => [String V]\n      hashmap pairs m =\n        | hm size m == 0 = []\n        | otherwise      = hm pairs loop (keys m) (hm vt (vals m)) ((hm size m) - 1) []\n```\n\n---\n\n## 36.5. Algorithmic Guarantees, `RMM1`/`RMM2` Memory, and the 5 Golden Rules of `hashmap`\n\n- **Algorithmic & Safety Guarantee**: The map is updated in place and grows by doubling, so `n` inserts cost $O(n)$ in total; always use the map an operation returns (`ADR-0009`). A random seed per map keeps an attacker from choosing keys that collide.\n- **$O(1)$ Stack Complexity via TCO**: Every recursive loop in `src/main/ridgun/lib/hashmap.ridgun` is in tail position, so `ridgunc` compiles them into native jumps with zero stack growth.\n- **Deterministic Memory (`RMM1`/`RMM2`)**: Zero garbage-collector pauses; all intermediate allocations are reclaimed deterministically on scope exit.\n- **Continuous Verification**: Statically checked via `stable check` and tested by the automated suite in `src/test/ridgun/test hashmap.ridgun`.\n\n### The 5 Golden Rules When Programming with `hashmap`\n\n1. **Declare `import hashmap` at the top of your file** and call its functions with spaces, exactly as they are declared, so your code reads like natural prose.\n2. **Align your data pipelines with `=`**: chain `hashmap` calls into named intermediate steps and let `stable format` align the columns.\n3. **Leverage `hashmap`'s total functions inside `|` guards**: inspect return values or unwrap ADTs via pattern matching rather than assuming external input is valid.\n4. **Avoid cloning large structures when only reading**: remember that under `RMM2`, function input arguments incur zero reference-count overhead (`+0` / `-0`).\n5. **Pair `hashmap` with `test` (`import test`)**: always lock in your domain invariants with `assert equals` or `assert true`.\n\n---\n\nIn **Chapter 37**, we will explore the **`tls`** lib in full depth (The `tls` Lib — TLS 1.3 and TLS 1.2 Client, X.509 Chain Validation, and Hostname Verification).\n"}, {"num": "36", "slug": "37-lib-tls-tls13-tls12-client-and-x509-validation", "file": "37-lib-tls-tls13-tls12-client-and-x509-validation.md", "title": "Chapter 37: The `tls` Lib — TLS 1.3 and TLS 1.2 Client, X.509 Chain Validation, and Hostname Verification", "short_title": "The `tls` Lib — TLS 1.3 and TLS 1.2 Client, X.509 Chain Validation, and Hostname Verification", "markdown": "# Chapter 37: The `tls` Lib — TLS 1.3 and TLS 1.2 Client, X.509 Chain Validation, and Hostname Verification\n\n## 37.1. Why Does the `tls` Lib Exist? (The Real-World Problem & Ridgun Philosophy)\n\n> *\"Why do I need a `tls` lib written from scratch in pure Ridgun instead of just linking a legacy C library?\"*\n\nThat is the first question every systems engineer asks when meeting `tls`. And the answer captures the entire philosophy of `ridgun-libs`:\n\nLet's be honest: almost every service a program talks to today sits behind TLS, and linking OpenSSL to reach it brings a C dependency of half a million lines, with its own allocator and its own calendar of security fixes.\n\nThe **`tls`** lib is a TLS client in pure Ridgun: **RFC 8446 TLS 1.3** and **RFC 5246 TLS 1.2**, with ECDHE key exchange (X25519, secp256r1) and AEAD suites only (AES-128-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305), **X.509** chain validation against a bundle of root certificates, **RFC 6125** hostname verification, SNI and ALPN. It takes its primitives from `crypto` and its connections from `socket`, and it has no option that skips the chain, expiry, signature or hostname checks.\n\nIn a traditional ecosystem, solving **`TLS`** tasks means pulling in external C dependencies, wrestling with raw pointers, opaque type conversions, unchecked exceptions, or unpredictable garbage-collector pauses. In Ridgun, the **`tls`** lib (`src/main/ridgun/lib/tls.ridgun`) tackles the problem with four non-negotiable principles:\n\n1. **Declare `import tls` (or `import tls as alias`) at the top of your file**: every lib defines its `module :: tls` namespace, and under `--strict` multi-word functions are always called with natural spaces.\n2. **Chain your data pipelines left-to-right with `->`**: write `input step one -> step two -> result`, use `(+ _ _ +)` sequence masks to destructure tuples/lists, and omit `_ =` on sequential statements (or discard with `-> ()`).\n3. **Tail-Call Optimization (TCO)**: all internal loops in `tls` are tail-recursive and compile into native hardware loops using $O(1)$ stack space.\n4. **Deterministic Memory (`RMM1` / `RMM2`)**: every intermediate allocation is reclaimed at the exact instruction where its last read finishes, with no Garbage Collector.\n\n---\n\n## 37.2. Native Artifacts, Imports, and Complete `tls` API Catalog\n\nIn `ridgun-libs`, **`tls`** is a first-class **lib** located at `src/main/ridgun/lib/tls.ridgun` (domain `TLS`). When built with `stable bundle`, it compiles into one native artifact:\n\n| Artifact | Path | Purpose |\n|---|---|---|\n| **Ridgun Bundle** | `target/bundles/tls.ridgunlib` | Portable distribution and direct `import tls` resolution |\n\n> Every lib declares its own namespace via `module :: tls`: simply write `import tls` (or `import tls as alias`) at the top and call its functions with natural spaces (`my fn x`) and left-to-right `->` pipelines (`x my fn -> result`).\n\n### 37.2.1. Summary of `tls` Functional Families\n\n| Signature / Function / Type | Purpose & Usage |\n|---|---|\n| `tls defaults / tls with roots / tls with root pem / tls with alpn / tls with timeout / tls with versions` | Configuration: trusted roots, ALPN protocols, timeout and accepted versions |\n| `tls connect host / tls connect addr / tls connect` | Handshake over a new connection by name or by address, or over an existing `Socket`, returning a `TlsResult` |\n| `tls send / tls recv / tls close` | Encrypted send, receive of up to `max` decrypted bytes, and `close_notify` plus close |\n| `tls is ok / tls unwrap / tls error kind / tls error reason` | Inspect the result: the connection, or one of seven typed errors (`TlsCertExpired`, `TlsHostnameMismatch`, `TlsInvalidChain`, ...) |\n| `tls verify chain / tls valid sni` | Validate a list of certificates for a server name without connecting, and check a name for SNI |\n\n### 37.2.2. Deep Dive into `tls`: Step-by-Step Examples for Every Feature\n\nA signature table alone is never enough: let's explore **every capability** of the `tls` lib through progressive, runnable Ridgun examples. We will start with two everyday tabular recipes and then walk through every functional scenario, transformation, and boundary condition verified in `src/test/ridgun/test tls.ridgun`.\n\n### 37.3.1. Example 1: Core Tabular Workflow with `tls`\n\nNotice how in Ridgun the `=` signs and transformation steps using `tls` align into a clean, scannable table without unnecessary mutable variables or hidden side effects:\n\n```ridgun\nimport tls\n\nfn :: leer cabecera TlsResult String => String\n      leer cabecera r host =\n        | tls is ok r = pedir cabecera (tls unwrap r) host\n        | otherwise   = (tls error kind r) + \": \" + (tls error reason r)\n\nfn :: pedir cabecera TlsConn String => String\n      pedir cabecera conn host =\n        tls send conn (\"HEAD / HTTP/1.1\\r\\nHost: \" + host + \"\\r\\nConnection: close\\r\\n\\r\\n\") -> enviados\n        tls recv conn 4096 -> respuesta\n        tls close conn\n        respuesta\n\nfn :: cabecera https String => String\n      cabecera https host =\n        leer cabecera (tls connect host host 443 (tls defaults)) host\n```\n\n### 37.3.2. Example 2: Safe Composition and Boundary Handling\n\nEvery function in the `tls` lib is designed to compose cleanly with boolean guards `|` and with the rest of the 38 libs in `ridgun-libs`:\n\n```ridgun\nimport tls\n\nfn :: conviene reintentar TlsResult => Bool\n      conviene reintentar r =\n        | tls is ok r                        = False\n        | (tls error kind r) == \"TlsTimeout\" = True\n        | (tls error kind r) == \"TlsIoError\" = True\n        | otherwise                          = False\n```\n\n### 37.3.3. Example 3: RFC 8448 §3: the TLS 1.3 Key Schedule and Record Protection against the Published Trace\n\nIn this hands-on walkthrough we thoroughly exercise how `tls` behaves across this functional area, covering standard inputs, parameter combinations, and corner cases:\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: test rfc8448 vectors => ()\n      test rfc8448 vectors =\n        failures = tls13 rfc8448 checks\n        print failures failures\n        assert true (tls13 rfc8448 self test) \"RFC 8448 §3 TLS 1.3 trace\" -> ()\n```\n\n### 37.3.4. Example 4: The TLS 1.2 PRF Vector, the Structure of the ClientHello, and the SNI Rules\n\nIn this hands-on walkthrough we thoroughly exercise how `tls` behaves across this functional area, covering standard inputs, parameter combinations, and corner cases:\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: test tls12 prf and hello => ()\n      test tls12 prf and hello =\n        prf = tls12 prf (hex to byte str \"9bbe436ba940f017b17652849a71db35\") \"test label\" (hex to byte str \"a0ba9f936cda311827a6f796ffd5198c\") 100\n        assert str eq (bytes to hex str prf) (\"e3f229ba727be17b8d122620557cd453c2aab21d07c3d495329b52d4e61edb5a6b301791e90d35c9c9a46b4e14baf9af0fa022f7077def17abfd3797c0564bab4fbc91666e9def9b97fce34f796789baa48082d122ee42c5a72e5a5110fff70187347b66\") \"TLS 1.2 PRF SHA-256\" -> ()\n        ch = tls client hello \"example.com\" (c repeat byte 7 32) (c repeat byte 9 32) ((tls be2 29) + (tls vec2 (c repeat byte 1 32))) \"\" (tls defaults)\n        assert eq (tls u8 ch 0) 1 -> ()\n        assert eq ((tls u24 ch 1) + 4) (str len ch) -> ()\n        assert true (str contains ch \"example.com\") \"ClientHello carries SNI\" -> ()\n        assert true (tls valid sni \"mail.example.com\") \"SNI accepts DNS names\" -> ()\n        assert false (tls valid sni \"192.168.1.1\") \"SNI rejects IPv4 literals\" -> ()\n        assert false (tls valid sni \"\") \"SNI rejects empty names\" -> ()\n        bad = tls connect host \"127.0.0.1\" 443 (tls defaults)\n        assert str eq (tls error kind bad) \"TlsIoError\" \"connect rejects IP literal as server name\" -> ()\n```\n\n### 37.3.5. Example 5: Chain Validation: Intermediates in Any Order, a Missing Intermediate, Untrusted Roots, Expiry, and Hostnames\n\nIn this hands-on walkthrough we thoroughly exercise how `tls` behaves across this functional area, covering standard inputs, parameter combinations, and corner cases:\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: test chain verification String => ()\n      test chain verification dir    =\n        leaf_ec  = pem ders (dir + \"/ec.pem\")\n        inter    = pem ders (dir + \"/int.pem\")\n        chain    = leaf_ec :: inter\n        cfg      = tls with root pem (tls defaults) (read file (dir + \"/ca.pem\"))\n        now      = (sys wall time ms) / 1000\n        assert str eq (chain kind chain \"localhost\" cfg) \"\" \"leaf + intermediate -> root verifies\" -> ()\n        noise    = pem ders (dir + \"/other.pem\")\n        assert str eq (chain kind (leaf_ec :: noise :: inter) \"localhost\" cfg) \"\" \"leaf first, extra and unordered certificates after it\" -> ()\n        assert str eq (chain kind leaf_ec \"localhost\" cfg) \"TlsInvalidChain\" \"missing intermediate is rejected\" -> ()\n        assert str eq (chain kind chain \"example.com\" cfg) \"TlsHostnameMismatch\" \"wrong host is rejected\" -> ()\n        assert str eq (chain kind chain \"localhost\" (tls with verify time cfg (now + (10 * 86400)))) \"TlsCertExpired\" \"expired chain is rejected\" -> ()\n        assert str eq (chain kind chain \"localhost\" (tls with verify time cfg 1000)) \"TlsCertExpired\" \"not-yet-valid chain is rejected\" -> ()\n        other    = tls with root pem (tls defaults) (read file (dir + \"/other.pem\"))\n        assert str eq (chain kind chain \"localhost\" other) \"TlsInvalidChain\" \"untrusted root is rejected\" -> ()\n        self     = pem ders (dir + \"/self.pem\")\n        assert str eq (chain kind self \"localhost\" cfg) \"TlsInvalidChain\" \"self-signed leaf is rejected\" -> ()\n        self_cfg = tls with root pem (tls defaults) (read file (dir + \"/self.pem\"))\n        assert str eq (chain kind self \"localhost\" self_cfg) \"\" \"explicitly trusted self-signed leaf verifies\" -> ()\n        empty    = tls with roots (tls defaults) \"/nonexistent/ca.pem\"\n        assert str eq (chain kind chain \"localhost\" empty) \"TlsInvalidChain\" \"no roots means no trust (no bypass, AC4)\" -> ()\n        assert str eq (chain kind [] \"localhost\" cfg) \"TlsInvalidChain\" \"empty certificate list is rejected\" -> ()\n        assert str eq (chain kind [\"garbage\"] \"localhost\" cfg) \"TlsInvalidChain\" \"malformed certificate is rejected\" -> ()\n```\n\n### 37.3.6. Example 6: Local Handshakes against `openssl s_server`: TLS 1.3 and 1.2, AES-128-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305, ECDSA and RSA\n\nIn this hands-on walkthrough we thoroughly exercise how `tls` behaves across this functional area, covering standard inputs, parameter combinations, and corner cases:\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: test local handshakes String => ()\n      test local handshakes dir    =\n        p   = base port\n        cfg = roots cfg dir\n        ec  = \"-cert ec.pem -key ec.key -cert_chain int.pem\"\n        rsa = \"-cert rsa.pem -key rsa.key -cert_chain int.pem\"\n        v1, s1, _ = local roundtrip dir p (ec + \" -tls1_3 -ciphersuites TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256\") cfg \"TLS 1.3 AES-128-GCM / ECDSA\"\n        assert eq v1 772 -> ()\n        assert eq s1 4865 -> ()\n        v2, s2, _ = local roundtrip dir (p + 1) (rsa + \" -tls1_3 -ciphersuites TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256\") cfg \"TLS 1.3 ChaCha20-Poly1305 / RSA-PSS\"\n        assert eq v2 772 -> ()\n        assert eq s2 4867 -> ()\n        v3, s3, _ = local roundtrip dir (p + 2) (ec + \" -tls1_3 -groups P-256\") cfg \"TLS 1.3 HelloRetryRequest to P-256\"\n        assert eq v3 772 -> ()\n        v4, s4, _ = local roundtrip dir (p + 3) (rsa + \" -tls1_2 -cipher ECDHE-RSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256\") cfg \"TLS 1.2 ECDHE-RSA-AES128-GCM\"\n        assert eq v4 771 -> ()\n        assert eq s4 49199 -> ()\n        v5, s5, _ = local roundtrip dir (p + 4) (ec + \" -tls1_2 -cipher ECDHE-ECDSA-CHACHA20-POLY1305\") cfg \"TLS 1.2 ECDHE-ECDSA-ChaCha20\"\n        assert eq v5 771 -> ()\n        assert eq s5 52393 -> ()\n        v6, s6, _ = local roundtrip dir (p + 5) (ec + \" -tls1_2 -cipher ECDHE-ECDSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256 -groups P-256\") cfg \"TLS 1.2 ECDHE P-256 / ECDSA\"\n        assert eq s6 49195 -> ()\n        _, _, a7  = local roundtrip dir (p + 6) (ec + \" -alpn h2,http/1.1\") (tls with alpn cfg [\"http/1.1\"]) \"ALPN\"\n        assert str eq a7 \"http/1.1\" \"ALPN selection\" -> ()\n```\n\n### 37.3.7. Example 7: Handshakes That Must Fail: Version Mismatch, Untrusted Root, and Typed Errors\n\nIn this hands-on walkthrough we thoroughly exercise how `tls` behaves across this functional area, covering standard inputs, parameter combinations, and corner cases:\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: test local failures String => ()\n      test local failures dir    =\n        p   = (base port) + 10\n        cfg = roots cfg dir\n        ec  = \"-cert ec.pem -key ec.key -cert_chain int.pem\"\n        assert true (start server dir p (ec + \" -tls1_2\")) \"s_server (TLS 1.2 only)\" -> ()\n        r1  = tls connect host \"localhost\" p (tls with versions cfg 772 772)\n        assert str eq (tls error kind r1) \"TlsUnsupportedVersion\" \"TLS 1.3-only client vs TLS 1.2-only server\" -> ()\n        assert true (start server dir (p + 1) ec) \"s_server (untrusted)\" -> ()\n        r2  = tls connect host \"localhost\" (p + 1) (tls with root pem cfg (read file (dir + \"/other.pem\")))\n        assert str eq (tls error kind r2) \"TlsInvalidChain\" \"server chain under an untrusted root\" -> ()\n        lrc, lfd = sys tcp listen \"127.0.0.1\" 0 8\n        assert eq lrc 0 -> ()\n        r3  = tls connect host \"localhost\" (sys local port lfd) (tls with timeout cfg 300)\n        assert str eq (tls error kind r3) \"TlsTimeout\" \"silent server times out\" -> ()\n        sys close lfd -> ()\n```\n\n### 37.3.8. Example 8: Live Servers: Public Sites and the Failure Cases of `badssl.com`\n\nIn this hands-on walkthrough we thoroughly exercise how `tls` behaves across this functional area, covering standard inputs, parameter combinations, and corner cases:\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: test live servers => ()\n      test live servers =\n        live \"www.debian.org\" 443 \"\" \"HEAD / HTTP/1.1\\r\\nHost: www.debian.org\\r\\nConnection: close\\r\\n\\r\\n\"\n        live \"smtp.gmail.com\" 465 \"\" \"QUIT\\r\\n\"\n        live \"tls-v1-2.badssl.com\" 1012 \"\" \"HEAD / HTTP/1.1\\r\\nHost: tls-v1-2.badssl.com\\r\\nConnection: close\\r\\n\\r\\n\"\n        live \"expired.badssl.com\" 443 \"TlsCertExpired\" \"\"\n        live \"wrong.host.badssl.com\" 443 \"TlsHostnameMismatch\" \"\"\n        live \"self-signed.badssl.com\" 443 \"TlsInvalidChain\" \"\"\n        live \"untrusted-root.badssl.com\" 443 \"TlsInvalidChain\" \"\"\n        live \"tls-v1-0.badssl.com\" 1010 \"TlsUnsupportedVersion TlsServerAlert\" \"\"\n```\n\n---\n\n## 37.4. Under the Hood: How `tls` Is Built in Pure Ridgun (`src/main/ridgun/lib/tls.ridgun`)\n\nOne of the biggest advantages of `ridgun-libs` is that **there are no C black boxes**. You can open `src/main/ridgun/lib/tls.ridgun` and read exactly how every operation is implemented using pattern matching, `|` / `|.` guard trees, and tail-call optimization (TCO). Let's inspect the key building blocks of its real implementation:\n\n### 37.4.1. Internal Implementation: Configuration (API-TLS-001)\n\nObserve how `tls.ridgun` declares explicit `fn :: ... => ...` contracts first and resolves each case through aligned equations and tail calls:\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: tls defaults => TlsConfig\n      tls defaults =  TlsConfig \"/etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt\" \"\" [] 771 772 10000 0\n\nfn :: tls with roots TlsConfig String => TlsConfig\n      tls with roots cfg       path   =  cfg with root_certs_path = path, root_certs_pem = \"\"\n\nfn :: tls with root pem TlsConfig String => TlsConfig\n      tls with root pem cfg       pem    =  cfg with root_certs_pem = pem\n\nfn :: tls with alpn TlsConfig [String] => TlsConfig\n      tls with alpn cfg       protos   =  cfg with alpn_protocols = protos\n\nfn :: tls with timeout TlsConfig Int => TlsConfig\n      tls with timeout cfg       ms  =  cfg with timeout_ms = ms\n\nfn :: tls with verify time TlsConfig Int => TlsConfig\n      tls with verify time cfg       sec =  cfg with verify_time_sec = sec\n\nfn :: tls with versions TlsConfig Int Int => TlsConfig\n      tls with versions cfg       lo  hi  =  cfg with min_version = lo, max_version = hi\n```\n\n### 37.4.2. Algorithmic Guarantees, `RMM1`/`RMM2` Memory, and the 5 Golden Rules of `tls`\n\n- **Algorithmic & Safety Guarantee**: Every handshake verifies the chain up to a trusted root, the validity dates, the handshake signature and the hostname, and only AEAD suites with ephemeral key exchange are offered: there is no option that turns a check off (`FR-TLS-001` AC4).\n- **$O(1)$ Stack Complexity via TCO**: Every recursive loop in `src/main/ridgun/lib/tls.ridgun` is in tail position, so `ridgunc` compiles them into native jumps with zero stack growth.\n- **Deterministic Memory (`RMM1`/`RMM2`)**: Zero garbage-collector pauses; all intermediate allocations are reclaimed deterministically on scope exit.\n- **Continuous Verification**: Statically checked via `stable check` and tested by the automated suite in `src/test/ridgun/test tls.ridgun`.\n\n### The 5 Golden Rules When Programming with `tls`\n\n1. **Declare `import tls` at the top of your file** and call its functions with spaces, exactly as they are declared, so your code reads like natural prose.\n2. **Align your data pipelines with `=`**: chain `tls` calls into named intermediate steps and let `stable format` align the columns.\n3. **Leverage `tls`'s total functions inside `|` guards**: inspect return values or unwrap ADTs via pattern matching rather than assuming external input is valid.\n4. **Avoid cloning large structures when only reading**: remember that under `RMM2`, function input arguments incur zero reference-count overhead (`+0` / `-0`).\n5. **Pair `tls` with `test` (`import test`)**: always lock in your domain invariants with `assert equals` or `assert true`.\n\n---\n\nIn **Chapter 38**, we will explore the **`mail`** lib in full depth (The `mail` Lib — RFC 5322 Messages and SMTP Submission over TLS).\n"}, {"num": "37", "slug": "38-lib-mail-rfc5322-messages-and-smtp-over-tls", "file": "38-lib-mail-rfc5322-messages-and-smtp-over-tls.md", "title": "Chapter 38: The `mail` Lib — RFC 5322 Messages and SMTP Submission over TLS", "short_title": "The `mail` Lib — RFC 5322 Messages and SMTP Submission over TLS", "markdown": "# Chapter 38: The `mail` Lib — RFC 5322 Messages and SMTP Submission over TLS\n\n## 38.1. Why Does the `mail` Lib Exist? (The Real-World Problem & Ridgun Philosophy)\n\n> *\"Why do I need a `mail` lib written from scratch in pure Ridgun instead of just linking a legacy C library?\"*\n\nThat is the first question every systems engineer asks when meeting `mail`. And the answer captures the entire philosophy of `ridgun-libs`:\n\nLet's be honest: sending the email that verifies an account looks like one line, until a subject with an accent arrives as question marks, a line that starts with a dot vanishes, or a form field with a line break adds a `Bcc:` header of the attacker's choice.\n\nThe **`mail`** lib builds and renders **RFC 5322** messages (RFC 2047 encoded-words for non-ASCII headers, quoted-printable bodies with lines of at most 76 bytes, `multipart/alternative` when there is text and HTML) and submits them with an **SMTP** client (RFC 5321, RFC 6409) over TLS: implicit TLS on port 465 (RFC 8314) or STARTTLS (RFC 3207), with `AUTH PLAIN` or `AUTH LOGIN` (RFC 4954) sent only after the TLS handshake. Header injection is rejected when the message is rendered, and every failure is a typed `SmtpError` that says whether a retry makes sense.\n\nIn a traditional ecosystem, solving **`MAIL`** tasks means pulling in external C dependencies, wrestling with raw pointers, opaque type conversions, unchecked exceptions, or unpredictable garbage-collector pauses. In Ridgun, the **`mail`** lib (`src/main/ridgun/lib/mail.ridgun`) tackles the problem with four non-negotiable principles:\n\n1. **Declare `import mail` (or `import mail as alias`) at the top of your file**: every lib defines its `module :: mail` namespace, and under `--strict` multi-word functions are always called with natural spaces.\n2. **Chain your data pipelines left-to-right with `->`**: write `input step one -> step two -> result`, use `(+ _ _ +)` sequence masks to destructure tuples/lists, and omit `_ =` on sequential statements (or discard with `-> ()`).\n3. **Tail-Call Optimization (TCO)**: all internal loops in `mail` are tail-recursive and compile into native hardware loops using $O(1)$ stack space.\n4. **Deterministic Memory (`RMM1` / `RMM2`)**: every intermediate allocation is reclaimed at the exact instruction where its last read finishes, with no Garbage Collector.\n\n---\n\n## 38.2. Native Artifacts, Imports, and Complete `mail` API Catalog\n\nIn `ridgun-libs`, **`mail`** is a first-class **lib** located at `src/main/ridgun/lib/mail.ridgun` (domain `MAIL`).
